atomic-structure.q: An atom’s valence electrons are found in which shell?
options: Whichever shell has the most electrons
atomic-structure.why: Valence electrons are the outermost shell’s electrons — the ones involved in bonding.

atomic-structure.q: Carbon (atomic number 6) has how many valence electrons?
atomic-structure.why: Carbon’s configuration is 1s² 2s² 2p² — the 2nd shell holds 4 electrons, all valence.

atomic-structure.q: Which subatomic particle determines an element’s identity?
atomic-structure.why: The number of protons (atomic number) defines which element an atom is.

atomic-structure.q: Which subatomic particle carries no electric charge?
atomic-structure.why: Neutrons are electrically neutral, unlike protons (+1) and electrons (−1); they add mass but no charge to the nucleus.

atomic-structure.q: Two isotopes of the same element always have the same number of:
atomic-structure.why: Isotopes share the same number of protons (same element) but differ in neutron count, which changes the mass number.

atomic-structure.q: In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons.
atomic-structure.why: Neutral atoms have no net charge, so the negative electrons exactly balance the positive protons.

atomic-structure.q: An atom's mass number is the sum of its:
atomic-structure.why: Electrons contribute negligible mass, so mass number counts only protons plus neutrons in the nucleus.

atomic-structure.q: A neutral atom that gains an extra electron becomes:
atomic-structure.why: Adding an electron gives the atom one more negative charge than positive, making it a negatively charged anion.

atomic-structure.q: Electrons travel around the nucleus in fixed, planet-like circular orbits.
atomic-structure.why: Modern quantum theory describes electrons as occupying probability clouds (orbitals), not fixed circular paths — the old planetary picture is an oversimplification.

atomic-structure.q: Nitrogen has atomic number 7. A neutral nitrogen atom contains how many protons?
atomic-structure.why: Atomic number is defined as the number of protons, so atomic number 7 means 7 protons (and, when neutral, 7 electrons).

atomic-structure.q: An oxygen atom (8 protons) that has gained 2 extra electrons (10 electrons total) carries an overall charge of:
atomic-structure.why: Charge equals protons minus electrons: 8 − 10 = −2, consistent with the oxide ion O²⁻ that oxygen commonly forms.

atomic-structure.q: All atoms of a given element must contain the same number of neutrons.
atomic-structure.why: Atoms of the same element can have different neutron counts — these variants are isotopes, and they still behave identically in chemical reactions.

atomic-structure.q: Nearly all of an atom's mass is concentrated in its:
atomic-structure.why: Protons and neutrons, both much heavier than electrons, reside in the tiny nucleus, which is why it holds almost all the atom's mass.

atomic-structure.q: The Pauli exclusion principle states that no two electrons in the same atom can have:
options: Identical sets of four quantum numbers
Opposite spins in the same orbital
atomic-structure.why: Every electron must be uniquely described by its quantum numbers; two electrons can share an orbital only if their spins differ.

atomic-structure.q: Hund's rule says that when filling a set of degenerate (equal-energy) orbitals, electrons will:
options: Pair up in the first orbital before occupying others
Always occupy the orbital closest to the nucleus first
Occupy separate orbitals singly before any pairing occurs
atomic-structure.why: Hund's rule minimizes electron-electron repulsion by spreading electrons into separate same-energy orbitals before any pairing happens.

atomic-structure.q: The second electron shell (n = 2) can hold a maximum of how many electrons?
atomic-structure.why: The second shell contains one 2s and three 2p orbitals (4 orbitals total), each holding 2 electrons, for a maximum of 8.

atomic-structure.q: Valence electrons are mainly responsible for an atom's:
atomic-structure.why: Valence (outermost) electrons are the ones available to be shared or transferred in bonds, so they govern how an atom reacts chemically.

atomic-structure.q: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are isotopes of carbon that differ in their number of:
atomic-structure.why: Both have 6 protons (defining them as carbon), but carbon-14 has 2 extra neutrons, giving it a higher mass number.

atomic-structure.q: Neutrons carry a positive electric charge.
atomic-structure.why: Neutrons are neutral (no charge); protons are the positively charged nuclear particles.

atomic-structure.q: How many valence electrons does a neutral nitrogen atom (group 15) have?
atomic-structure.why: Nitrogen is in group 15, and for main-group elements the group number corresponds to 5 valence electrons.

atomic-structure.q: How many valence electrons does a neutral oxygen atom (group 16) have?
atomic-structure.why: Oxygen sits in group 16, so it has 6 valence electrons — which is why it typically forms 2 bonds to complete an octet.

atomic-structure.q: Chlorine is in period 3, group 17. How many valence electrons does it have?
atomic-structure.why: For main-group elements, the group number (17, or 7A) gives 7 valence electrons, explaining why chlorine needs just one more electron for a full octet.

atomic-structure.q: The periodic table arranges elements in order of increasing:
atomic-structure.why: Elements are ordered by increasing atomic number (proton count), which also roughly tracks increasing mass for most elements.

atomic-structure.q: Electrons are located inside the nucleus along with protons and neutrons.
atomic-structure.why: Only protons and neutrons occupy the nucleus; electrons exist in surrounding orbitals/shells outside the nucleus.

atomic-structure.q: Elements in the same column (group) of the periodic table share similar chemical properties mainly because they have:
options: The same number of total electrons
The same number of valence electrons
atomic-structure.why: Chemical behavior is driven by valence electrons, and elements in a group share the same valence electron count, giving them similar reactivity.

atomic-structure.q: Which particle has dramatically smaller mass than the other two?
atomic-structure.why: An electron has roughly 1/1800th the mass of a proton or neutron, so electrons contribute almost nothing to an atom's total mass.

atomic-structure.q: Which quantum number describes an electron's intrinsic spin?
atomic-structure.why: The spin quantum number (m_s = +1/2 or −1/2) distinguishes the two electrons that can occupy the same orbital.

atomic-structure.q: Fluorine (7 valence electrons) strongly tends to:
options: Gain one electron to form F⁻ anions
atomic-structure.why: Being one electron short of an octet, fluorine strongly favors gaining an electron to form the stable F⁻ ion rather than losing one.

atomic-structure.q: An atom's atomic number is defined by its number of protons, not its number of neutrons or electrons.
atomic-structure.why: Atomic number is fixed by proton count; this is what defines which element an atom is, regardless of isotope or ionic charge.

atomic-structure.q: Sodium (Na) readily loses one electron to form Na⁺. This is best explained by sodium having:
options: 1 valence electron, easily lost to reach a stable noble-gas configuration
atomic-structure.why: Sodium (group 1) has just 1 valence electron; losing it leaves sodium with the same stable electron configuration as neon, a noble gas.

orbitals.q: Which orbital shape is dumbbell-shaped with two lobes?
orbitals.why: p orbitals have two lobes on either side of the nucleus along one axis; s orbitals are spherical.

orbitals.q: How many electrons can a single orbital hold at most?
orbitals.why: The Pauli exclusion principle allows at most 2 electrons per orbital, and they must have opposite spins.

orbitals.q: Which orbital fills first: 4s or 3d?
orbitals.why: By the (n+l) filling order, 4s (4+0=4) fills before 3d (3+2=5).

orbitals.q: Which orbital shape is spherical?
orbitals.why: The s orbital is the only orbital type with a simple spherical shape centered on the nucleus.

orbitals.q: How many individual orbitals make up a p subshell?
orbitals.why: A p subshell consists of three orbitals (px, py, pz), oriented along the three perpendicular axes.

orbitals.q: How many individual orbitals make up an s subshell?
orbitals.why: An s subshell has just one spherical orbital, regardless of which energy level it belongs to.

orbitals.q: A d subshell contains 5 orbitals.
orbitals.why: The d subshell has five distinct orbitals, each able to hold up to 2 electrons, for a maximum of 10 electrons.

orbitals.q: What is the maximum number of electrons a full p subshell (3 orbitals) can hold?
orbitals.why: Each of the 3 p orbitals holds up to 2 electrons, so 3 orbitals × 2 electrons = 6 electrons maximum.

orbitals.q: What is the maximum number of electrons the entire 2p subshell can hold?
orbitals.why: Like any p subshell, 2p has three orbitals that each hold 2 electrons, giving a maximum of 6 electrons.

orbitals.q: Why can a single orbital hold at most 2 electrons?
options: The Pauli exclusion principle requires the two electrons to have opposite spins, and a third would have to match an existing set of quantum numbers
Orbitals are physically too small for more
Electrons repel beyond a distance limit set by orbital shape
Only s orbitals can hold 2 electrons
orbitals.why: Two electrons can occupy one orbital only if their spins are opposite; a third electron would necessarily duplicate a full set of quantum numbers, which the Pauli exclusion principle forbids.

orbitals.q: Orbitals represent fixed, definite paths that electrons travel along.
orbitals.why: Orbitals are regions of space describing the probability of finding an electron, not fixed trajectories — this is a key distinction from the outdated Bohr model.

orbitals.q: A sigma (σ) bond forms from which type of orbital overlap?
options: Head-on, direct overlap along the bond axis
orbitals.why: Sigma bonds result from orbitals overlapping end-to-end directly along the axis connecting the two nuclei, giving strong, rotation-tolerant bonding.

orbitals.q: A pi (π) bond forms from which type of orbital overlap?
options: Head-on overlap along the bond axis
Side-by-side overlap of parallel unhybridized p orbitals
orbitals.why: Pi bonds arise when two parallel, unhybridized p orbitals overlap side-by-side above and below the bond axis, creating electron density off the direct line between nuclei.

orbitals.q: Which bond type, sigma or pi, allows free rotation around the bond axis?
orbitals.why: Sigma bonds are symmetric around the bond axis, so rotating one end doesn't disrupt the overlap, unlike pi bonds whose parallel-p-orbital overlap would be destroyed by rotation.

orbitals.q: Hybrid orbitals (like sp3) are formed by mathematically mixing together:
options: s and p orbitals from the same atom
Only p orbitals from different atoms
orbitals.why: Hybridization combines an atom's own s and p orbitals into new, equivalent hybrid orbitals (sp, sp2, or sp3) better suited for bonding geometry.

orbitals.q: How many total orbitals exist in the entire n = 2 shell (2s + 2p)?
orbitals.why: The n=2 shell has one 2s orbital plus three 2p orbitals, totaling 4 orbitals (which can hold up to 8 electrons).

orbitals.q: Why does the 4s orbital fill with electrons before the 3d orbital, even though n=3 is lower than n=4?
options: 4s orbitals are physically larger so they fill first by convention
3d orbitals don't exist until after period 4
In multi-electron atoms, 4s is actually lower in energy than 3d due to shielding effects, so the Aufbau principle has electrons fill it first
Electrons always fill orbitals in strict numerical order of n
orbitals.why: Electron-electron shielding changes the relative energies of orbitals in multi-electron atoms, making 4s slightly lower in energy than 3d, so it fills first according to the Aufbau principle.

orbitals.q: p orbitals have two lobes with a node (zero probability) at the nucleus.
orbitals.why: Unlike the spherical s orbital, a p orbital has a dumbbell shape with two lobes separated by a node right at the nucleus.

orbitals.q: A node in an orbital represents a region where:
options: The electron probability is at its maximum
The electron probability is exactly zero
orbitals.why: A node is a location where the probability of finding the electron drops to zero, separating regions (lobes) of the orbital.

orbitals.q: Which letter designates the orbital type with a spherical shape (zero angular momentum)?
orbitals.why: The s designation corresponds to orbitals with zero orbital angular momentum, which are spherically symmetric.

orbitals.q: The three p orbitals (px, py, pz) are oriented:
options: In a random arrangement that varies by element
orbitals.why: The three p orbitals point along the x, y, and z axes, perpendicular to one another, minimizing their mutual overlap.

orbitals.q: An s orbital has the same basic spherical shape at every energy level, just larger at higher levels.
orbitals.why: 1s, 2s, 3s, etc. are all spherically symmetric; higher-energy s orbitals are simply larger (with additional internal nodes) but keep the overall spherical shape.

orbitals.q: When two p orbitals overlap end-to-end along the axis connecting two nuclei, what type of bond results?
orbitals.why: Even p orbitals can form a sigma bond if they overlap directly along the internuclear axis, concentrating electron density between the nuclei.

orbitals.q: Two parallel p orbitals overlapping side-by-side (not along the bond axis) form what type of bond?
orbitals.why: Side-by-side, parallel overlap of p orbitals places electron density above and below the bond axis, which is the defining feature of a pi bond.

orbitals.q: Orbitals are best described as:
options: Regions of space with a high probability of finding an electron
Fixed circular paths electrons travel along
Solid physical structures inside the atom
Empty space with no electrons at all
orbitals.why: Quantum mechanics describes orbitals as three-dimensional probability distributions for where an electron is likely to be found, not fixed paths.

orbitals.q: How many individual orbitals make up an f subshell?
orbitals.why: The f subshell contains seven orbitals, each capable of holding 2 electrons, for a maximum of 14 electrons.

orbitals.q: What is the maximum number of electrons that can occupy the entire n = 3 shell (3s + 3p + 3d)?
orbitals.why: The n=3 shell has 1 s-orbital, 3 p-orbitals, and 5 d-orbitals (9 orbitals total), each holding 2 electrons, for a maximum of 18.

orbitals.q: Two electrons occupying the same orbital must have opposite spins.
orbitals.why: The Pauli exclusion principle requires that the two electrons sharing an orbital differ in their spin quantum number, since all their other quantum numbers are identical.

orbitals.q: Which bond type results from orbital overlap directly along the internuclear axis, maximizing electron density between the two nuclei?
orbitals.why: A sigma bond's defining feature is head-on overlap along the axis connecting the nuclei, giving the strongest, most direct electron density between them.

orbitals.q: A g subshell (theoretical, not used in ground-state atoms found in nature) would contain how many individual orbitals, following the same pattern as s, p, d, f?
orbitals.why: Subshell orbital counts follow 2l+1: s=1, p=3, d=5, f=7, g=9 — each subsequent subshell type has 2 more orbitals than the last.

hybridization.q: A carbon with one double bond and two single bonds (3 total attachments, trigonal planar) is hybridized as:
hybridization.why: Three regions of electron density (trigonal planar) come from mixing one s and two p orbitals — sp².

hybridization.q: An sp carbon (like in a triple bond) has a bond angle of about:
hybridization.why: sp hybridization gives 2 regions of electron density arranged linearly, 180° apart.

hybridization.q: A carbon with 2 sigma bonds and 2 pi bonds (a triple bond partner) is hybridized as:
hybridization.why: 2 regions of electron density (linear) come from mixing one s and one p orbital — sp, leaving 2 unhybridized p orbitals for the 2 pi bonds.

hybridization.q: A tetrahedral sp3 carbon (4 single bonds, no pi bonds) has a bond angle of about:
hybridization.why: sp3 hybrid orbitals point toward the corners of a tetrahedron, giving the characteristic 109.5° bond angle.

hybridization.q: An sp3 hybridized carbon has no unhybridized p orbitals left, meaning it cannot form any pi bonds.
hybridization.why: sp3 hybridization uses all of the atom's s and p orbitals (one s and all three p's), leaving none available for pi bonding.

hybridization.q: An sp2 hybridized carbon (trigonal planar) has a bond angle of about:
hybridization.why: The three sp2 hybrid orbitals spread out evenly in a plane, 120° apart, to minimize electron repulsion.

hybridization.q: A carbon atom with four single bonds and no multiple bonds is hybridized as:
hybridization.why: With 4 sigma bonds and 0 lone pairs (steric number 4), the carbon mixes one s and three p orbitals into four sp3 hybrid orbitals.

hybridization.q: In ammonia (NH3), nitrogen has 3 bonds and 1 lone pair. What is nitrogen's hybridization?
hybridization.why: Counting 3 sigma bonds plus 1 lone pair gives a steric number of 4, corresponding to sp3 hybridization, even though one 'position' is a lone pair rather than a bond.

hybridization.q: In water (H2O), oxygen has 2 bonds and 2 lone pairs. What is oxygen's hybridization?
hybridization.why: Adding 2 sigma bonds and 2 lone pairs gives a steric number of 4, so oxygen is sp3 hybridized despite forming only 2 visible bonds.

hybridization.q: An atom's hybridization can be determined by counting its number of sigma bonds plus lone pairs (its steric number).
hybridization.why: Steric number 2 gives sp, 3 gives sp2, and 4 gives sp3 — this simple count is the standard shortcut for assigning hybridization.

hybridization.q: A carbonyl carbon (C=O, plus two other single bonds) is hybridized as:
hybridization.why: The carbonyl carbon has 3 sigma bonds total (the double bond counts once for sigma purposes) and 0 lone pairs, giving a steric number of 3 and sp2 hybridization.

hybridization.q: How many unhybridized p orbitals remain on an sp hybridized carbon?
hybridization.why: sp hybridization mixes only one s and one p orbital, leaving 2 p orbitals unhybridized and available to form two pi bonds.

hybridization.q: How many unhybridized p orbitals remain on an sp2 hybridized carbon?
hybridization.why: sp2 hybridization mixes one s orbital with two p orbitals, leaving exactly 1 p orbital unhybridized for pi bonding.

hybridization.q: Why does an sp2 hybridized carbon have exactly one unhybridized p orbital left over?
options: Because carbon only has one p orbital to begin with
Because sp2 carbons never form pi bonds
Because the unhybridized orbital is destroyed during hybridization
Because sp2 hybridization mixes one s orbital with two of the three p orbitals, leaving the third p orbital unused
hybridization.why: Hybridization combines one s and two p orbitals into three sp2 orbitals; the one remaining, un-mixed p orbital is what allows sp2 carbons to form a pi bond.

hybridization.q: A terminal alkyne's C–H bond (attached to an sp carbon) is more acidic than a C–H bond on an sp3 carbon mainly because:
options: sp orbitals have more s-character, holding the bonding electrons closer to carbon and better stabilizing the resulting negative charge
sp carbons are less electronegative than sp3 carbons
Triple bonds weaken all nearby C–H bonds
hybridization.why: Higher s-character (50% in sp vs 25% in sp3) pulls electron density closer to the carbon nucleus, which better stabilizes the negative charge left behind when that C–H bond's proton is removed.

hybridization.q: As the s-character of a carbon's hybrid orbitals increases (sp3 → sp2 → sp), the ideal bond angle around that carbon:
hybridization.why: More s-character spreads the hybrid orbitals further apart in angle — from 109.5° (sp3) to 120° (sp2) to 180° (sp).

hybridization.q: Which C–H bond is generally the shortest?
options: They are all identical in length
hybridization.why: Greater s-character pulls the bonding electron pair closer to the carbon nucleus, making sp C–H bonds shorter (and stronger) than sp2 or sp3 C–H bonds.

hybridization.q: Any atom with exactly 4 sigma bonds, 0 pi bonds, and 0 lone pairs is sp3 hybridized.
hybridization.why: A steric number of 4 with no lone pairs always corresponds to sp3 hybridization and a tetrahedral arrangement of bonds.

hybridization.q: In an imine (C=N), the nitrogen has one double bond, one single bond, and one lone pair. What is nitrogen's hybridization?
hybridization.why: Counting 2 sigma bonds plus 1 lone pair gives a steric number of 3, so the imine nitrogen is sp2 hybridized, just like the carbon it's double-bonded to.

hybridization.q: Boron in BF3 (3 bonds, no lone pair, electron-deficient) is hybridized as:
hybridization.why: With 3 sigma bonds and no lone pairs, boron has a steric number of 3, giving sp2 hybridization and a trigonal planar shape, even though boron lacks a full octet.

hybridization.q: In allene (H2C=C=CH2), the central carbon is bonded via two separate double bonds. What is its hybridization?
hybridization.why: The central carbon has only 2 sigma bonds (one to each neighboring carbon, with each double bond contributing one sigma and one pi bond), giving a steric number of 2 and sp hybridization.

hybridization.q: Among sp3, sp2, and sp hybrid orbitals, which has the greatest percentage of s-character?
hybridization.why: sp hybrids are formed from one s and one p orbital (50% s-character), more than sp2 (about 33%) or sp3 (25%), making sp orbitals hold electrons closest to the nucleus.

hybridization.q: sp2 hybridized atoms arrange their three hybrid orbitals in a single plane, 120° apart from each other.
hybridization.why: Trigonal planar geometry is the direct geometric consequence of mixing one s and two p orbitals into three equivalent sp2 hybrids.

hybridization.q: A carbocation carbon (3 bonds, no lone pair, empty p orbital) is hybridized as:
hybridization.why: With only 3 sigma bonds and no lone pair, the carbocation's steric number is 3, giving sp2 hybridization and a trigonal planar shape with an empty, unhybridized p orbital.

hybridization.q: In a carbonyl group (C=O), the oxygen has 1 sigma bond to carbon, a pi bond, and 2 lone pairs. What is oxygen's hybridization?
hybridization.why: Counting 1 sigma bond plus 2 lone pairs gives a steric number of 3, so the carbonyl oxygen is sp2 hybridized, matching its planar carbon partner.

hybridization.q: A steric number of 4 (sigma bonds plus lone pairs) on a central atom corresponds to which hybridization?
hybridization.why: A steric number of 4 means the atom mixes one s and all three p orbitals together, producing four sp3 hybrid orbitals.

hybridization.q: A steric number of 2 (sigma bonds plus lone pairs) on a central atom corresponds to which hybridization?
hybridization.why: A steric number of 2 means only one s and one p orbital are mixed, leaving two p orbitals unhybridized and giving a linear sp arrangement.

hybridization.q: A carbon atom's hybridization can change during a reaction, such as going from sp3 to sp2 when a leaving group departs to form a carbocation.
hybridization.why: Hybridization reflects the current bonding situation, not a fixed property, so it shifts as bonds break and form — here losing a sigma bond drops the steric number from 4 to 3.

hybridization.q: Which hybridization state is associated with linear molecular geometry at the hybridized atom?
hybridization.why: sp hybrid orbitals point exactly 180° apart from each other, producing a linear arrangement around that atom.

hybridization.q: Why do the two hybrid orbitals on an sp carbon point exactly 180° apart?
options: Because mixing one s orbital and one p orbital produces exactly two hybrid orbitals that point in opposite directions to minimize repulsion
Because carbon always forms linear molecules
Because sp carbons have no unhybridized orbitals
Because triple bonds force a fixed 180° angle regardless of hybridization
hybridization.why: Combining one s and one p orbital mathematically yields two equivalent hybrid orbitals oriented oppositely (180° apart), which is the geometric root of every linear sp center.

bonding.q: How many total bonds (σ + π) does a triple bond have?
bonding.why: A triple bond is 1 sigma bond plus 2 pi bonds — 3 total.

bonding.q: Why can’t you freely rotate around a C=C double bond?
options: The sigma bond is too short
The pi bond’s sideways p-orbital overlap would break on twisting
Double bonds have no sigma component
bonding.why: Twisting misaligns the parallel p orbitals that form the pi bond, breaking that overlap — sigma bonds alone allow free rotation.

bonding.q: Which bond is shorter: C=C or C–C?
bonding.why: More bonds between the same two atoms pulls the nuclei closer together, so C=C (~134 pm) is shorter than C–C (~154 pm).

bonding.q: A single bond consists of how many sigma and pi bonds?
bonding.why: A single bond is exactly one sigma bond; no pi bonds are involved.

bonding.q: A double bond consists of how many sigma and pi bonds?
bonding.why: A double bond is always composed of exactly one sigma bond plus one pi bond, never two sigma bonds.

bonding.q: A pi bond is always stronger than a sigma bond between the same two atoms.
bonding.why: Pi bonds form from side-by-side p-orbital overlap, which is generally less effective than the direct head-on overlap of a sigma bond, making pi bonds typically weaker.

bonding.q: Which type of bond forms from direct, head-on orbital overlap along the axis connecting two nuclei?
bonding.why: Sigma bonds are defined by overlap directly along the internuclear axis, concentrating electron density right between the two nuclei.

bonding.q: Which type of bond forms from side-by-side overlap of parallel p orbitals above and below the bond axis?
bonding.why: Pi bonds arise specifically from parallel p orbitals overlapping off to the sides of the bond axis, not along it.

bonding.q: Why is a C≡C triple bond shorter than a C=C double bond between the same two carbons?
options: Triple bonds have less electron density pulling the nuclei together
Bond length is unrelated to bond order
The extra pi bond adds more electron density between the nuclei, pulling them closer together
bonding.why: Each additional bond (sigma or pi) increases the electron density held between the two nuclei, which pulls them closer together and shortens the bond.

bonding.q: Ionic bonds typically form between two nonmetal atoms with similar electronegativity.
bonding.why: Ionic bonds form when there's a large electronegativity difference, typically between a metal (low electronegativity) and a nonmetal (high electronegativity), not between two similar nonmetals.

bonding.q: A covalent bond is best described as:
options: Sharing of a pair of electrons between two atoms
Complete transfer of an electron from one atom to another
bonding.why: Covalent bonding involves two atoms sharing a pair of electrons, as opposed to ionic bonding's complete electron transfer.

bonding.q: An ionic bond is best described as:
options: Transfer of one or more electrons from one atom to another, creating oppositely charged ions
A covalent bond with no polarity
bonding.why: Ionic bonding occurs when electrons are essentially transferred rather than shared, producing a cation and an anion held together by electrostatic attraction.

bonding.q: The O–H bonds within a single water molecule are an example of what type of bond?
bonding.why: Bonds within a molecule connecting atoms like O and H, where electrons are shared, are covalent bonds (here, polar covalent).

bonding.q: Given equally good orbital overlap, which is generally the stronger bond: a sigma bond or a pi bond?
options: They are always equal in strength
bonding.why: Head-on sigma overlap is more efficient than the side-by-side overlap of a pi bond, so sigma bonds are typically stronger per bond.

bonding.q: Why does rotating around a C=C double bond require breaking the pi bond?
options: The parallel p orbitals forming the pi bond must stay aligned for overlap; twisting one carbon misaligns the orbitals and destroys that overlap
Rotation has no effect on pi bonds
Sigma bonds are what get disrupted by rotation
Double bonds don't actually involve p orbitals
bonding.why: The pi bond depends on two p orbitals staying parallel to overlap; rotating one end of the double bond twists the orbitals out of alignment, breaking the pi bond's overlap.

bonding.q: Which bond type allows free rotation around the bond axis?
options: Both sigma and pi bonds equally
bonding.why: Because a sigma bond's overlap is symmetric around the bond axis, rotating the atoms at either end doesn't disrupt the bonding — unlike a pi bond.

bonding.q: Carbon typically forms a total of 4 bonds in stable, neutral organic molecules.
bonding.why: With 4 valence electrons and a strong drive to complete an octet, neutral carbon almost always forms exactly 4 total bonds (counting each bond in a double or triple bond separately).

bonding.q: What is the bond order of a single bond?
bonding.why: Bond order simply counts the number of shared electron pairs between two atoms; a single bond has exactly one.

bonding.q: What is the bond order of a triple bond?
bonding.why: A triple bond consists of 1 sigma plus 2 pi bonds, for a total bond order of 3.

bonding.q: As bond order increases from single to double to triple between the same two atoms, bond length generally:
bonding.why: More shared electron pairs pull the two nuclei closer together, so higher bond order consistently means shorter bond length.

bonding.q: As bond order increases from single to double to triple, bond dissociation energy (strength) generally:
bonding.why: More shared electron pairs create a stronger overall attraction holding the atoms together, so higher bond order means more energy is needed to break the bond.

bonding.q: Bond strength increases but bond length also increases when going from a single to a triple bond between the same two atoms.
bonding.why: The opposite is true: as bond order increases, bond length decreases while bond strength increases — both trends move together, not apart.

bonding.q: Which best describes a polar covalent bond?
options: Electrons are shared exactly equally between two identical atoms
One atom completely transfers an electron to another
Electrons are shared unequally because the two bonded atoms have different electronegativities
No electrons are involved in the bond
bonding.why: Polar covalent bonds occur when the bonded atoms differ enough in electronegativity that the shared electrons spend more time near the more electronegative atom.

bonding.q: A nonpolar covalent bond is most likely to form between two atoms with:
options: A full octet on only one atom
bonding.why: When two bonded atoms have essentially the same electronegativity, the shared electrons are distributed evenly, producing a nonpolar bond.

bonding.q: Which of these bonds is purely (or nearly) nonpolar?
bonding.why: A bond between two identical carbon atoms has zero electronegativity difference, making it essentially nonpolar, unlike bonds to more electronegative heteroatoms.

bonding.q: Why can't a pi bond exist on its own between two atoms without an accompanying sigma bond in typical organic molecules?
options: Pi bonds always form before sigma bonds
The sigma bond establishes the fixed internuclear distance and axis that allows the parallel p orbitals of a pi bond to properly align and overlap
Pi bonds don't actually involve orbital overlap
Atoms can only have one type of bond between them at a time
bonding.why: The sigma bond holds the two atoms at the right distance and orientation; without it, there would be no stable framework for the p orbitals to align and form a pi bond.

bonding.q: A triple bond between two carbons consists of 2 pi bonds and 1 sigma bond.
bonding.why: A carbon-carbon triple bond is made of one sigma bond plus two perpendicular pi bonds, totaling three bonds overall.

bonding.q: In a typical C=C double bond, which bond (sigma or pi) is generally easier to break, making it more reactive toward addition reactions?
bonding.why: The pi bond's electrons are held less tightly (weaker, more exposed overlap above and below the bond axis), making it the part of the double bond that typically reacts first in addition reactions.

bonding.q: Ionic, covalent, and metallic bonding fundamentally differ in:
options: The total number of electrons in the atoms involved
Whether atoms are involved at all
The color of the resulting compound
How electrons are shared or transferred between the atoms involved
bonding.why: The key distinction between bonding types is the behavior of the valence electrons — transferred in ionic bonds, shared between specific atoms in covalent bonds, and delocalized across many atoms in metallic bonds.

bonding.q: A double bond between two atoms is made up of two identical sigma bonds.
bonding.why: A double bond is one sigma bond plus one pi bond — these are fundamentally different types of overlap, not two sigma bonds.

electronegativity.q: Across a period (left to right), electronegativity generally:
electronegativity.why: Nuclear charge increases across a period while shielding stays roughly constant, pulling electrons in more tightly.

electronegativity.q: Which element is the most electronegative?
electronegativity.why: Fluorine is the most electronegative element on the periodic table.

electronegativity.q: Down a group (top to bottom), electronegativity generally:
electronegativity.why: Atomic radius increases down a group, so the valence electrons are farther from the nucleus and less tightly held — electronegativity decreases.

electronegativity.q: Electronegativity measures an atom's ability to:
options: Lose electrons completely in a reaction
Attract shared electrons toward itself within a bond
electronegativity.why: Electronegativity is specifically about how strongly an atom pulls on the electrons it is sharing in a covalent bond.

electronegativity.q: Which is more electronegative: oxygen or carbon?
electronegativity.why: Oxygen (electronegativity ≈ 3.5) is significantly more electronegative than carbon (≈ 2.5), reflecting oxygen's position further right on the periodic table.

electronegativity.q: Electronegativity describes the pulling power of an atom only when it exists completely alone, unbonded to anything.
electronegativity.why: Electronegativity specifically describes an atom's behavior within a bond, pulling on shared electrons — it's meaningless for a truly isolated, unbonded atom.

electronegativity.q: Nitrogen and phosphorus are in the same group. Which is more electronegative?
electronegativity.why: Electronegativity decreases down a group, so nitrogen (higher up, smaller atom) is more electronegative than phosphorus below it.

electronegativity.q: Rank F, Cl, and Br from highest to lowest electronegativity.
electronegativity.why: Electronegativity decreases going down a group, and fluorine, chlorine, and bromine appear in that order from top to bottom, so F is most electronegative and Br is least.

electronegativity.q: A bond between two identical atoms (like H–H) is essentially:
electronegativity.why: With zero electronegativity difference between identical atoms, the shared electrons are distributed perfectly evenly, making the bond nonpolar.

electronegativity.q: Why is fluorine the most electronegative element on the periodic table?
options: Its small atomic radius combined with high effective nuclear charge lets it pull bonding electrons very strongly toward its nucleus
It has the largest atomic radius of any element
It has the most valence electrons of any element
electronegativity.why: Fluorine's small size means its nucleus is close to the bonding electrons, and its high effective nuclear charge gives it an especially strong pull on those shared electrons.

electronegativity.q: Metals generally have lower electronegativity values than nonmetals.
electronegativity.why: Metals tend to lose electrons easily (low electronegativity), while nonmetals tend to attract electrons strongly (high electronegativity) — this split underlies much of ionic bonding.

electronegativity.q: Which group of elements generally has the lowest electronegativity values (excluding noble gases)?
electronegativity.why: Alkali metals sit at the far left of the periodic table, where atoms are large and electronegativity is at its lowest for that period.

electronegativity.q: Given carbon (≈2.5) and hydrogen (≈2.1) electronegativities, a typical C–H bond is considered:
options: Purely nonpolar with zero electronegativity difference
electronegativity.why: The small electronegativity difference (about 0.4) between carbon and hydrogen makes C–H bonds only weakly polar, often treated as essentially nonpolar in practice.

electronegativity.q: Which bond is more polar: C–F or C–Cl?
electronegativity.why: Fluorine (≈4.0) is more electronegative than chlorine (≈3.0), giving the C–F bond a larger electronegativity difference and therefore greater polarity.

electronegativity.q: Which trend correctly describes electronegativity across period 2, from lithium to fluorine?
electronegativity.why: Moving left to right across a period, increasing nuclear charge with similar shielding pulls electrons more strongly, so electronegativity rises steadily from Li to F.

electronegativity.q: Electronegativity values generally increase toward the upper right corner of the periodic table (excluding noble gases).
electronegativity.why: Electronegativity increases across a period (left to right) and decreases down a group (top to bottom), so the highest values cluster in the upper right, with fluorine as the extreme.

electronegativity.q: Why does electronegativity decrease going down a group, despite the increasing number of protons in the nucleus?
options: The added protons exactly cancel out any attraction
Increasing atomic radius and additional electron shielding outweigh the added nuclear charge, so bonding electrons feel a weaker net pull
Electronegativity doesn't actually depend on nuclear charge
Lower elements in a group have fewer valence electrons
electronegativity.why: Even though nuclear charge increases down a group, the valence electrons are farther from the nucleus and more shielded by inner electrons, so the net attraction on bonding electrons actually weakens.

electronegativity.q: Which is more electronegative: oxygen or nitrogen?
options: Nitrogen, because it has fewer bonds
electronegativity.why: Oxygen sits one position to the right of nitrogen in period 2, and electronegativity increases across a period, so oxygen is more electronegative.

electronegativity.q: Which is more electronegative: chlorine or sulfur (same period, chlorine further right)?
electronegativity.why: Within the same period, electronegativity increases moving rightward, and chlorine sits to the right of sulfur, making it more electronegative.

electronegativity.q: The most commonly used electronegativity scale in chemistry is named after:
electronegativity.why: Linus Pauling developed the widely used electronegativity scale, assigning fluorine the highest value (about 4.0).

electronegativity.q: The electronegativity difference between two bonded atoms determines whether a covalent bond is polar or nonpolar.
electronegativity.why: A small or zero electronegativity difference gives a nonpolar bond, while a moderate difference gives a polar covalent bond — this difference is the key diagnostic.

electronegativity.q: Two bonded atoms with an electronegativity difference of roughly 1.7-2.0 or greater tend to form a bond that is best described as:
electronegativity.why: Very large electronegativity differences pull shared electrons so strongly toward one atom that the bond behaves more like a full electron transfer — approaching ionic character.

electronegativity.q: Which is more electronegative: carbon or silicon (same group, carbon above silicon)?
electronegativity.why: Electronegativity decreases down a group, so carbon, sitting above silicon, is more electronegative.

electronegativity.q: Moving left to right across a period, atomic radius generally decreases while electronegativity generally:
electronegativity.why: A smaller atomic radius means the nucleus is closer to the bonding electrons, strengthening its pull on them and increasing electronegativity across the period.

electronegativity.q: Why does a smaller atomic radius within the same period generally correlate with higher electronegativity?
options: The nucleus is physically closer to the bonding electrons, so it exerts a stronger attractive pull on them
Smaller atoms have more valence electrons to share
Atomic radius has no real effect on electronegativity
electronegativity.why: Within the same period, a shorter distance between the nucleus and the outer (bonding) electrons lets the nucleus attract those electrons more strongly, raising electronegativity.

electronegativity.q: Among C–N, C–O, and C–F bonds, which is the most polar?
electronegativity.why: Fluorine has the highest electronegativity of the three, giving the C–F bond the largest electronegativity difference and therefore the greatest polarity.

electronegativity.q: Within the same row of the periodic table, the element farthest to the left (an alkali metal) is generally the least electronegative.
electronegativity.why: Electronegativity increases from left to right across a period, so the leftmost element (an alkali metal) has the lowest electronegativity in that row.

electronegativity.q: Among the halogens F, Cl, Br, and I, which is the least electronegative?
electronegativity.why: Electronegativity decreases down a group, and iodine is the lowest (largest, furthest down) of these four common halogens.

electronegativity.q: Sulfur and oxygen are in the same group and both have 6 valence electrons. Why is oxygen more electronegative?
options: Oxygen has more protons overall than sulfur
Electronegativity doesn't depend on position within a group
Oxygen's smaller atomic radius (being higher in the group) lets its nucleus attract bonding electrons more strongly
electronegativity.why: Being higher up the group, oxygen is smaller than sulfur, so its bonding electrons sit closer to the nucleus and experience a stronger pull, despite both elements sharing the same valence electron count.

electronegativity.q: A carbon-hydrogen bond (ΔEN ≈ 0.4) is usually treated as essentially nonpolar in practice, even though there is a small electronegativity difference.
electronegativity.why: The C-H electronegativity difference is small enough that chemists commonly treat it as nonpolar for most practical purposes, even though a slight polarity technically exists.

formal-charge.q: Formal charge = (valence electrons) − (nonbonding electrons) − ?
formal-charge.why: Formal charge = valence e⁻ − nonbonding e⁻ − ½(bonding e⁻), since each atom "owns" half of each shared bond.

formal-charge.q: A nitrogen with 4 bonds and no lone pairs has a formal charge of:
formal-charge.why: N normally has 5 valence e⁻; with 4 bonds (8 shared e⁻, 4 "owned") and 0 lone pairs: 5 − 0 − 4 = +1.

formal-charge.q: An oxygen with 1 bond and 3 lone pairs has a formal charge of:
formal-charge.why: O normally has 6 valence e⁻; with 1 bond (1 "owned" electron) and 3 lone pairs (6 nonbonding e⁻): 6 − 6 − 1 = −1.

formal-charge.q: What is the complete formula for formal charge?
formal-charge.why: Formal charge subtracts an atom's nonbonding electrons and half of its bonding (shared) electrons from its normal number of valence electrons.

formal-charge.q: A carbon atom with 4 bonds and no lone pairs has a formal charge of:
formal-charge.why: 4 valence electrons − 0 nonbonding − 1/2(8 bonding) = 4 − 0 − 4 = 0, matching carbon's normal, neutral bonding pattern.

formal-charge.q: The sum of all formal charges in a neutral molecule must equal zero.
formal-charge.why: Formal charges are a bookkeeping device, and for consistency they must sum to the molecule's actual overall charge — zero for any neutral molecule.

formal-charge.q: A carbon atom with only 3 bonds and no lone pairs (as in a carbocation) has a formal charge of:
formal-charge.why: 4 valence electrons − 0 nonbonding − 1/2(6 bonding) = 4 − 0 − 3 = +1, consistent with the positive charge of a carbocation.

formal-charge.q: A carbon atom with 3 bonds and 1 lone pair has a formal charge of:
formal-charge.why: 4 valence electrons − 2 nonbonding − 1/2(6 bonding) = 4 − 2 − 3 = -1, consistent with a carbanion.

formal-charge.q: An oxygen atom with 2 bonds and 2 lone pairs (as in water) has a formal charge of:
formal-charge.why: 6 valence electrons − 4 nonbonding − 1/2(4 bonding) = 6 − 4 − 2 = 0, matching oxygen's usual neutral bonding pattern.

formal-charge.q: An oxygen atom with 3 bonds and 1 lone pair has a formal charge of:
formal-charge.why: 6 valence electrons − 2 nonbonding − 1/2(6 bonding) = 6 − 2 − 3 = +1, which is why an oxygen with 3 bonds (like a protonated ether oxygen) carries a positive formal charge.

formal-charge.q: A nitrogen atom with 3 bonds and 1 lone pair (a typical neutral amine nitrogen) has a formal charge of:
formal-charge.why: 5 valence electrons − 2 nonbonding − 1/2(6 bonding) = 5 − 2 − 3 = 0, confirming that a nitrogen with 3 bonds and 1 lone pair is neutral, as expected.

formal-charge.q: A nitrogen atom with only 2 bonds and 2 lone pairs has a formal charge of:
formal-charge.why: 5 valence electrons − 4 nonbonding − 1/2(4 bonding) = 5 − 4 − 2 = -1, which is why a nitrogen with only 2 bonds typically carries a negative formal charge.

formal-charge.q: Formal charge is a bookkeeping tool used mainly to compare competing Lewis structures, rather than a measure of the literal true charge on an atom.
formal-charge.why: Formal charge assumes perfectly even sharing of bonding electrons, which isn't physically exact, but it's extremely useful for judging which of several Lewis structures is more reasonable.

formal-charge.q: In the ammonium ion NH4+, nitrogen has 4 bonds and no lone pairs. Its formal charge is:
formal-charge.why: 5 valence electrons − 0 nonbonding − 1/2(8 bonding) = 5 − 0 − 4 = +1, matching the overall +1 charge carried by the ammonium ion.

formal-charge.q: When two Lewis structures are both chemically valid for the same molecule, which is generally preferred?
options: The one with formal charges minimized and placed on the most electronegative atoms possible
The one with the most total bonds
The one drawn with the least symmetry
The one using the most lone pairs overall
formal-charge.why: Structures with smaller (closer to zero) formal charges, and with any unavoidable negative formal charge on the more electronegative atom, are considered more stable and realistic.

formal-charge.q: When a negative formal charge cannot be avoided in a structure, it is generally best placed on:
options: Whichever atom is in the center
formal-charge.why: More electronegative atoms are better able to stabilize extra electron density, so placing a negative formal charge there produces a more reasonable, lower-energy structure.

formal-charge.q: A Lewis structure with a negative formal charge on oxygen is generally more stable than one with the same negative charge placed on carbon.
formal-charge.why: Oxygen's high electronegativity makes it far better suited to hold extra negative charge than carbon, so structures matching charge to electronegativity are favored.

formal-charge.q: In one common Lewis structure for carbon monoxide (C≡O with one lone pair on each atom), the formal charges work out to:
formal-charge.why: Giving carbon 1 lone pair and 3 bonds yields a formal charge of -1, while oxygen with 1 lone pair and 3 bonds yields +1 — an unusual but correct result for CO.

formal-charge.q: A hydrogen atom with 1 bond and no lone pairs has a formal charge of:
formal-charge.why: 1 valence electron − 0 nonbonding − 1/2(2 bonding) = 1 − 0 − 1 = 0, the normal, neutral state for bonded hydrogen.

formal-charge.q: A fluorine atom with 1 bond and 3 lone pairs (its typical neutral bonding pattern) has a formal charge of:
formal-charge.why: 7 valence electrons − 6 nonbonding − 1/2(2 bonding) = 7 − 6 − 1 = 0, matching fluorine's usual neutral, single-bonded state.

formal-charge.q: A fluorine atom with 0 bonds and 4 lone pairs (as in the fluoride ion F−) has a formal charge of:
formal-charge.why: 7 valence electrons − 8 nonbonding − 1/2(0 bonding) = 7 − 8 − 0 = -1, matching the known -1 charge of the fluoride ion.

formal-charge.q: In the nitrate ion (NO3−, overall charge -1), a common structure has nitrogen at +1 and the three oxygens collectively totaling -2 (two at 0, one at -1). Do these formal charges correctly represent the ion?
options: No, because formal charges must always be zero on every atom
No, because nitrogen can never have a positive formal charge
Yes, because they sum to -1, matching the ion's overall charge
No, oxygen atoms can never carry formal charge
formal-charge.why: Formal charges don't need to be zero individually — they only need to sum to the species' true overall charge, and +1 + 0 + 0 + (-1) = 0... more precisely +1 and three oxygens summing to -2 gives an overall -1, matching the nitrate ion.

formal-charge.q: It is acceptable for individual atoms within a polyatomic ion to carry nonzero formal charges, as long as all the formal charges sum to the ion's overall charge.
formal-charge.why: Unlike neutral molecules (which must sum to zero), ions are expected to have formal charges summing to their actual net charge, whether +1, -1, or otherwise.

formal-charge.q: A boron atom in the tetrafluoroborate ion (BF4−) with 4 bonds and no lone pair has a formal charge of:
formal-charge.why: 3 valence electrons − 0 nonbonding − 1/2(8 bonding) = 3 − 0 − 4 = -1, consistent with boron's contribution to the ion's overall -1 charge.

formal-charge.q: If a lone pair on one atom becomes a new pi bond to a neighboring atom (to relieve that neighbor's negative formal charge), how does the first atom's own formal charge change?
formal-charge.why: Converting 2 nonbonding electrons into 2 bonding electrons removes 2 from the nonbonding count (+2 to formal charge) but only adds 1 to the half-bonding count (-1 to formal charge), for a net change of +1.

formal-charge.q: For a neutral molecule, the sum of the formal charges on all its atoms must equal:
formal-charge.why: Since a neutral molecule has no net charge, all of its individual atomic formal charges must add up to zero overall.

formal-charge.q: In the bicarbonate ion HCO3− (overall charge -1), the -1 formal charge is most likely located on:
options: It cannot be located on any single atom
formal-charge.why: Oxygen's high electronegativity and its role as a terminal atom with extra lone pairs make it the atom that typically carries the ion's formal negative charge.

formal-charge.q: A carbon atom can never have a nonzero formal charge in any valid Lewis structure.
formal-charge.why: Carbocations (+1) and carbanions (-1) are valid, commonly drawn species in organic chemistry, showing that carbon's formal charge is not always zero.

formal-charge.q: If an atom's number of bonds exactly matches its typical valence (carbon with 4, nitrogen with 3, oxygen with 2, a halogen with 1), its formal charge is generally:
options: Impossible to determine without more information
formal-charge.why: These are each atom's 'normal' bonding patterns in a neutral molecule, for which the formal charge works out to zero by design.

formal-charge.q: Phosphorus in PCl5 has 5 bonds and no lone pair (an expanded octet). What is phosphorus's formal charge?
formal-charge.why: 5 valence electrons − 0 nonbonding − 1/2(10 bonding) = 5 − 0 − 5 = 0, showing that an expanded octet on a period-3+ element doesn't automatically create a formal charge.

lewis-structures.q: What is the first step in drawing a Lewis structure?
options: Add lone pairs to satisfy the octet
lewis-structures.why: You need the total valence electron count before you can distribute bonds and lone pairs correctly.

lewis-structures.q: In a good Lewis structure, the central atom is usually:
lewis-structures.why: Less electronegative atoms tend to form more bonds and sit centrally; hydrogen can never be central (only 1 bond).

lewis-structures.q: If, after distributing bonds and lone pairs, an atom is short of an octet, what should you try next?
options: Leave it short — octets are optional
Remove an atom from the molecule
Form a double or triple bond using an adjacent lone pair
lewis-structures.why: Converting a lone pair on a neighboring atom into a pi bond (multiple bond) often completes the octet without changing the molecular formula.

lewis-structures.q: In a Lewis structure, a shared pair of bonding electrons is typically drawn as:
options: An arrow pointing away from the atom
A line (or two dots) between two atoms
lewis-structures.why: A bonding pair is represented either as two dots between the bonded atoms or, more commonly, as a single line connecting them.

lewis-structures.q: A lone (nonbonding) pair of electrons is drawn in a Lewis structure as:
options: Two dots placed on a single atom, not between atoms
lewis-structures.why: Lone pairs belong to just one atom, so they're shown as a pair of dots on that atom rather than as a line connecting to another atom.

lewis-structures.q: Hydrogen can never be the central atom in a Lewis structure.
lewis-structures.why: Hydrogen can form only one bond (it has just one valence electron and no available orbitals to expand), so it must always be a terminal (outer) atom, never central.

lewis-structures.q: For methane, CH4, how many total valence electrons must be distributed in the Lewis structure?
lewis-structures.why: Carbon contributes 4 valence electrons and each of the 4 hydrogens contributes 1, giving 4 + 4(1) = 8 total valence electrons.

lewis-structures.q: For carbon dioxide, CO2, how many total valence electrons are there to distribute?
lewis-structures.why: Carbon contributes 4 and each oxygen contributes 6, giving 4 + 6 + 6 = 16 total valence electrons.

lewis-structures.q: For the carbonate ion, CO3²−, how many total valence electrons should be used, accounting for the charge?
lewis-structures.why: Carbon (4) plus three oxygens (6 each = 18) gives 22, plus 2 extra electrons for the 2− charge, totaling 24.

lewis-structures.q: When drawing a Lewis structure for a polyatomic ion with a negative charge, you should add that many extra electrons to the total electron count.
lewis-structures.why: A negative charge means the species has gained that many extra electrons beyond the neutral sum of its atoms' valence electrons, so they must be added to the total before distributing them.

lewis-structures.q: After connecting all atoms to the central atom with single bonds, what is the typical next step in drawing a Lewis structure?
options: Distribute the remaining electrons as lone pairs, usually completing the outer atoms' octets first
Immediately add a triple bond to every atom
Erase the bonds and start over
Place all remaining electrons on the central atom regardless of outer atoms
lewis-structures.why: Once the basic skeleton is bonded, remaining electrons are placed as lone pairs, typically satisfying the outer (terminal) atoms' octets before addressing the central atom.

lewis-structures.q: When drawing SO2, sulfur initially ends up short of a full octet after single bonds and lone pairs are placed. The standard fix is to:
options: Leave sulfur with an incomplete octet permanently
Convert a lone pair on one oxygen into a pi bond, forming a double bond to sulfur
Remove electrons from the structure entirely
Make oxygen the central atom instead
lewis-structures.why: Moving a lone pair from an outer atom into a new pi bond gives the electron-deficient central atom the electrons it needs without changing the total electron count.

lewis-structures.q: Why do ions like NO3− often require multiple resonance structures rather than one single Lewis structure?
options: Because the molecule constantly changes its actual atomic connectivity
Because resonance structures are simply alternate, equally wrong guesses
Because no single static structure fully captures the real, averaged (delocalized) distribution of electrons across equivalent positions
Because nitrogen cannot form double bonds
lewis-structures.why: The true electron distribution in such ions is an average (delocalized) across several equivalent arrangements, which a single fixed structure can't represent alone — resonance structures together approximate the real picture.

lewis-structures.q: In a correctly drawn Lewis structure, the total number of electrons shown (in bonds and lone pairs) must equal:
options: Twice the number of atoms in the molecule
The atomic number of the central atom
The total valence electron count calculated at the very start
lewis-structures.why: Every valence electron counted up front must appear somewhere in the final structure — none can be added or left out along the way.

lewis-structures.q: Which type of atom is typically a terminal (outer) atom rather than a candidate for the central position?
lewis-structures.why: Hydrogen and the halogens generally form only one bond each, making them well suited as terminal atoms rather than as a central, multiply-bonded atom.

lewis-structures.q: Period 3 and beyond elements, such as sulfur or phosphorus, can sometimes exceed a simple octet in a valid Lewis structure.
lewis-structures.why: Elements in period 3 or lower have accessible d orbitals (or simply larger atomic size) that allow them to accommodate more than 8 electrons around them, unlike strict period-2 elements.

lewis-structures.q: Which of these atoms is NOT generally allowed to exceed an octet in a standard Lewis structure?
lewis-structures.why: Carbon, a period-2 element, has no available orbitals beyond 2s and 2p, so it is strictly limited to 8 electrons, unlike period-3+ elements that can expand their octets.

lewis-structures.q: What is the very first practical step before placing any electrons in a Lewis structure?
options: Draw all the lone pairs first
Guess the final shape of the molecule
Count the total number of valence electrons available from all atoms (adjusting for any overall charge)
Assign formal charges to every atom
lewis-structures.why: Knowing the total electron budget up front is essential — every later step (bonds, lone pairs, multiple bonds) depends on correctly distributing that fixed total.

lewis-structures.q: When more than one atom could plausibly be the central atom, which is generally chosen?
options: The least electronegative atom available, which is typically capable of forming the most bonds
lewis-structures.why: Less electronegative atoms are usually less 'greedy' for electrons and can form more bonds, making them well suited to sit at the center, surrounded by more electronegative terminal atoms.

lewis-structures.q: Why is a single, fixed Lewis structure inadequate for describing the bonding in the azide ion N3−?
options: Several equivalent arrangements of double/triple bonds and lone pairs are possible, and the true structure is a delocalized average of them, which resonance structures together approximate
Nitrogen cannot form any bonds at all
Azide has no valence electrons to draw
The ion does not actually exist
lewis-structures.why: Just as with nitrate, azide's electron density is spread across multiple equivalent bonding arrangements, and drawing several resonance structures better represents the real, delocalized bonding than any single structure alone.

lewis-structures.q: Carbon almost always forms exactly 4 total bonds in a valid, neutral Lewis structure.
lewis-structures.why: With 4 valence electrons, neutral carbon needs 4 more (shared) to complete its octet, so it reliably forms 4 total bonds (single, double, and triple bonds all counted toward that total).

lewis-structures.q: In a neutral, uncharged Lewis structure, oxygen typically forms how many total bonds?
lewis-structures.why: With 6 valence electrons, oxygen needs 2 more to complete an octet, so it typically forms 2 total bonds (plus 2 lone pairs) when neutral.

lewis-structures.q: In a neutral, uncharged Lewis structure, nitrogen typically forms how many total bonds?
lewis-structures.why: With 5 valence electrons, nitrogen needs 3 more to complete an octet, so it typically forms 3 total bonds (plus 1 lone pair) when neutral.

lewis-structures.q: If a period-2 central atom like carbon or nitrogen ends up surrounded by 10 electrons in a drawn structure, this most likely indicates:
options: That the atom has a formal charge of -2
An error — period-2 elements cannot legitimately exceed an octet of 8 electrons
lewis-structures.why: Period-2 elements like carbon and nitrogen lack accessible orbitals beyond the octet, so any structure giving them more than 8 electrons signals a mistake that needs correcting.

lewis-structures.q: Which molecule requires an expanded octet on its central atom to be drawn correctly: SF6 or CH4?
lewis-structures.why: Sulfur in SF6 forms 6 bonds (12 electrons around it), which is only possible because sulfur, a period-3 element, can exceed the standard octet — something carbon in CH4 (period 2) cannot do.

lewis-structures.q: Drawing the skeletal structure (atom connectivity) before placing electrons matters because it:
options: Has no real effect on the final structure
Determines which atoms are bonded to which before any electrons are distributed, which directly shapes the rest of the process
Is only a formality with no chemical significance
Replaces the need to count valence electrons
lewis-structures.why: Electrons can only be placed once you know which atoms are actually connected — getting the skeleton right first is essential to arriving at a sensible final structure.

lewis-structures.q: A correct Lewis structure must account for every single valence electron counted at the start — none can be left out or added extra.
lewis-structures.why: The entire process is essentially careful electron bookkeeping: the total electrons placed in bonds and lone pairs must exactly match the total counted up front.

lewis-structures.q: In formaldehyde, H2CO, which best describes the central carbon's bonding?
options: Four single bonds, no lone pairs
Two double bonds and no single bonds
A double bond to oxygen and two single bonds to hydrogen, with no lone pairs on carbon
A single bond to oxygen and three single bonds to hydrogen
lewis-structures.why: Carbon forms a C=O double bond plus two C–H single bonds (4 bonds total, 0 lone pairs), giving it a complete octet with no formal charge.

lewis-structures.q: Why is fluorine essentially never chosen as a central atom when other options are available?
options: Fluorine always forms ionic bonds, never covalent ones
Fluorine is highly electronegative and typically forms only 1 bond, making it a better fit as a terminal atom
lewis-structures.why: Since fluorine needs only 1 bond to complete its octet, it naturally sits at the edge of a structure rather than at the center, where more bonds are usually needed.

lewis-structures.q: Which best explains why many molecules and ions require more than one valid Lewis structure (resonance) to be fully described?
options: Electrons in certain pi bonds or lone pairs can be delocalized across multiple equivalent positions, and no single static structure fully captures this
The rules for Lewis structures are inconsistent and unreliable
Resonance structures are simply different molecules entirely
Only charged species ever need more than one structure
lewis-structures.why: When electron density can be equally well placed in more than one equivalent arrangement, drawing several resonance structures together gives a more accurate picture of the real, averaged bonding than any single structure alone.

molecular-geometry.q: A central atom with 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs has what geometry?
molecular-geometry.why: 4 electron domains with no lone pairs arrange tetrahedrally (VSEPR) — 109.5° angles.

molecular-geometry.q: Why does water (2 bonding pairs, 2 lone pairs) have a bent shape instead of linear?
options: Lone pairs take up space and push the bonding pairs together
Hydrogen atoms repel each other more than electrons do
molecular-geometry.why: VSEPR counts lone pairs as occupying space — with 4 total domains around O, the electron geometry is tetrahedral, but the molecular shape (just the atoms) comes out bent.

molecular-geometry.q: A central atom with 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair has what molecular shape?
molecular-geometry.why: 4 total electron domains give a tetrahedral electron geometry, but with one domain as a lone pair, the atoms alone form a trigonal pyramidal shape (like NH₃).

molecular-geometry.q: A central atom with 2 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs has what molecular geometry?
molecular-geometry.why: With only 2 electron groups and no lone pairs to push them around, they spread as far apart as possible: 180° apart, giving a linear shape.

molecular-geometry.q: A central atom with 3 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs has what molecular geometry?
molecular-geometry.why: Three electron groups with no lone pairs spread out evenly in a single plane, 120° apart, giving a trigonal planar shape.

molecular-geometry.q: VSEPR theory predicts molecular shape based on minimizing repulsion between electron groups around a central atom.
molecular-geometry.why: VSEPR (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion) theory's core idea is that electron groups (bonds and lone pairs) arrange themselves to be as far apart as possible, minimizing repulsion.

molecular-geometry.q: What is the key difference between 'electron-pair geometry' and 'molecular geometry'?
options: They are always identical with no difference
Electron-pair geometry accounts for all electron groups (bonds plus lone pairs), while molecular geometry describes only the arrangement of the bonded atoms themselves
Molecular geometry ignores bonding electrons entirely
Electron-pair geometry only applies to ions
molecular-geometry.why: Electron-pair geometry considers every region of electron density (including invisible lone pairs), while molecular geometry describes the shape traced out by the actual atoms, which can look different when lone pairs are present.

molecular-geometry.q: Ammonia (NH3) has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair around nitrogen. What is its molecular (atoms-only) shape?
molecular-geometry.why: Although the electron-pair geometry is tetrahedral (4 total electron groups), one position is a lone pair, so only 3 atoms are visible, giving a trigonal pyramidal shape.

molecular-geometry.q: Water's H–O–H bond angle (104.5°) is smaller than ammonia's H–N–H angle (107°), which is smaller than methane's H–C–H angle (109.5°). Why does water compress the most?
options: Water has fewer total electron groups than ammonia
Oxygen is larger than nitrogen and carbon
Water's bonds are longer than ammonia's
Water has 2 lone pairs (versus ammonia's 1), and lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, compressing the bond angle further
molecular-geometry.why: Each extra lone pair adds more repulsion pushing the bonding pairs closer together; with 2 lone pairs instead of ammonia's 1, water's H–O–H angle gets squeezed down the most.

molecular-geometry.q: Lone pairs occupy more space around a central atom than bonding pairs, causing greater repulsion on neighboring electron groups.
molecular-geometry.why: Because lone pairs aren't held between two nuclei, they spread out more and exert stronger repulsive forces, compressing bond angles involving bonding pairs nearby.

molecular-geometry.q: What is the ideal bond angle for tetrahedral molecular geometry (4 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs)?
molecular-geometry.why: Four identical electron groups with no lone pairs spread out symmetrically to 109.5° apart, the ideal tetrahedral angle.

molecular-geometry.q: What is the ideal bond angle for trigonal planar geometry?
molecular-geometry.why: Three electron groups with no lone pairs spread evenly in a plane at 120° apart to minimize repulsion.

molecular-geometry.q: What is the ideal bond angle for linear geometry?
molecular-geometry.why: With only 2 electron groups and no lone pairs, the maximum possible separation is a straight 180° angle.

molecular-geometry.q: A central atom with 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs has what molecular shape?
molecular-geometry.why: The underlying electron-pair geometry is tetrahedral (4 total groups), but with 2 lone pairs removed from view, only the 2 bonded atoms remain visible, producing a bent shape.

molecular-geometry.q: Sulfur dioxide (SO2) has sulfur with 2 bonds and 1 lone pair (using a resonance structure). Why is SO2 bent rather than linear, since it only has 2 terminal atoms?
options: The lone pair on sulfur occupies one of the three electron-group positions, forcing a trigonal-planar-based (bent) arrangement instead of a linear one
Sulfur is too large to form a linear molecule
Oxygen atoms repel each other directly, bending the molecule
SO2 doesn't actually have a defined shape
molecular-geometry.why: With 3 total electron groups (2 bonds + 1 lone pair), the electron-pair geometry is trigonal planar; removing the invisible lone pair from the picture leaves the 2 oxygens in a bent arrangement, not a straight line.

molecular-geometry.q: A central atom with 5 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs (an expanded octet, as in PCl5) has what geometry?
molecular-geometry.why: Five electron groups with no lone pairs arrange themselves into a trigonal bipyramidal shape, with three equatorial and two axial positions.

molecular-geometry.q: A central atom with 6 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs (an expanded octet, as in SF6) has what geometry?
molecular-geometry.why: Six electron groups with no lone pairs spread into an octahedral arrangement, the most symmetric way to separate 6 groups evenly.

molecular-geometry.q: Molecular geometry describes only the positions of bonded atoms, even though lone pairs still influence the overall observed shape.
molecular-geometry.why: Lone pairs aren't drawn into the final molecular shape, but their repulsive effect on the bonding pairs still shapes the angles and arrangement that we actually observe.

molecular-geometry.q: For a tetrahedral carbon with 4 different substituents, roughly how many of the bond angles between pairs of substituents are approximately equal?
options: All of the pairwise bond angles, at about 109.5° each
molecular-geometry.why: In an ideal tetrahedral arrangement, every pair of substituents around the central atom is separated by approximately the same 109.5° angle.

molecular-geometry.q: Why does ammonia's trigonal pyramidal shape differ from a full tetrahedron, even though both arise from a tetrahedral electron-pair geometry?
options: One 'corner' of the tetrahedral electron arrangement is occupied by an invisible lone pair instead of an atom, so only 3 atom positions (plus the center) are observed, giving a pyramid shape
Ammonia's nitrogen is a different element entirely
Ammonia doesn't actually have a tetrahedral electron-pair geometry
Nitrogen has fewer valence electrons than carbon
molecular-geometry.why: The electron-pair geometry (4 total groups) is tetrahedral, but since one of those groups is an unseen lone pair, only 3 hydrogen atoms plus the nitrogen are visible, producing the trigonal pyramidal molecular shape.

molecular-geometry.q: In formaldehyde, the carbon has 3 bonding groups (one of which is a double bond to oxygen) and 0 lone pairs. What is its molecular geometry?
molecular-geometry.why: A double bond still counts as just one electron group for VSEPR purposes, so with 3 total groups and no lone pairs, the carbon is trigonal planar.

molecular-geometry.q: In VSEPR theory, a double or triple bond between the central atom and another atom counts as how many electron groups for determining geometry?
options: 2 for a double bond, 3 for a triple bond
1, regardless of how many bonds (sigma + pi) it contains
It varies depending on the atoms involved
molecular-geometry.why: VSEPR treats an entire multiple bond (single, double, or triple) as one region of electron density occupying one position around the central atom, since the pi bonds don't point in separate directions.

molecular-geometry.q: A double bond counts as two separate electron groups when determining a central atom's steric number for VSEPR purposes.
molecular-geometry.why: A double bond occupies only one spatial position around the central atom (toward the same neighboring atom), so it always counts as a single electron group, not two.

molecular-geometry.q: A carbocation carbon with 3 bonds and no lone pair (and an empty p orbital) adopts what molecular geometry?
molecular-geometry.why: With only 3 electron groups (the 3 bonds) and no lone pair present, the 3 substituents spread out in a plane at 120°, giving trigonal planar geometry.

molecular-geometry.q: Why do carbocations adopt a trigonal planar geometry rather than a tetrahedral one?
options: They have only 3 bonding groups and an empty orbital (not a lone pair) providing no extra repulsive electron density, so VSEPR predicts a planar arrangement for just the 3 substituents
Carbocations always have a hidden lone pair forcing a pyramid shape
Carbocations cannot be described by VSEPR theory at all
Carbocations actually have 4 bonds, one of which is invisible
molecular-geometry.why: An empty orbital holds no electrons and therefore exerts no repulsion, so with only 3 true electron groups present, the molecule minimizes repulsion by going flat (120° apart) rather than puckering into a tetrahedron.

molecular-geometry.q: Which steric number (total electron groups) gives a linear electron-pair geometry?
molecular-geometry.why: With just 2 total electron groups and no other groups to consider, the only way to minimize repulsion is to place them 180° apart, giving a linear arrangement.

molecular-geometry.q: How many total electron groups (bonding pairs plus lone pairs) surround the central oxygen in a water molecule?
molecular-geometry.why: Water's oxygen has 2 bonding pairs (to the 2 hydrogens) plus 2 lone pairs, for a total steric number of 4, even though the visible molecular shape only shows 2 atoms.

molecular-geometry.q: A tetrahedral electron-pair geometry always results in a tetrahedral molecular geometry.
molecular-geometry.why: A tetrahedral electron-pair geometry only produces a tetrahedral molecular shape when there are no lone pairs; if lone pairs are present, the molecular shape becomes trigonal pyramidal or bent instead.

molecular-geometry.q: What is the molecular geometry of the central carbon in CO2, which has 2 double bonds and 0 lone pairs?
molecular-geometry.why: Each double bond counts as just one electron group, so carbon has 2 total groups with no lone pairs, giving a linear molecule with 180° bond angles.

molecular-geometry.q: A central atom with 2 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs, and no ability to expand its octet, will have what molecular geometry?
molecular-geometry.why: Two electron groups with nothing else around the central atom always spread as far apart as possible, producing a straight, linear shape.

bond-polarity.q: A bond is considered polar covalent when the electronegativity difference is roughly:
bond-polarity.why: Small/zero difference = nonpolar covalent; moderate difference (~0.4–1.7) = polar covalent; large difference = ionic.

bond-polarity.q: In a C–O bond, which atom carries the partial negative charge?
bond-polarity.why: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so it pulls the shared electron density toward itself, becoming δ⁻.

bond-polarity.q: A molecule can have polar bonds but still be a nonpolar molecule overall if:
options: It has no bonds at all
It contains only carbon and hydrogen
The bond dipoles are arranged symmetrically and cancel out
It has an odd number of atoms
bond-polarity.why: Molecular polarity depends on the vector sum of all bond dipoles — symmetric arrangements (like CO₂ or CCl₄) can cancel polar bonds into a net nonpolar molecule.

bond-polarity.q: In a C–H bond, which atom carries the slight partial negative charge?
options: Neither — the bond is perfectly nonpolar
bond-polarity.why: Carbon (electronegativity ≈ 2.5) is slightly more electronegative than hydrogen (≈ 2.1), so carbon pulls the shared electrons marginally toward itself, giving it a small partial negative charge.

bond-polarity.q: In an O–H bond, which atom carries the partial positive charge?
bond-polarity.why: Oxygen is far more electronegative than hydrogen, pulling the shared electrons toward itself and leaving hydrogen with a partial positive charge.

bond-polarity.q: A bond between two identical atoms (such as C–C) is always nonpolar.
bond-polarity.why: Identical atoms have exactly equal electronegativity, so there is zero tendency for the shared electrons to shift toward one side, making the bond perfectly nonpolar.

bond-polarity.q: Which bond is more polar: C–Cl or C–Br?
options: Neither bond is polar at all
bond-polarity.why: Chlorine is more electronegative than bromine, so the C–Cl bond has a larger electronegativity difference and is therefore more polar than C–Br.

bond-polarity.q: Which of these bonds has the greatest electronegativity difference and the most ionic character: C–F, C–N, or C–O?
bond-polarity.why: Fluorine is the most electronegative of the three atoms, giving C–F the largest electronegativity gap and the greatest degree of ionic character among typical organic bonds.

bond-polarity.q: In a polar bond, the dipole arrow (pointing from partial positive to partial negative) points toward:
options: The smaller atom, regardless of electronegativity
bond-polarity.why: The dipole arrow represents the net pull on the shared electrons, which always points toward the more electronegative (more electron-hungry) atom in the bond.

bond-polarity.q: The symbol δ+ placed near an atom indicates:
options: That the atom has gained an electron
bond-polarity.why: The delta (δ) symbol denotes a partial charge resulting from unequal electron sharing in a polar covalent bond, not a full formal ionic charge.

bond-polarity.q: The symbol δ− placed near an atom indicates:
options: That the atom has lost an electron
bond-polarity.why: Like δ+, the δ− symbol represents a partial charge from unequal electron sharing, showing which end of a polar bond carries extra (but not whole) negative character.

bond-polarity.q: Carbon dioxide (CO2) has two polar C=O bonds but is overall a nonpolar molecule. Why?
options: The C=O bonds are actually nonpolar
Carbon is more electronegative than oxygen, canceling the effect
CO2's linear shape points the two bond dipoles in exactly opposite directions, so they cancel out
CO2 has no dipole moments to begin with
bond-polarity.why: Because CO2 is linear and symmetric, the two equal-but-opposite C=O dipoles point directly away from each other and sum to zero, leaving no net molecular dipole.

bond-polarity.q: What single factor most directly determines whether a bond is classified as ionic, polar covalent, or nonpolar covalent?
options: The total number of atoms in the molecule
The number of lone pairs on each atom
The electronegativity difference between the two bonded atoms
