bond-polarity.why: The size of the electronegativity difference between two bonded atoms is the standard criterion used to classify a bond along the spectrum from nonpolar covalent to polar covalent to ionic.

bond-polarity.q: Why is carbon tetrachloride (CCl4) a nonpolar molecule despite having 4 individually polar C–Cl bonds?
options: The 4 bond dipoles are arranged symmetrically (tetrahedrally) around carbon and cancel each other out
Chlorine atoms are not very electronegative
CCl4 doesn't actually have any C–Cl bonds
bond-polarity.why: Because CCl4's tetrahedral geometry places the 4 equal C–Cl dipoles in perfectly symmetric directions, their vector sum is zero, making the overall molecule nonpolar even though each bond is polar.

bond-polarity.q: Is the C–C bond in ethane (CH3–CH3) considered polar or nonpolar?
bond-polarity.why: Since both atoms in the bond are carbon, there is zero electronegativity difference, making the C–C bond essentially nonpolar.

bond-polarity.q: An electronegativity difference close to zero between two bonded atoms typically results in what kind of bond?
options: A nonpolar (or nearly nonpolar) covalent bond
bond-polarity.why: When two atoms have essentially equal electronegativity, the shared electrons are distributed evenly, producing little to no bond polarity.

bond-polarity.q: An electronegativity difference greater than roughly 1.7-2.0 between two bonded atoms typically signals:
options: No chemical bond can form at all
A bond with mostly ionic character
bond-polarity.why: Once the electronegativity gap is large enough, the bonding electrons are held so strongly by one atom that the bond is better described as mostly ionic rather than simply polar covalent.

bond-polarity.q: If a molecule has individual polar bonds, the overall molecule must always be polar as well.
bond-polarity.why: Bond polarity and molecular polarity don't always match — if a molecule's shape is symmetric enough, individual bond dipoles can cancel out, leaving a nonpolar molecule despite polar bonds.

bond-polarity.q: Which bond is more polar: N–H or C–H?
bond-polarity.why: Nitrogen is more electronegative than carbon, so the N–H bond has a larger electronegativity difference from hydrogen than C–H does, making N–H more polar.

bond-polarity.q: In the carbonyl group C=O, the oxygen end of the dipole is best described as:
bond-polarity.why: Oxygen's much higher electronegativity pulls the shared pi and sigma electrons toward itself, giving it the partial negative (δ−) end of the carbonyl dipole.

bond-polarity.q: Why does the carbon in a Grignard reagent's C–Mg bond carry the partial negative charge, rather than the metal?
options: Magnesium is more electronegative than carbon
Carbon always carries negative charge in every bond
Carbon is more electronegative than the metal magnesium, so it pulls the shared electrons toward itself
Magnesium has no valence electrons to share
bond-polarity.why: Even though carbon is usually the less electronegative partner compared to oxygen or nitrogen, it is considerably more electronegative than a metal like magnesium, reversing the usual polarity seen in most organic bonds.

bond-polarity.q: Which is more polar: S–H or O–H?
bond-polarity.why: Oxygen is more electronegative than sulfur (despite being in the same group), giving O–H a larger electronegativity difference and therefore greater polarity than S–H.

bond-polarity.q: The greater the electronegativity difference between two bonded atoms, the more polar that bond generally is.
bond-polarity.why: Electronegativity difference is essentially a direct proxy for bond polarity — bigger gaps mean more unequal electron sharing and a more polar bond.

bond-polarity.q: Chloromethane (CH3Cl) is an overall polar molecule mainly because:
options: Its single C–Cl bond dipole has nothing to cancel it out, giving the whole molecule a net dipole moment
It has no polar bonds at all
Carbon and hydrogen have very different electronegativities
Chlorine has no effect on molecular polarity
bond-polarity.why: With only one strongly polar C–Cl bond and three much weaker C–H dipoles that don't offset it, the molecule ends up with an unbalanced, net dipole moment overall.

bond-polarity.q: Which bond is essentially nonpolar due to a very small electronegativity difference: C–H or O–H?
bond-polarity.why: The electronegativity difference between carbon and hydrogen (about 0.4) is much smaller than between oxygen and hydrogen (about 1.4), making C–H nearly nonpolar by comparison.

bond-polarity.q: Why is a C=O bond more polar overall than a typical C–O single bond?
options: Single bonds are always more polar than double bonds
The C=O bond has more total shared electron density (from both a sigma and a pi bond) pulled toward the more electronegative oxygen, increasing the overall charge separation
Oxygen becomes less electronegative in a double bond
bond-polarity.why: Because a double bond includes both a sigma and a pi bond, there's more total electron density being pulled toward the electronegative oxygen, amplifying the charge separation compared to a single C–O bond.

bond-polarity.q: In trans-1,2-dichloroethene, the two C–Cl bond dipoles point in opposite directions across the double bond. This makes the molecule:
options: More polar than the cis isomer
Exactly as polar as a single C–Cl bond
Much less polar (nearly nonpolar) compared to the cis isomer
bond-polarity.why: Because the trans arrangement places the two equal C–Cl dipoles pointing opposite each other, they largely cancel, giving the trans isomer a much smaller net dipole than the cis isomer, where the dipoles add together.

bond-polarity.q: Which of these bonds would you expect to be purely (or nearly) nonpolar: H–H, H–Cl, or H–F?
bond-polarity.why: H–H connects two identical atoms with zero electronegativity difference, making it the only purely nonpolar bond among these three options.

bond-polarity.q: A chemical bond must be classified as either purely covalent or purely ionic, with no middle ground between the two.
bond-polarity.why: Bonding actually exists along a continuous spectrum, with nonpolar covalent and ionic bonds as the two extremes and polar covalent bonds occupying the wide middle ground.

bond-polarity.q: Why does water (H2O) have a net dipole moment even though it is made of individual polar O–H bonds pointing in specific directions?
options: Water's bent shape means the two O–H bond dipoles don't point in opposite directions, so they add together into a net dipole pointing toward the oxygen
Water has no lone pairs to consider
The hydrogens cancel out the oxygen's electronegativity
bond-polarity.why: Because water is bent (not linear), the two O–H dipoles reinforce rather than cancel each other, summing into a single net molecular dipole pointing toward the electronegative oxygen.

resonance.q: Resonance structures differ only in the position of:
options: The net charge of the molecule
resonance.why: Resonance structures show the same atoms in the same positions — only electron placement (lone pairs/pi bonds) differs.

resonance.q: The real structure of a resonance-stabilized species is:
options: Whichever single structure is drawn first
An average (hybrid) of all valid resonance structures
Constantly flipping between structures over time
resonance.why: The actual molecule is a single resonance hybrid — a weighted average of the contributing structures, not an equilibrium between them.

resonance.q: Which resonance structure generally contributes most to the real hybrid?
options: The one with the most atoms
The one with complete octets, minimal formal charges, and negative charge on the most electronegative atom
Whichever has the most double bonds regardless of charge
resonance.why: Lower-energy (more stable) resonance structures — full octets, minimized/well-placed formal charges — contribute more to the actual hybrid.

resonance.q: Resonance structures must all have the same:
options: Number of lone pairs on each atom
resonance.why: Only electrons move between resonance structures — the atoms themselves never move, so connectivity (which atom is bonded to which) is identical in every resonance structure.

resonance.q: Drawing multiple resonance structures for a molecule means the molecule rapidly interconverts between two or more distinct forms.
resonance.why: This is a common misconception. The molecule has only one real structure, a hybrid of all the contributing structures; it never actually becomes any single drawn structure.

resonance.q: In the carbonate ion (CO3^2-), how many equivalent resonance structures contribute to the hybrid?
resonance.why: The negative charge and the C=O double bond can each be placed on any of the three equivalent oxygens, giving three equivalent resonance structures that average to give each C–O bond equal, partial double-bond character.

resonance.q: Resonance stabilization generally makes a molecule or ion:
options: Less stable than any single contributing structure
More stable than any single contributing structure
Exactly as stable as the average of the contributing structures' energies
Unstable unless all structures are equivalent
resonance.why: Delocalizing electrons over more atoms lowers the overall energy of the real hybrid below that of any one localized contributing structure — this is the resonance (delocalization) energy.

resonance.q: Which pair of features makes a resonance structure a poor (minor) contributor?
options: Full octets on all atoms and no charge separation
Negative charge on the more electronegative atom
A carbon atom bearing a positive charge and broken octets
Charges that are close together but opposite in sign
resonance.why: Structures with incomplete octets on carbon, or other atoms that normally want 8 electrons, are high in energy and contribute very little to the real hybrid.

resonance.q: Placing a negative formal charge on oxygen is generally more favorable than placing it on carbon in a resonance structure.
resonance.why: Electronegative atoms like oxygen stabilize negative charge better than carbon does, so resonance structures with negative charge on O are usually major contributors.

resonance.q: For an allylic cation (CH2=CH–CH2+), the curved arrow used to draw its second resonance structure moves electrons from:
options: The empty p orbital into the pi bond
A C–H sigma bond into the cation
The cation directly into a lone pair on carbon
The pi bond into the empty p orbital, shifting the positive charge
resonance.why: The adjacent pi bond's electrons shift toward the empty orbital on the cationic carbon, moving the double bond over by one position and relocating the positive charge to the far end.

resonance.q: Why does an amide (R–CO–NH2) have a C–N bond that is shorter and stronger than a typical amine C–N bond?
options: The nitrogen lone pair delocalizes into the carbonyl, giving the C–N bond partial double-bond character
Nitrogen is more electronegative than it appears
Amides are always planar regardless of electronics
Hydrogen bonding shortens the C–N bond
resonance.why: A resonance structure places the nitrogen lone pair in a pi bond to carbon (with the negative charge moving to oxygen), giving real double-bond character to the C–N bond and restricting its rotation.

resonance.q: Rank the following resonance contributors of an enolate (CH2=CH–O^-  versus  ^-CH2–CH=O) by how much they contribute to the real hybrid.
options: Both contribute roughly equally; neither dominates
The structure with negative charge on oxygen dominates over the one with negative charge on carbon
The structure with negative charge on carbon dominates over the one with negative charge on oxygen
Neither structure is a valid resonance form
resonance.why: Negative charge is better stabilized on the more electronegative oxygen, so the O-centered structure is the major contributor even though both are valid resonance forms.

resonance.q: A nitro group (R–NO2) is often drawn with one N=O double bond and one N–O single bond bearing a negative charge, but both N–O bonds are experimentally found to have equal, intermediate length.
resonance.why: Two equivalent resonance structures (swapping which oxygen carries the double bond and which carries the negative charge) mean the real structure is a hybrid with both N–O bonds equivalent and of intermediate bond order.

resonance.q: Which of the following is a requirement for two structures to be valid resonance forms of each other?
options: They must have the same formal charges on every atom
They must have the same number of electrons and the same connectivity, differing only in electron placement
They must differ in which atoms are sp2 vs sp3 hybridized
resonance.why: Resonance structures share identical atomic connectivity and total electron count; only the positions of pi electrons and lone pairs differ, which can indeed change individual atoms' formal charges.

resonance.q: Benzene's six C–C bonds are all the same length (intermediate between single and double bond length) because:
options: Benzene rapidly isomerizes between two Kekule structures
Benzene has no double bonds at all
Each carbon alternates hybridization over time
The true structure is a hybrid of two equivalent Kekule resonance structures with the pi electrons delocalized around the ring
resonance.why: The two Kekule structures are equal contributors, so the actual molecule has six equivalent bonds with bond order 1.5, not alternating single and double bonds.

resonance.q: A curved arrow used to generate a new resonance structure can show a lone pair moving to form a new pi bond, or a pi bond's electrons moving to become a lone pair.
resonance.why: Both directions are valid ways of redistributing electrons between resonance structures, as long as connectivity and total charge are conserved.

resonance.q: Why can the lone pair on the nitrogen of pyrrole delocalize into the aromatic ring, while the lone pair on the nitrogen of pyridine cannot?
options: Pyrrole's nitrogen lone pair sits in a p orbital aligned with the ring's pi system, while pyridine's lone pair sits in an sp2 orbital in the plane of the ring
Pyridine nitrogen has no lone pair
Pyrrole nitrogen is not part of the ring
resonance.why: In pyrrole the N–H leaves the lone pair in a p orbital that overlaps the ring pi system (delocalized), whereas in pyridine the lone pair occupies an in-plane sp2 orbital perpendicular to the pi system and cannot delocalize.

resonance.q: Which contributing structure of the carboxylate ion (RCOO^-) is the major contributor?
options: The one with the double bond to the oxygen nearer the alkyl chain
Neither — both C–O resonance structures contribute equally
There is only one resonance structure possible for carboxylate
The one with the negative charge on carbon
resonance.why: The two oxygens in a carboxylate are equivalent by symmetry, so the two resonance structures (negative charge/double bond swapped between the two oxygens) contribute equally, giving two identical C–O bond lengths.

resonance.q: A resonance structure with separated formal charges (+ and -) generally contributes more than one with no charge separation, as long as both satisfy the octet rule.
resonance.why: Minimizing formal charge and charge separation generally increases a structure's stability and contribution; a neutral, fully-satisfied-octet structure is usually favored over one with separated charges.

resonance.q: For the allyl radical (CH2=CH–CH2•), resonance predicts that the unpaired electron is:
options: Localized entirely on the original radical carbon
Located only on the central carbon
Delocalized, with significant radical character on both terminal carbons
Impossible to delocalize because radicals never show resonance
resonance.why: Like allylic cations and anions, an allylic radical has resonance structures that place the odd electron on either terminal carbon, so the true structure has partial radical character spread over both ends.

resonance.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes resonance structures from isomers?
options: Isomers have the same connectivity but resonance structures do not
Resonance structures and isomers are the same thing
Resonance structures always have different molecular formulas than each other
Resonance structures depict the same single species with different electron arrangements, while isomers are genuinely different molecules with different energies
resonance.why: Isomers are distinct, isolable compounds, whereas resonance structures are just different ways of drawing electrons in the one real molecule; you cannot isolate a single resonance structure.

resonance.q: In a resonance structure for the phenoxide ion (deprotonated phenol), the negative charge can be placed at the ortho and para ring carbons as well as on oxygen.
resonance.why: Pushing electrons from the oxygen lone pair into the ring, and then around the ring pi system, generates resonance structures with negative charge at the ortho and para positions, explaining phenoxide's extra stability and its reactivity there.

resonance.q: Comparing a resonance structure where a positive charge sits on oxygen (with three bonds, full octet) to one where it sits on carbon (with only three bonds, incomplete octet), which generally contributes more?
options: The oxygen-centered one, because it has a complete octet despite oxygen being electronegative
The carbon-centered one, because carbon is less electronegative
Neither is a valid resonance structure
resonance.why: A complete octet is usually weighted more heavily than minimizing which atom bears a positive charge; an atom with an incomplete octet is a high-energy, minor contributor.

resonance.q: How many total pi electrons are shown as delocalized across the three resonance structures typically drawn for the nitrate ion (NO3^-)?
resonance.why: Nitrate has one N=O pi bond (2 electrons) that resonance delocalizes across the three equivalent N–O linkages, plus the overall negative charge; conventionally two pi electrons are shown shifting position among the three equivalent structures.

resonance.q: A molecule with more significant resonance structures (more ways to delocalize charge) is generally more stable than one with fewer.
resonance.why: Greater delocalization spreads charge or electron density over more atoms, lowering the energy of the real structure relative to a localized one — more good resonance structures usually means more stabilization.

resonance.q: Why is it misleading to say a resonance hybrid is a 'mixture' of its contributing structures?
options: Because only one contributing structure actually exists at any given time
Because resonance structures are not related to each other at all
Because 'mixture' implies separate molecules in different flasks, while a resonance hybrid is a single molecule with one unchanging electronic structure that is only approximated by multiple drawings
Because mixtures cannot have delocalized electrons
resonance.why: A resonance hybrid is one real, single structure; the multiple drawings are just an artificial way of depicting delocalized electron density using the tools of simple bonding diagrams, not a literal equilibrium or blend of separate species.

resonance.q: Which of these changes between two drawn Lewis structures would disqualify them from being true resonance structures of each other?
options: Moving a lone pair to form a new pi bond
Moving a pi bond to become a lone pair on an adjacent atom
Changing the formal charge on an atom by shifting electron density
Moving a hydrogen atom from one carbon to another
resonance.why: Resonance structures never move atoms (including hydrogens) — only electrons move. Moving an atom creates a different molecule (often a tautomer), not a resonance structure.

resonance.q: The cyclopentadienyl anion is unusually stable in part because its negative charge can be delocalized by resonance onto every carbon of the five-membered ring.
resonance.why: Each ring carbon bears a p orbital that is part of a continuous conjugated system, allowing the lone pair (and thus negative charge) to be distributed by resonance across all five equivalent carbons.

resonance.q: In the acetate ion's major resonance structures, what happens to the C–O bond lengths compared to a simple ester's C=O and C–O–R bonds?
options: Both acetate C–O bonds become identical and intermediate in length between a single and double bond
One bond becomes much longer than any single bond and the other much shorter than any double bond
The bond lengths are unaffected by resonance
Only the C–C bond length changes
resonance.why: Because the two equivalent resonance structures contribute equally, the real acetate ion has two identical C–O bonds with bond order about 1.5, not one single and one double bond.

resonance.q: Predict which resonance structure of an enamine (R2N–CH=CH2) contributes more: the neutral form, or the zwitterionic form with a positive charge on nitrogen and a negative charge on the terminal carbon.
options: The zwitterionic form, because separating charges is always favorable
The neutral form, because it avoids charge separation and keeps full octets without extra energy cost
Neither is a legitimate resonance structure of an enamine
resonance.why: Charge-separated resonance structures are generally higher in energy and minor contributors; the neutral structure (with the lone pair still largely on nitrogen in the parent drawing, or no charge separation) is favored, even though the zwitterion correctly predicts the nucleophilic character of the terminal carbon.

curved-arrows.q: A curved arrow in a mechanism always starts at:
options: A source of electrons (lone pair or bond)
curved-arrows.why: Curved arrows track electron movement — they start where electrons already are (a lone pair or an existing bond).

curved-arrows.q: Where does a curved arrow’s head point?
options: Where the electrons are leaving from
Where the electrons are going to
curved-arrows.why: The arrowhead marks the destination of the moving electron pair — a new bond or a new lone pair.

curved-arrows.q: In an acid-base proton transfer, where does the curved arrow showing the base attacking start from?
options: The base’s lone pair (or pi bond)
curved-arrows.why: The arrow starts at the electron source doing the attacking — the base’s lone pair — and points to the proton it is grabbing.

curved-arrows.q: A curved arrow can legally start from a positively charged atom with no electrons to give.
curved-arrows.why: A curved arrow always represents electrons moving, so its tail must start at a source of electron density (a lone pair, a bond, or a negative charge), never at an empty orbital or cation.

curved-arrows.q: When a pi bond attacks an electrophile, the curved arrow's tail is placed on:
options: One of the two atoms of the double bond
The midpoint of the double bond line, between the two atoms
curved-arrows.why: Because both electrons of the pi bond move together as a unit, the tail is drawn from the middle of the double bond line, not from either individual atom.

curved-arrows.q: In an SN2 reaction, how many curved arrows are minimally needed to show the nucleophile displacing the leaving group?
curved-arrows.why: One arrow shows the nucleophile's lone pair attacking the carbon, and a second arrow shows the C–leaving group bond breaking as electrons move onto the leaving group.

curved-arrows.q: A curved arrow drawn from a C–H sigma bond directly into an adjacent pi system (hyperconjugation/elimination step) has its head pointing at:
options: The space between the two carbons where the new pi bond will form
The carbon bearing the leaving group only
curved-arrows.why: When a C–H bond's electrons become a new pi bond (as in E1/E2 elimination), the arrowhead points to the middle of the forming C=C double bond, not at an individual atom.

curved-arrows.q: Curved arrows are only used to draw mechanisms involving charged species, never neutral radicals.
curved-arrows.why: Radical mechanisms use single-barbed 'fishhook' arrows to show one electron moving, which is a variant of curved-arrow notation — curved arrows (full double-barbed) are used for two-electron (ionic) steps, but electron-movement notation exists for radicals too.

curved-arrows.q: If you draw a curved arrow from a lone pair on oxygen toward a neighboring carbon, but that carbon already has four bonds and no leaving group departing, what is wrong with the arrow?
options: Nothing is wrong; carbon can have five bonds temporarily
The arrow should instead start from carbon
The arrow would give carbon five bonds, violating the octet rule unless something simultaneously leaves that carbon
Oxygen cannot have lone pairs that move
curved-arrows.why: Carbon can never exceed four bonds (an octet at most); forming a new bond to carbon requires that carbon simultaneously break an existing bond (a leaving group departing) unless it already has room, such as being cationic.

curved-arrows.q: In drawing a mechanism step, the tail of a curved arrow can be placed on a formal negative charge even if no explicit lone pair is drawn.
curved-arrows.why: A formal negative charge implies an available lone pair at that position, so the arrow tail may start there even without redrawing the dots explicitly.

curved-arrows.q: Which of these is an invalid use of a curved arrow?
options: Tail on a lone pair, head pointing to form a new bond
Tail on a pi bond, head pointing toward an electrophilic atom
Tail on a sigma bond, head pointing to an adjacent atom as a leaving group departs
Tail on a proton (H+), head pointing toward a base's lone pair
curved-arrows.why: A bare proton (H+) has no electrons to donate, so an arrow can never start from H+; instead, the arrow starts from the base's lone pair and points to the H, while a separate arrow shows the H–X bond breaking.

curved-arrows.q: When two curved arrows are drawn for a single mechanistic step, they must be drawn simultaneously to represent a concerted process, not as two separate sequential steps.
curved-arrows.why: Multiple arrows within one mechanism arrow-pushing 'step' (one structure to the next) represent bond-breaking and bond-forming events happening at the same time, i.e., concertedly.

curved-arrows.q: For an intramolecular ring-closing step where a nucleophile inside the same molecule attacks an electrophilic carbon, how many curved arrows are typically needed if the electrophilic carbon also loses a leaving group?
options: It cannot be shown with curved arrows
curved-arrows.why: As in any nucleophilic substitution, one arrow shows the nucleophile (even if intramolecular) attacking, and a second shows the leaving group departing, regardless of whether the nucleophile is in the same molecule.

curved-arrows.q: A curved arrow's tail placed in between two atoms on a bond line, rather than directly on an atom, specifically indicates:
options: A full bond's worth of electrons (sigma or pi) is moving as a unit
curved-arrows.why: Placing the tail on the bond line itself (rather than on an atom's lone pair) shows that the whole bonding pair associated with that bond is the electron source.

curved-arrows.q: In the mechanism for acid-catalyzed protonation of an alkene, the curved arrow showing the alkene attacking H+ starts from the pi bond and points to:
options: A lone pair on the acid's conjugate base
curved-arrows.why: The pi electrons act as the nucleophile and are shown attacking the electrophilic proton; the arrowhead lands on the H atom that is being bonded.

curved-arrows.q: Why is it mechanistically incorrect to draw a single curved arrow going directly from a leaving group's departing bond to the incoming nucleophile's final bonding position in an SN2 reaction?
options: It is actually correct and commonly drawn that way
Because SN2 has no leaving group
Because nucleophiles never have electrons to give
Electrons flow from electron-rich sources to electron-poor sinks, not from one bond directly 'into' another unrelated bond without passing through the reacting atom
curved-arrows.why: Each arrow must independently originate from a genuine source of electrons (the nucleophile's lone pair, or the breaking bond) and terminate at a genuine electron sink; you cannot draw one continuous arrow that skips the reacting carbon.

curved-arrows.q: A curved arrow used to show a carbocation rearrangement (1,2-hydride shift) has its tail on:
options: The C–H sigma bond adjacent to the cation
The empty p orbital of the cation
A lone pair on the cationic carbon
curved-arrows.why: The electrons of the adjacent C–H bond shift to fill the empty orbital on the cationic carbon, so the tail starts on that C–H sigma bond and the head points to the cationic carbon.

curved-arrows.q: Which statement about curved arrows and formal charge is correct?
options: Curved arrows determine formal charges only at the start of a mechanism, not throughout

Every curved arrow tail removes electron density (tends to increase/make-more-positive the formal charge) from its origin atom, and every arrowhead adds electron density (tends to decrease/make-more-negative) at its destination
Curved arrows have no effect on formal charge
Formal charge only changes when atoms move, not electrons
curved-arrows.why: Since formal charge tracks an atom's electron count relative to its neutral state, moving electrons away from an atom (tail) raises its formal charge while electrons arriving (head) lower the formal charge at the destination.

curved-arrows.q: In an E2 elimination, three curved arrows are typically drawn in one step: one for the base removing a proton, one for the C–H bond forming the new pi bond, and one for:
options: A lone pair returning to the base
The C–leaving group bond breaking as electrons leave with the leaving group
curved-arrows.why: E2 is a single concerted step: base removes the beta-hydrogen, those electrons form the new pi bond, and simultaneously the leaving group departs with the sigma bond electrons — three synchronized arrows.

curved-arrows.q: Every curved arrow tail must originate exactly where the electrons physically are before the step, and every arrowhead must point to exactly where they end up after the step.
curved-arrows.why: Curved arrows are a precise bookkeeping tool: tails mark the electrons' starting location and heads mark their ending location, corresponding exactly to the bonding changes between the starting and product structures.

curved-arrows.q: A student draws an arrow from a lone pair on a neutral amine nitrogen pointing toward a proton on a neutral water molecule, forming an ammonium ion and hydroxide. Is this arrow correctly placed?
options: No, the arrowhead should point to the oxygen instead, since oxygen is the more electronegative atom
No, arrows cannot involve neutral species
No, the tail should be on the water molecule instead
Yes, this correctly shows the amine acting as a base
curved-arrows.why: The amine's lone pair is the base's electron source (tail), and it forms a new bond to the acidic proton (head); a second arrow would then show the O–H bond breaking, with electrons going to oxygen.

curved-arrows.q: Why can't a curved arrow ever have its head pointing at a plain, unlabeled blank space with no atom or bond present?
options: Arrowheads must point to where a new bond or lone pair is forming, which is always located at or between specific atoms
Blank space is reserved for labeling formal charges
It actually can, when drawing resonance structures
Curved arrows never have heads, only tails
curved-arrows.why: An arrowhead marks the destination of electron density — either a new bond (so it points between two specific atoms) or a new lone pair (so it points at a specific atom) — never an arbitrary empty location.

curved-arrows.q: In a mechanism, using a curved arrow to move electrons from a C=C pi bond to form a new bond to a proton, while a separate arrow shows nothing happening to the leaving group, would violate which rule if the starting material was neutral and had no leaving group to begin with?
options: The octet rule is always violated in this case
No rule is violated; this correctly describes protonation of an alkene to form a carbocation
This is never a valid step because alkenes have no available electrons
A curved arrow can never point to a proton
curved-arrows.why: Protonating an alkene needs only one arrow (the pi bond attacking H+) because the resulting carbocation, while electron-deficient, doesn't violate any rule since carbocations legitimately have fewer than 8 electrons around carbon.

curved-arrows.q: When two separate curved arrows point to the same single atom in one mechanistic step, that atom would end up with too many bonds unless something simultaneously leaves.
curved-arrows.why: If two new bonds or lone pairs are being added to one atom in the same step without anything leaving, that atom would exceed its normal valence (e.g., carbon exceeding four bonds), which is why such steps require a compensating departure.

curved-arrows.q: A Grignard reagent's carbanion-like carbon attacks the carbon of a ketone's C=O. Which two curved arrows are needed for this addition step?
options: One arrow from oxygen to carbon, and one arrow from magnesium to carbon
Only one arrow is needed, from carbon to carbon
One arrow from the C–Mg bond to the ketone carbon, and one arrow from the C=O pi bond to the oxygen
One arrow from the ketone oxygen to the Grignard carbon, and nothing else
curved-arrows.why: The polarized C–Mg bond's electrons attack the electrophilic carbonyl carbon (first arrow), and the pi electrons of C=O simultaneously shift onto oxygen to avoid carbon exceeding four bonds (second arrow), generating an alkoxide.

curved-arrows.q: A curved arrow can start from a sigma bond between two carbons (a C–C bond) in certain rearrangement or fragmentation mechanisms.
curved-arrows.why: While less common in introductory reactions than lone pairs or pi bonds, C–C sigma bonds can act as electron sources in rearrangements (such as carbocation rearrangements where an alkyl group shifts), so this is valid.

curved-arrows.q: Which best describes the overall direction curved arrows flow in virtually every organic mechanism?
options: From electron-poor regions to electron-rich regions
In a direction chosen arbitrarily by the person drawing the mechanism
Only from negatively charged atoms to other negatively charged atoms
From electron-rich regions (nucleophiles, lone pairs, pi bonds) to electron-poor regions (electrophiles, positive charges)
curved-arrows.why: Curved arrows track the flow of electron density, and electrons always flow from a source with available density toward a site that can accept it (an electrophile), never the reverse.

curved-arrows.q: In drawing the mechanism for forming a hemiacetal from an aldehyde and an alcohol (acid-catalyzed), the very first curved arrow in the overall sequence typically shows:
options: A lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen attacking a proton on the acid catalyst
The alcohol oxygen attacking the carbonyl carbon directly
The carbonyl carbon attacking the alcohol's oxygen
A C–H bond breaking on the aldehyde
curved-arrows.why: Under acid catalysis, the mechanism usually begins with protonation of the carbonyl oxygen (its lone pair attacks H+), which increases the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon before the alcohol attacks.

curved-arrows.q: If a curved arrow's tail is drawn on an atom with no lone pairs, no negative charge, and no bond to break from that position, the arrow is invalid.
curved-arrows.why: Every arrow tail needs a genuine electron source at that exact location — a lone pair, a bond, or charge implying available electrons; an atom with none of these cannot be a valid tail location.

curved-arrows.q: In the reaction of a carboxylic acid with a base, which is the correct single curved arrow showing the acid donating its proton to the base, assuming the O–H bond breaking is shown as a second arrow?
options: From the acidic hydrogen to the base
From the base's lone pair to the acidic hydrogen
From the carbonyl oxygen to the base
From the O–H bond directly to the base's nucleus
curved-arrows.why: The base supplies the electrons that form the new bond to the proton, so the arrow tail sits on the base's lone pair and the head points at the hydrogen; a separate arrow then shows the O–H bond breaking toward oxygen.

nucleophiles.q: A nucleophile is best described as:
nucleophiles.why: Nucleophiles ("nucleus-loving") are electron-rich species that donate an electron pair to form a new bond.

nucleophiles.q: Which factor generally makes a species a better nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent?
options: Larger atomic size down a group (more polarizable)
Being neutral instead of negatively charged
nucleophiles.why: Larger, more polarizable atoms (like I⁻ vs F⁻) donate electron density more easily, making them better nucleophiles especially in aprotic solvents.

nucleophiles.q: Why is a negatively charged nucleophile (like OH⁻) generally stronger than its neutral conjugate acid (H₂O)?
options: Charge has no effect on nucleophilicity
Negative charge means more electron density available to donate
nucleophiles.why: The extra negative charge makes the lone pairs more available/reactive, generally making anions better nucleophiles than their neutral conjugate acids.

nucleophiles.q: Which of the following is NOT typically classified as a nucleophile?
nucleophiles.why: A bare proton has no electrons to donate and is instead a classic electrophile; true nucleophiles must have a lone pair, negative charge, or pi bond available to donate.

nucleophiles.q: Nucleophilicity and basicity measure exactly the same property and always rank species in the same order.
nucleophiles.why: Basicity is thermodynamic (affinity for a proton at equilibrium), while nucleophilicity is kinetic (rate of attack on an electrophilic carbon); steric bulk and solvent can make the two rankings diverge, as with bulky bases that are poor nucleophiles.

nucleophiles.q: Going down a column of the periodic table (e.g., F- to Cl- to Br- to I-), nucleophilicity in a polar aprotic solvent generally:
options: Increases because larger, more polarizable atoms donate electron density more readily
nucleophiles.why: Larger, more polarizable atoms have a more diffuse, easily distorted electron cloud that can reach out and begin bond formation with an electrophile more effectively, increasing nucleophilicity down a group.

nucleophiles.q: In a protic solvent like water or methanol, I- is typically a better nucleophile than F-, but in a polar aprotic solvent like DMSO, the order can reverse.
nucleophiles.why: Protic solvents hydrogen-bond strongly to small, localized-charge anions like F-, caging it and lowering its reactivity; in aprotic solvents with no hydrogen bonding, F- is not solvated as heavily and its small size/high charge density can make it more nucleophilic than I-.

nucleophiles.q: Which of these is the best nucleophile in a protic solvent, assuming all are similarly charged halides?
nucleophiles.why: In protic solvents, strong solvation (hydrogen bonding) cripples small, charge-dense nucleophiles like F-; the large, weakly solvated, highly polarizable I- is freest to attack and is the best nucleophile.

nucleophiles.q: A bulky nucleophile like tert-butoxide (tBuO-) is generally a weaker nucleophile (in the SN2 sense) than a less hindered one like methoxide (CH3O-), even though both are strong bases.
nucleophiles.why: Steric bulk around the nucleophilic atom hinders its ability to approach and bond with an electrophilic carbon in an SN2-type attack, reducing nucleophilicity even when basicity (proton affinity) remains high.

nucleophiles.q: Why is a thiolate (RS-) generally a stronger nucleophile than an alkoxide (RO-), even though alkoxide is the stronger base?
options: Sulfur is more electronegative than oxygen
Thiolates carry a smaller negative charge
Sulfur's larger, more polarizable electron cloud and lower electronegativity make it donate electron density more readily in the rate-determining nucleophilic attack
Alkoxides cannot act as nucleophiles at all
nucleophiles.why: Sulfur is larger and more polarizable than oxygen, so its lone pairs can more easily reach out and form a new bond, even though its lone pairs are held less tightly (making it a weaker base) than oxygen's.

nucleophiles.q: An uncharged species such as ammonia (NH3) can never act as a nucleophile because it carries no negative charge.
nucleophiles.why: Neutral species with an available lone pair (like NH3, H2O, or amines) are common, effective nucleophiles; a negative charge increases nucleophilicity but is not required.

nucleophiles.q: Rank CH3O-, CH3NH2, and CH3COO- in order of decreasing nucleophilicity toward a simple alkyl halide (all else being similar solvent conditions).
nucleophiles.why: A localized, non-resonance-stabilized alkoxide is a stronger nucleophile than a neutral amine, and the resonance-stabilized, delocalized carboxylate is the weakest of the three because its negative charge is spread out and less available.

nucleophiles.q: A pi bond, such as the C=C of an alkene, can act as a nucleophile even though it carries no lone pair or formal negative charge.
nucleophiles.why: The electron density of a pi bond is available to attack an electrophile (as in addition of HBr to an alkene), making alkenes legitimate, if relatively weak, nucleophiles.

nucleophiles.q: Which factor does NOT generally increase nucleophilicity?
options: Increasing electronegativity of the reactive atom (holding size/charge constant)
Increasing negative charge on the reactive atom
Increasing polarizability (size) of the reactive atom
Decreasing steric bulk around the reactive atom
nucleophiles.why: Higher electronegativity means an atom holds its electrons more tightly, making it less willing to donate them to an electrophile, which generally decreases (not increases) nucleophilicity.

nucleophiles.q: Why does resonance delocalization (as in a carboxylate or enolate) generally reduce nucleophilicity compared to a non-delocalized anion of similar charge?
options: Delocalization has no effect on reactivity
Spreading the negative charge over multiple atoms lowers the electron density available at any single atom for forming a new bond
Delocalized anions are always positively charged instead
Resonance makes an anion smaller in physical size
nucleophiles.why: When charge is shared across several atoms via resonance, less electron density sits at any one reactive site, so the species is both more stable (weaker base/nucleophile) and slower to attack an electrophile.

nucleophiles.q: Between H2O and OH-, which is the better nucleophile, and why?
options: H2O, because it is more abundant in aqueous solution
OH-, because its negative charge gives it higher electron density and less attraction holding that density to its own nucleus
nucleophiles.why: Removing a proton from water to give hydroxide increases the electron density around oxygen without adding extra nuclear charge to hold it, making the anion considerably more reactive as a nucleophile (and stronger base).

nucleophiles.q: A good nucleophile must always also be a good leaving group in the reverse reaction.
nucleophiles.why: Good nucleophiles and good leaving groups tend to have opposite characteristics (strong nucleophiles are typically poor leaving groups, like amines or alkoxides, and vice versa, like halides or sulfonates), so this statement is false in general.

nucleophiles.q: Which statement best explains why cyanide (CN-) is an effective nucleophile despite carbon (not nitrogen) usually being the attacking atom?
options: Cyanide has no lone pairs at all
Nitrogen is physically incapable of attacking anything
Cyanide only reacts through its negative formal charge on nitrogen
The carbon end bears significant electron density and is less sterically hindered/more accessible, even though nitrogen is more electronegative
nucleophiles.why: Although formal charge considerations might suggest nitrogen, the carbon atom of cyanide is the kinetically preferred nucleophilic site in most SN2-type reactions due to its orbital characteristics and accessibility.

nucleophiles.q: Increasing solvent polarity in a protic solvent (like going from methanol to water) generally affects the nucleophilicity of a small anion like F- by:
options: Decreasing it further, because stronger solvation more tightly cages the anion's electron density
Increasing it, because polar solvents always activate nucleophiles
Converting the anion into an electrophile
nucleophiles.why: More polar protic solvents solvate small, charge-dense anions even more strongly via hydrogen bonding, further shielding their electron density and reducing their ability to attack an electrophile.

nucleophiles.q: An sp3-hybridized nitrogen lone pair (as in a trialkylamine) is generally a better nucleophile than an sp2-hybridized nitrogen lone pair (as in pyridine), all else equal.
nucleophiles.why: An sp3 lone pair has less s-character than an sp2 lone pair, so it sits farther from the nucleus and is held less tightly, making it somewhat more available to donate; this fits pyridine's sp2 nitrogen being a weaker nucleophile and base than a typical sp3 trialkylamine.

nucleophiles.q: What makes a carbanion (such as an acetylide ion, HC≡C-) an especially strong nucleophile?
options: Carbon is the least electronegative common atom bearing a negative charge, so it holds its extra electron density loosely and readily shares it
Carbanions always carry a formal positive charge
Acetylide ions have no lone pairs
nucleophiles.why: Because carbon is not very electronegative, a negative charge on carbon is poorly stabilized and very reactive, making carbanions some of the strongest nucleophiles (and bases) encountered in introductory organic chemistry.

nucleophiles.q: Which best describes an 'ambident' nucleophile like the cyanide or enolate ion?
options: A nucleophile that cannot react under any conditions
A nucleophile found only in aromatic compounds
A nucleophile with two different atoms that could each act as the site of attack, potentially giving different products
A nucleophile that is also simultaneously an electrophile at all times
nucleophiles.why: Ambident nucleophiles (like enolates, which can react through carbon or oxygen, or cyanide through carbon or nitrogen) have more than one potential reactive atom, and which one reacts can depend on conditions.

nucleophiles.q: In general, across a single row of the periodic table (e.g., comparing C, N, O, F anions of similar charge), nucleophilicity tends to decrease as electronegativity increases left to right.
nucleophiles.why: Moving right across a period, atoms hold electron density more tightly due to increasing electronegativity, so their lone pairs are less available to donate, generally reducing both basicity and nucleophilicity.

nucleophiles.q: Why does steric hindrance near the nucleophilic atom matter more for SN2 reactivity than for simple proton-transfer basicity?
options: Steric hindrance does not matter for either process
Basicity is always more sensitive to sterics than nucleophilicity
Protons are larger than the carbon electrophiles in SN2
SN2 requires close, backside approach to a crowded carbon, which bulky groups physically block, whereas proton transfer to a small, exposed H atom is less sensitive to bulk
nucleophiles.why: Because an SN2 nucleophile must approach a tetrahedral, often crowded carbon from a specific backside angle, bulky substituents on the nucleophile or substrate create steric clashes that aren't nearly as significant when a small, exposed proton is simply being removed by a base.

nucleophiles.q: Azide ion (N3-) is generally considered a good nucleophile in SN2 reactions.
nucleophiles.why: Azide is a small, negatively charged, relatively unhindered nucleophile commonly used in SN2 substitutions to introduce a nitrogen functional group, later reducible to an amine.

nucleophiles.q: Which change would most directly increase a nucleophile's reactivity toward a given alkyl halide substrate, without changing the nucleophile's identity or charge?
options: Switching from a polar protic solvent (like ethanol) to a polar aprotic solvent (like acetone or DMSO)
Switching from a polar aprotic solvent (like acetone) to a polar protic solvent (like ethanol)
Adding more of the alkyl halide substrate
nucleophiles.why: Polar aprotic solvents cannot hydrogen-bond to and cage anionic nucleophiles the way protic solvents do, leaving the nucleophile's electron density more exposed and reactive.

nucleophiles.q: Which of the following pairs correctly identifies the stronger nucleophile based primarily on charge alone, holding the rest of the structure constant?
options: RO- is a weaker nucleophile than ROH
R3N is a weaker nucleophile than R3NH+ cation remaining neutral (trick: the cation has no lone pair left)
RS- is a weaker nucleophile than RSH
RNH2 is a weaker nucleophile than RNH3+
nucleophiles.why: Protonating an amine's lone pair to form an ammonium cation consumes that lone pair entirely, leaving the cation with no nucleophilic site at all, so it is not merely weaker but essentially non-nucleophilic compared to the neutral amine.

nucleophiles.q: A tertiary amine (R3N) generally makes a better nucleophile than a primary amine (RNH2) of similar electronic character because it has more alkyl substituents donating electron density, outweighing any steric penalty in most simple cases used in intro courses.
nucleophiles.why: In typical introductory treatments, additional alkyl groups are electron-donating and increase electron density on nitrogen, generally increasing nucleophilicity/basicity unless steric bulk becomes severe (as with very hindered tertiary amines), which intro courses usually simplify away.

nucleophiles.q: A hydride ion (H-) delivered from a reagent like NaBH4 or LiAlH4 acts as a nucleophile in reducing a carbonyl. What is it attacking?
options: The electrophilic carbon of the carbonyl
nucleophiles.why: Hydride attacks the electron-poor carbonyl carbon, with its electron pair forming a new C–H bond while the C=O pi electrons shift onto oxygen, ultimately giving an alkoxide (and after protonation, an alcohol).

nucleophiles.q: Why is water generally considered a weaker nucleophile than hydroxide, yet water is still used as a nucleophile in many SN1 and addition reactions?
options: Water has no lone pairs available
Water is actually a stronger nucleophile than hydroxide in all cases
Water cannot participate in organic mechanisms at all
Water's oxygen still retains two lone pairs even though it is neutral, so it can still attack electrophiles, just less readily than the negatively charged, more electron-rich hydroxide
nucleophiles.why: Neutral nucleophiles like water are weaker than their anionic counterparts but are still perfectly capable nucleophiles, especially toward highly reactive electrophiles such as carbocations formed in SN1 pathways.

electrophiles.q: An electrophile is best described as:
electrophiles.why: Electrophiles ("electron-loving") are electron-poor and accept an electron pair to form a new bond.

electrophiles.q: A carbonyl carbon (C=O) is a good electrophile because:
options: Carbon is more electronegative than oxygen
Oxygen pulls electron density away, leaving the carbon partially positive
It has a full negative charge
Carbonyl carbons have no bonds available
electrophiles.why: Oxygen’s electronegativity polarizes the C=O bond, giving carbon a δ+ that nucleophiles attack.

electrophiles.q: Which of these is typically NOT a good electrophile?
electrophiles.why: Hydroxide is electron-rich (a nucleophile/base), not electron-poor — it seeks to donate electrons, not accept them.

electrophiles.q: Which of these species is NOT typically a good electrophile?
electrophiles.why: Hydroxide is electron-rich and negatively charged, making it a nucleophile/base rather than an electrophile; electrophiles are electron-poor and seek electron density.

electrophiles.q: An electrophile must always carry a full positive formal charge.
electrophiles.why: Many electrophiles are neutral but electron-poor (such as the carbon of a carbonyl group, or boron in BF3), so a full positive charge is not required, only a deficiency of electron density at the reactive atom.

electrophiles.q: Why is the carbon of an epoxide ring a good electrophile even though the molecule overall is neutral?
options: Epoxide carbons carry a partial positive charge due to the electronegative oxygen, and ring strain makes them especially reactive to nucleophilic attack
Epoxide carbons are always negatively charged
Oxygen in the ring is the electrophilic atom, not carbon
Epoxides have no dipole at all
electrophiles.why: The electronegative oxygen pulls electron density from the ring carbons (inducing partial positive charge), and the strained three-membered ring geometry adds extra driving force for nucleophiles to open the ring at carbon.

electrophiles.q: Rank BF3, CH4, and CH3Cl in order of decreasing electrophilicity at their central/relevant carbon or boron atom.
electrophiles.why: BF3's boron has an empty p orbital and no octet, making it a very strong electrophile (Lewis acid); CH3Cl's carbon is moderately electrophilic due to the polar C–Cl bond; CH4 has no polarized bonds and is essentially non-electrophilic.

electrophiles.q: A carbonyl carbon (C=O) is a good electrophile primarily because:
options: Carbon is more electronegative than oxygen
The carbonyl has no polarity at all
Oxygen's electronegativity pulls electron density away from carbon, leaving it partially positive (δ+) and the pi bond is easily attacked
Oxygen donates extra electrons to carbon
electrophiles.why: Oxygen's high electronegativity polarizes the C=O bond, leaving carbon electron-deficient (δ+) and well-suited to accept an incoming nucleophile's electron pair, with the pi electrons shifting onto oxygen.

electrophiles.q: Adding an electron-withdrawing group (such as a second carbonyl or a halogen) near a carbonyl carbon generally makes that carbonyl carbon:
options: Less electrophilic, because electron-withdrawing groups donate electrons
More electrophilic, because electron-withdrawing groups pull additional electron density away from the already positive carbon
electrophiles.why: Electron-withdrawing groups intensify the positive character at the carbonyl carbon by further depleting its electron density, which is why acid chlorides and anhydrides are more electrophilic (more reactive to nucleophiles) than simple ketones or esters.

electrophiles.q: A carbocation is generally considered one of the strongest electrophiles in organic chemistry because it has an empty orbital and carries a full positive charge.
electrophiles.why: Carbocations are highly electron-deficient, with an empty p orbital and a full positive charge on carbon, making them extremely reactive toward any available nucleophile or pi bond.

electrophiles.q: Why is the carbon attached to a leaving group in an alkyl halide (e.g., the carbon in CH3–Br) considered electrophilic even though it is tetravalent and neutral?
options: Bromine's greater electronegativity polarizes the C–Br bond, giving carbon a partial positive charge that a nucleophile can attack as the bond breaks
The hydrogens on that carbon make it electrophilic
Bromine is more electron-poor than carbon
Alkyl halides are not electrophilic at all
electrophiles.why: The polar C–Br bond leaves carbon partially positive (δ+), and because Br- can leave as a stable anion, a nucleophile can attack that carbon while the C–Br bond breaks, as in SN1/SN2 reactions.

electrophiles.q: Which halogen-containing species acts as the electrophile when Br2 reacts with an alkene in a bromination addition reaction?
options: The alkene is the electrophile in this reaction
Br2 itself, polarized by the approaching electron-rich alkene into a bromonium-forming electrophile
electrophiles.why: As the alkene's pi electrons approach Br2, they induce a dipole in the Br–Br bond, making one bromine electrophilic; the alkene attacks it, displacing bromide and forming a bromonium ion intermediate.

electrophiles.q: A Lewis acid such as AlCl3 is classified as an electrophile because it:
options: Has a complete octet and no room to accept electrons
Has an incomplete octet (empty orbital) on aluminum and readily accepts an electron pair from a Lewis base
electrophiles.why: Aluminum in AlCl3 has only six electrons around it (no octet), giving it a strongly electron-accepting empty orbital, which is the hallmark of a Lewis acid/electrophile used to activate other electrophiles in reactions like Friedel-Crafts.

electrophiles.q: Protonation of an alcohol by a strong acid converts the alcohol's oxygen region into a better leaving group, but does this make the adjacent carbon a better or worse electrophile?
options: Worse electrophile, because protonation adds more electron density
No change in electrophilicity at all
The carbon becomes a nucleophile instead
Better electrophile, because the now-positively-charged oxygen further withdraws electron density from the attached carbon
electrophiles.why: Protonating the oxygen gives it a formal positive charge, which pulls even more electron density away from the attached carbon through the sigma bond, increasing that carbon's electrophilicity and making it far more reactive to nucleophilic attack or departure as a leaving group.

electrophiles.q: Which of the following carbonyl-containing compounds has the most electrophilic carbonyl carbon, making it the most reactive toward nucleophiles?
electrophiles.why: Chlorine is a strong electron-withdrawing group and a poor electron donor by resonance, leaving the acid chloride's carbonyl carbon the most electron-poor and electrophilic; amides are the least electrophilic because nitrogen donates its lone pair into the carbonyl most effectively, reducing electrophilicity.

electrophiles.q: A carboxylate ion (RCOO-) is generally a poor electrophile at its carbonyl carbon.
electrophiles.why: The negative charge and resonance delocalization in a carboxylate actually increase electron density at the carbonyl carbon (compared to a neutral ester or acid), making it a very poor electrophile and resistant to nucleophilic attack.

electrophiles.q: Why can a simple, unactivated alkane like ethane not act as an electrophile under ordinary conditions?
options: It has too many electrons overall
Its C–C and C–H bonds are nonpolar (similar electronegativities) and there is no electron-deficient atom or accessible empty orbital for a nucleophile to attack
Alkanes react instantly with every nucleophile
electrophiles.why: Without a polarized bond, an empty orbital, or a good leaving group, there is no electron-poor site available, so simple alkanes are essentially unreactive toward nucleophiles under standard conditions.

electrophiles.q: In an SN1 mechanism, which species formed as an intermediate is the actual electrophile attacked by the incoming nucleophile?
options: The original alkyl halide before ionization
The leaving group itself after it departs
The carbocation intermediate formed after the leaving group departs
electrophiles.why: Once the leaving group departs in the first (rate-determining) step, a planar carbocation intermediate forms with an empty p orbital, and this highly electrophilic cation is what the nucleophile subsequently attacks.

electrophiles.q: An aldehyde's carbonyl carbon is generally more electrophilic than a ketone's carbonyl carbon because:
options: Aldehydes have an extra electron-withdrawing oxygen
Ketones have no carbonyl carbon at all

A ketone has two alkyl groups donating electron density (weakly) and providing more steric shielding, while an aldehyde has only one alkyl group (or none) and a hydrogen, leaving its carbonyl carbon more exposed and electron-poor
electrophiles.why: Alkyl groups are weakly electron-donating and bulky; a ketone has two of them stabilizing and shielding the carbonyl carbon, while an aldehyde's single alkyl group (plus a small hydrogen) leaves it more electrophilic and more accessible to nucleophiles.

electrophiles.q: An aromatic ring undergoing electrophilic aromatic substitution reacts with an electrophile such as Br+ generated from Br2 and a Lewis acid catalyst.
electrophiles.why: In electrophilic aromatic substitution, a Lewis acid (like FeBr3) helps generate a highly electrophilic species (such as Br+) that the electron-rich aromatic ring then attacks as the nucleophile.

electrophiles.q: Which statement correctly relates electrophile strength to reaction rate with a given nucleophile?
options: Stronger electrophiles (more electron-poor, more accessible) generally react faster with a given nucleophile, all else equal
Stronger electrophiles generally react more slowly because they are more stable
Electrophile strength has no bearing on reaction rate
Only nucleophile strength affects reaction rate, never electrophile strength
electrophiles.why: Just as nucleophile strength affects rate, a more electron-deficient and accessible electrophile is attacked more readily and rapidly by a given nucleophile, since there is a greater driving force for electron transfer.

electrophiles.q: A proton (H+) is considered the simplest electrophile because it has:
options: A full valence shell with extra electrons to share
No electrons at all and a strong positive charge, making it eager to accept any available electron pair
electrophiles.why: A bare proton has zero electrons and a full positive charge, making it an extremely strong and simple electrophile that reacts instantly with essentially any available lone pair or pi bond.

electrophiles.q: Why does conjugation of a carbonyl with an adjacent C=C double bond (as in an enone, an alpha,beta-unsaturated ketone) create a second electrophilic site at the beta carbon?
options: Conjugation has no effect on electrophilicity anywhere in the molecule
The beta carbon becomes negatively charged instead
Resonance delocalization places partial positive character on the beta carbon by shifting the pi electrons toward oxygen through the conjugated system
Only the carbonyl carbon is ever electrophilic in an enone
electrophiles.why: A resonance structure of an enone shows the C=C pi electrons shifting all the way to the very electronegative oxygen, leaving a positive charge on the beta carbon; this explains why nucleophiles can add either directly to the carbonyl carbon or to this more remote beta carbon (conjugate addition).

electrophiles.q: Which of the following best explains why CO2 (carbon dioxide) reacts readily as an electrophile with strong nucleophiles like Grignard reagents?
options: CO2's oxygen atoms are the electrophilic sites, not carbon
CO2 cannot react with any nucleophile
CO2's carbon is flanked by two electronegative oxygens, making it highly electron-poor and susceptible to nucleophilic attack despite being a small, simple molecule
electrophiles.why: The two electronegative oxygens withdraw significant electron density from the central carbon, making it quite electrophilic; Grignard reagents readily attack this carbon to eventually form a carboxylic acid after workup.

electrophiles.q: Increasing the positive character of a Lewis acid's central atom (for example, comparing BF3 to BH3) tends to increase its strength as an electrophile when the substituents are strongly electron-withdrawing.
electrophiles.why: Fluorines are highly electronegative and can withdraw electron density (inductively) even while donating some back by resonance in certain cases, but generally a boron center surrounded by electron-withdrawing groups maintains strong electrophilic (Lewis acidic) character, accepting electron pairs readily.

electrophiles.q: A terminal alkyne's acidic proton can be removed by a strong base. In this acid-base reaction, which species is acting as the electrophile?
options: The acidic hydrogen atom on the terminal alkyne carbon
electrophiles.why: The acidic C–H proton is the electrophilic site being attacked by the base's lone pair; the carbon framework itself is not what is directly attacked in this proton-transfer step.

electrophiles.q: What makes sulfonate esters (like tosylates, R-OTs) useful electrophiles in substitution reactions, much like alkyl halides?
options: Sulfonates make carbon into a nucleophile
The carbon attached to the sulfonate oxygen is electron-poor due to the electronegative oxygen, and the sulfonate anion is an excellent, stable leaving group once the bond breaks
Sulfonate esters have no leaving group at all
Sulfur is the site that nucleophiles attack, not carbon
electrophiles.why: Like halides, the oxygen in a sulfonate ester polarizes the attached carbon (making it electrophilic), and the resulting sulfonate anion is exceptionally stable (weak base) due to extensive resonance and charge delocalization, making it depart easily as a leaving group.

electrophiles.q: In general, increasing the number of electron-donating alkyl substituents directly on an electrophilic carbon tends to:
options: Increase its electrophilicity by adding more positive character
Have absolutely no effect on electrophilicity under any circumstances
Decrease its electrophilicity somewhat, since alkyl groups donate electron density and add steric bulk that shields the site
Convert the carbon into a full nucleophile
electrophiles.why: Alkyl groups are weak electron donors (by induction/hyperconjugation) and also physically block approach, so more substitution at a potentially electrophilic carbon generally reduces how strongly and how accessibly electrophilic it is (this is part of why more substituted carbonyls are less reactive toward nucleophiles).

electrophiles.q: A tertiary carbocation is generally a better (more stabilized, and therefore more readily formed, though still highly electrophilic) intermediate than a primary carbocation.
electrophiles.why: Alkyl groups stabilize an adjacent positive charge through hyperconjugation and induction, so tertiary carbocations are more stable and form more readily than primary ones, even though all carbocations remain strong electrophiles once formed.

electrophiles.q: Which best explains why methyl iodide (CH3I) is often used as a model electrophile in SN2 reactions despite iodine being a relatively weak inductive electron-withdrawer compared to fluorine?
options: Iodine makes the carbon extremely electron-rich
Methyl iodide has no electrophilic carbon
Fluorine is always a better leaving group than iodine
The C–I bond is weak and long, and iodide is an excellent, highly polarizable leaving group, so even modest electrophilicity at carbon is enough to react quickly once a nucleophile attacks
electrophiles.why: Even though the C–I bond is only modestly polarized, the weak, long C–I bond breaks easily and iodide is a very stable, weakly basic leaving group, so the overall reaction is fast even if carbon itself is not the most electron-poor among the halomethanes.

leaving-groups.q: A good leaving group is generally one that is:
options: Stable once it departs with the electron pair (weak base)
Unable to hold a negative charge
leaving-groups.why: Good leaving groups are stable as the departed anion/molecule — i.e., weak bases, since weak bases are comfortable holding the extra electron density.

leaving-groups.q: Which of these is typically the best leaving group?
leaving-groups.why: Iodide is a large, very weak base — very stable once it leaves — making it an excellent leaving group, unlike OH⁻, NH₂⁻, or CH₃⁻ which are strong bases.

leaving-groups.q: Why is F⁻ generally a poor leaving group compared to the other halides?
options: It is the strongest base among the halides, making it less stable once departed
leaving-groups.why: Among the halide ions, F⁻ is the strongest base (least electronegative-stabilized charge relative to its small size/high charge density), so it’s the worst leaving group of the group.

leaving-groups.q: A good leaving group should be the conjugate base of a:
leaving-groups.why: Good leaving groups are stable, weak bases, which are exactly the conjugate bases of strong acids (like HI, HBr, or TsOH); weak bases hold their extra electron pair loosely and leave readily.

leaving-groups.q: Hydroxide (OH-) is generally an excellent leaving group in substitution reactions on alcohols without any activation.
leaving-groups.why: Hydroxide is a strong base (conjugate base of water, a weak acid), so it is a poor leaving group; alcohols typically need to be protonated (forming water as the leaving group) or converted to a sulfonate/halide before substitution proceeds well.

leaving-groups.q: Rank Cl-, Br-, and I- in order of decreasing ability to act as a leaving group.
options: All three are identical leaving groups
leaving-groups.why: Leaving group ability tracks with anion stability (weak basicity); I- is the weakest base of the three halides and the most stable once it leaves, making it the best leaving group, followed by Br- then Cl-.

leaving-groups.q: Why is F- generally a poor leaving group compared to the other halides even though fluorine is the most electronegative halogen?
options: Fluorine cannot form a stable anion
Fluorine's small size and high electronegativity make it hold its negative charge very tightly, making it a comparatively strong base that resists leaving
The C–F bond is the weakest of all the C–halogen bonds
Fluoride is actually the best leaving group of the halides
leaving-groups.why: F- is a much stronger base than the other halide ions because its small size concentrates negative charge, making the C–F bond strong and fluoride reluctant to depart with the electron pair, unlike the larger, more stable, weaker-base halide ions.

leaving-groups.q: A tosylate group (OTs-, the conjugate base of a strong sulfonic acid) is considered an excellent leaving group for the same general reason that halides are, namely:
options: It is a strong base that holds electrons tightly
It has no negative charge when it leaves
It is a very weak, highly resonance-stabilized base that readily accommodates the departing negative charge
It forms only under basic conditions
leaving-groups.why: The negative charge on a sulfonate leaving group is delocalized over multiple oxygens by resonance (and stabilized further by the electron-withdrawing sulfonyl group), making it a very weak base and thus an excellent, stable leaving group.

leaving-groups.q: Amide ion (NH2-) is generally considered one of the worst common leaving groups in organic chemistry.
leaving-groups.why: NH2- is the conjugate base of ammonia, an extremely weak acid, making amide ion an extremely strong base that holds on tightly to its electrons and essentially never leaves under normal conditions.

leaving-groups.q: Why does protonating the oxygen of an alcohol (forming R-OH2+) convert a poor leaving group into a good one?
options: Protonation removes the leaving group entirely
Protonation has no effect on leaving group ability
Protonation makes oxygen a better nucleophile instead
Protonation converts the leaving group from hydroxide (strong base) to neutral water (weak base, conjugate base of the strong acid H3O+), which departs far more readily
leaving-groups.why: Once protonated, the group that leaves is neutral water rather than negatively charged hydroxide; water is a much weaker base (conjugate base of the strong acid H3O+) and leaves far more easily, which is why acid catalysis activates alcohols for substitution/elimination.

leaving-groups.q: Which of the following is generally NOT a good leaving group under typical SN1/SN2 conditions?
leaving-groups.why: A carbanion like CH3- is an extraordinarily strong base (conjugate base of methane, an exceedingly weak acid) and essentially never acts as a leaving group under normal conditions, unlike halides or neutral water.

leaving-groups.q: Resonance stabilization of the departing anion (as in a sulfonate or carboxylate leaving group) generally makes that group a better leaving group.
leaving-groups.why: Delocalizing the negative charge over several atoms lowers the energy of the anion, making it more stable (a weaker base) and thus more willing to depart, which is exactly why sulfonate esters are popular synthetic leaving groups.

leaving-groups.q: In the reaction of an epoxide with a nucleophile under basic conditions, what effectively serves as the leaving group when the ring opens?
options: The ring oxygen, which becomes an alkoxide as the strained C–O bond breaks
leaving-groups.why: As a nucleophile attacks a ring carbon, the strained C–O bond breaks and the oxygen (now bearing the electron pair) becomes an alkoxide leaving group still attached elsewhere in the molecule, relieving ring strain.

leaving-groups.q: Why is it generally true that weaker bases make better leaving groups?
options: Weak bases are more electronegative than strong bases in every case
Weak bases always carry a positive charge

A weak base is, by definition, a species that is comfortable holding extra negative charge/electron density, so it departs from a bond more readily without needing to hold onto the bonding electrons as tightly
There is no real relationship between base strength and leaving group ability
leaving-groups.why: Base strength measures how strongly a species wants to grab and hold a proton (or, analogously, electron density); weak bases are inherently stable on their own and 'happy' to leave with the bonding electron pair, which is the core reason leaving group ability and base strength are inversely related.

leaving-groups.q: Which species would you predict to be a better leaving group: the conjugate base of acetic acid (CH3COO-, pKa of acid ≈ 4.8) or the conjugate base of ethanol (CH3CH2O-, pKa of acid ≈ 16)?
options: Ethoxide, because alcohols are weaker acids
They are equally good leaving groups
Neither can ever act as a leaving group
Acetate, because it is the conjugate base of the stronger acid and is therefore a weaker, more stable base
leaving-groups.why: Acetic acid (pKa ≈ 4.8) is a much stronger acid than ethanol (pKa ≈ 16), meaning acetate is a much weaker base than ethoxide and therefore a considerably better leaving group.

leaving-groups.q: A carbocation can be thought of as having 'lost' a leaving group from the original substrate. Which best describes the leaving group's role right before departure?
options: It must be able to stabilize the negative charge (or simply depart as a relatively neutral/stable species) that results from taking the bonding electron pair with it
It must remain a strong nucleophile even as it departs
It must become more reactive after leaving
It plays no role in determining the reaction rate
leaving-groups.why: Because the leaving group departs with the bonding electrons, its ability to stabilize that extra electron density (i.e., be a weak, stable base) directly controls how readily ionization occurs and therefore the rate of SN1/E1 reactions.

leaving-groups.q: Converting an alcohol's -OH into a mesylate (OMs) or tosylate (OTs) group before a substitution reaction is a common strategy because:
options: It makes the oxygen a stronger base
It converts a poor leaving group (hydroxide) into an excellent one (a resonance-stabilized sulfonate) without needing strongly acidic conditions
Mesylates and tosylates are never good leaving groups
It removes the need for any leaving group at all
leaving-groups.why: Sulfonate esters are prepared under mild, non-acidic conditions and then provide a highly stabilized, weak-base leaving group, giving chemists a practical alternative to strongly acidic activation of alcohols.

leaving-groups.q: In an E1 elimination mechanism, the leaving group departs in the same step as the base removing a proton.
leaving-groups.why: E1 is a two-step (stepwise) mechanism: the leaving group departs first to form a carbocation intermediate, and only afterward does a base remove a proton to form the alkene; this differs from E2, where both events are concerted.

leaving-groups.q: Which leaving group would most likely make an SN2 reaction proceed fastest, all else being equal: Cl-, Br-, or a tosylate (OTs-)?
options: Cl-, because it is the smallest
Br-, because halides are always best
Tosylate, because its charge is extensively resonance-delocalized, making it an exceptionally weak, stable base
All three give identical reaction rates
leaving-groups.why: Tosylate's negative charge is spread over three oxygens and stabilized further by the adjacent aromatic sulfonyl group, making it one of the best common leaving groups, generally outperforming simple halides.

leaving-groups.q: An amine (NH2R) attached directly to a carbon is typically a poor leaving group unless it is first protonated to become a neutral amine leaving as RNH2 from a positively charged ammonium-like carbon, or otherwise activated.
leaving-groups.why: A simple amide anion (R-NH-) would be much too strong a base to leave; however, once protonated so the leaving species is neutral (or the nitrogen already bears a positive charge, as in some quaternary ammonium salts), the departing amine becomes weak-base-like and feasible as a leaving group.

leaving-groups.q: Why does pKa of the leaving group's conjugate acid serve as a useful predictor of leaving group ability?
options: Higher pKa always means a better leaving group
pKa has no relationship to leaving group ability
pKa only matters for nucleophiles, not leaving groups
Lower pKa (stronger conjugate acid) generally corresponds to a weaker conjugate base, meaning the leaving group is more stable and leaves more easily
leaving-groups.why: Since leaving groups are conjugate bases, the pKa of their conjugate acid directly reflects base strength: a low pKa (strong acid) means a weak, stable conjugate base, and therefore a good leaving group.

leaving-groups.q: Which of these would you predict to be the best leaving group based on its conjugate acid's strength: leaving group X whose conjugate acid has pKa 9, or leaving group Y whose conjugate acid has pKa -7?
options: Leaving group Y, because its conjugate acid is a much stronger acid, meaning Y is a much weaker, more stable base and better leaving group
Leaving group X, because higher pKa means a better leaving group
Both are equally good leaving groups regardless of pKa
pKa values cannot be used to compare leaving groups
leaving-groups.why: A conjugate acid pKa of -7 corresponds to an extremely strong acid (such as HI), meaning its conjugate base is extremely weak and stable — exactly the profile of an excellent leaving group, far better than one with a conjugate acid pKa of 9.

leaving-groups.q: Cyanide ion (CN-) is generally a poor leaving group.
leaving-groups.why: HCN is only a moderately weak acid (pKa around 9), making cyanide a fairly strong base relative to halides or sulfonates, so it does not readily depart as a leaving group under typical substitution conditions.

leaving-groups.q: In a Grignard or organolithium reagent, the carbon bonded to the metal behaves as a strong nucleophile/base. If this carbon were instead asked to act as a leaving group, what would you predict?
options: It would be an excellent leaving group, since strong bases always make excellent leaving groups too

It would be an extremely poor leaving group, since the same property that makes it a strong base/nucleophile (holding electron density tightly and reactively) makes it resistant to departing with that electron pair
Leaving group ability is unrelated to nucleophilicity or basicity in this case
