Carbanions cannot be discussed in terms of leaving group ability at all
leaving-groups.why: Because strong bases/nucleophiles and good leaving groups are generally opposite ends of the same stability spectrum, a reactive carbanion (strong base) is a very poor leaving group — it simply does not want to depart and take the electron pair in an already-stable low-energy form elsewhere.

leaving-groups.q: Which best explains why water (H2O) can act as a leaving group in acid-catalyzed reactions but hydroxide (OH-) generally cannot under the same mild acidic conditions?
options: Water and hydroxide are equally good leaving groups always
Hydroxide has no electron pairs to take with it
Neutral water is the conjugate base of the strong acid H3O+ and is a weak base, whereas hydroxide is the conjugate base of the much weaker acid water, making it a stronger base that resists leaving
Water cannot leave under any circumstances
leaving-groups.why: Protonation shifts the leaving species from hydroxide (conjugate base of water, pKa ≈ 15.7, a fairly strong base) to water itself (conjugate base of H3O+, pKa ≈ -1.7, a very weak base), dramatically improving its willingness to leave.

leaving-groups.q: A leaving group's steric bulk (size) plays as large a role in determining its leaving group ability as its base strength does.
leaving-groups.why: Leaving group ability is governed overwhelmingly by stability of the resulting anion (base strength/pKa of the conjugate acid), not primarily by steric bulk; steric effects matter more for the nucleophile's approach than for how readily a group departs.

leaving-groups.q: Phosphate groups (such as those in ATP) are biologically important leaving groups. Why are they effective leaving groups despite carrying a full negative charge?
options: Phosphate has no resonance stabilization at all
Phosphate groups are actually poor leaving groups in every biological context
Phosphate always leaves as a neutral, uncharged species
The negative charge on a departing phosphate group is delocalized over multiple oxygens by resonance, similar to a sulfonate, stabilizing it as a weak base
leaving-groups.why: Like sulfonates and carboxylates, phosphate leaving groups spread their negative charge over several oxygen atoms via resonance, lowering their basicity and making them effective leaving groups despite the formal negative charge, which is central to many biochemical substitution reactions.

leaving-groups.q: Which of the following best ranks typical leaving group ability from best to worst: I-, OH-, OTs-?
leaving-groups.why: Tosylate and iodide are both excellent, weak-base leaving groups (conjugate bases of strong acids), while hydroxide is a comparatively strong base and a poor leaving group, so the order is OTs- > I- >> OH-.

leaving-groups.q: A trifluoromethanesulfonate group (triflate, OTf-) is considered one of the best leaving groups known, even better than tosylate, largely because of the strongly electron-withdrawing fluorines.
leaving-groups.why: The three highly electronegative fluorine atoms further withdraw electron density and help delocalize/stabilize the negative charge on the departing sulfonate oxygen, making triflate an exceptionally weak base and outstanding leaving group, even better than a simple tosylate.

leaving-groups.q: If a leaving group is a poor one (a strong base) in a proposed SN1 mechanism, what is the most likely consequence for the reaction?
options: The reaction proceeds at the same rate regardless of leaving group quality
Ionization (loss of the leaving group) becomes the slow, rate-limiting step, and the overall reaction is very slow or does not proceed without some form of activation
The reaction mechanism switches automatically to E2
leaving-groups.why: Since SN1 rate depends on how readily the substrate ionizes, a poor leaving group (strong base, high-energy anion) makes that ionization step slow or unfavorable, often requiring the substrate to be activated first (e.g., protonation or conversion to a sulfonate) before substitution can proceed.

electron-rich-poor.q: An electron-rich atom in a mechanism tends to act as a(n):
electron-rich-poor.why: Electron-rich atoms have extra electron density to donate, making them nucleophilic.

electron-rich-poor.q: Why is the carbon of C=O electron-poor while the oxygen is electron-rich?
options: Oxygen’s higher electronegativity pulls shared electron density toward itself
There is no difference — they’re equal
electron-rich-poor.why: The electronegativity difference polarizes the pi bond, making O δ− (electron-rich) and C δ+ (electron-poor).

electron-rich-poor.q: In a C–Mg bond (as in a Grignard reagent), which atom is electron-rich?
electron-rich-poor.why: Carbon is more electronegative than magnesium, so the bonding electrons sit closer to carbon, making it electron-rich (and strongly nucleophilic/basic).

electron-rich-poor.q: An electron-poor atom in a mechanism generally acts as a(n):
electron-rich-poor.why: Electron-poor atoms lack sufficient electron density and therefore seek it out from an electron-rich partner, which is exactly the defining behavior of an electrophile.

electron-rich-poor.q: A carbon bonded directly to a highly electronegative atom like oxygen, nitrogen, or a halogen is generally electron-poor relative to a carbon bonded only to other carbons and hydrogens.
electron-rich-poor.why: Electronegative substituents pull electron density away from the attached carbon through the polar sigma bond (an inductive effect), leaving that carbon partially positive (δ+) relative to one surrounded only by similarly electronegative C and H.

electron-rich-poor.q: In a C–Mg bond (as in a Grignard reagent, R–MgBr), which atom is electron-rich?
options: Carbon, because magnesium is significantly less electronegative than carbon
Magnesium, because metals are always electron-poor
Bromine, because halogens are always electron-rich
electron-rich-poor.why: Magnesium is a much less electronegative (more electropositive) element than carbon, so the bonding electrons sit closer to carbon, making the carbon electron-rich (carbanion-like) and strongly nucleophilic/basic.

electron-rich-poor.q: In an enolate, the negative charge is delocalized between the alpha carbon and the carbonyl oxygen. Which site is more electron-rich in the major resonance contributor?
options: The alpha carbon, since carbon always holds more electron density than oxygen
The oxygen, since it is more electronegative and better able to stabilize the negative charge
Both are equally electron-rich with no distinction possible
Neither site carries any electron density
electron-rich-poor.why: The resonance structure placing the negative charge on oxygen is the larger contributor to the hybrid, since oxygen is far better suited to stabilize a negative charge than carbon is — making the oxygen the more electron-rich site overall.

electron-rich-poor.q: An aromatic ring substituted with an electron-donating group, such as an amine or alkoxy group, becomes more electron-rich overall, making it more reactive toward electrophiles.
electron-rich-poor.why: Electron-donating substituents push additional electron density into the aromatic ring (by resonance and/or induction), increasing the ring's overall nucleophilicity and accelerating electrophilic aromatic substitution.

electron-rich-poor.q: Which atom in a hydrogen halide (H–X, such as H–Cl) is electron-poor and thus reacts as the acidic proton source?
options: Neither atom has any partial charge
electron-rich-poor.why: The halogen is more electronegative than hydrogen, pulling bonding electron density toward itself and leaving hydrogen partially positive (δ+), which is why H–X compounds act as proton (acid) sources.

electron-rich-poor.q: A nitro group (-NO2) attached to an aromatic ring makes the ring more electron-rich due to strong electron donation by resonance.
electron-rich-poor.why: The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing (both by induction and resonance, since nitrogen is positively charged with electronegative oxygens), making an attached ring more electron-poor, not electron-rich.

electron-rich-poor.q: Why does an alkene substituted with several alkyl groups (a more substituted alkene) tend to be more electron-rich and thus a better nucleophile than a less substituted one?
options: Alkyl groups withdraw electron density from the pi bond through induction
Substitution pattern has no effect on an alkene's electron density
More substituted alkenes always have fewer electrons overall
Alkyl groups donate electron density into the pi system via hyperconjugation and induction, increasing electron density at the double bond
electron-rich-poor.why: Alkyl groups are weak electron donors (through hyperconjugation with adjacent C–H/C–C bonds and simple induction), so each additional alkyl substituent on a double bond increases the electron density of the pi bond, making the alkene a better nucleophile.

electron-rich-poor.q: Comparing a C–F bond to a C–I bond, which carbon is more electron-poor (more δ+)?
options: The carbon bonded to fluorine, because fluorine is far more electronegative and polarizes the bond more strongly
The carbon bonded to iodine, because iodine is larger
Both carbons have identical electron density
electron-rich-poor.why: Fluorine's very high electronegativity creates a strongly polarized C–F bond, pulling substantial electron density away from carbon, more so than the much less electronegative iodine does in a C–I bond, even though the C–I bond is actually weaker and breaks more easily.

electron-rich-poor.q: A carbanion is an example of an electron-rich carbon species, while a carbocation is an example of an electron-poor carbon species.
electron-rich-poor.why: A carbanion carries a full negative charge and a lone pair (electron-rich, nucleophilic), while a carbocation has an empty orbital and a full positive charge (electron-poor, electrophilic) — they sit at opposite ends of the electron-density spectrum.

electron-rich-poor.q: In an enol (the tautomer of a ketone with a C=C–OH arrangement), which carbon is electron-rich and acts as the nucleophilic site?
options: The carbon bonded directly to oxygen
The carbon at the far end of the double bond, away from oxygen (the alpha carbon)
Neither carbon has extra electron density
The oxygen atom itself is the only reactive site
electron-rich-poor.why: A resonance structure of the enol places a lone pair from oxygen into the pi system, shifting electron density to the terminal (alpha) carbon and giving it significant nucleophilic, electron-rich character, which is why enols react with electrophiles at that carbon.

electron-rich-poor.q: Why is the nitrogen of an amide less electron-rich (less basic/nucleophilic) than the nitrogen of a simple amine?
options: Amide nitrogen has no lone pair at all
Amide nitrogen is bonded to more hydrogens than amine nitrogen
The amide nitrogen's lone pair is delocalized by resonance into the adjacent carbonyl, reducing the electron density actually available on nitrogen itself
There is no difference between amide and amine nitrogen electron density
electron-rich-poor.why: Conjugation of the nitrogen lone pair with the carbonyl pi system pulls electron density away from nitrogen toward the electronegative oxygen, leaving the amide nitrogen considerably less electron-rich than an isolated amine nitrogen.

electron-rich-poor.q: Which of these atoms, all found within a molecule of acetonitrile (CH3-C≡N), is the most electron-rich and would be expected to act as a nucleophile/base site?
options: All atoms have identical electron density
The nitrogen atom, due to its lone pair
electron-rich-poor.why: The nitrogen of a nitrile carries a lone pair in an sp orbital and, despite nitrogen's electronegativity pulling some density toward it within the triple bond, this lone pair is the most electron-rich, available site for interacting with electrophiles or protons.

electron-rich-poor.q: A carbon directly bonded to a strongly electron-withdrawing group such as a trifluoromethyl group (CF3) is generally more electron-poor than the same carbon bonded only to hydrogens.
electron-rich-poor.why: The three highly electronegative fluorines in a CF3 group inductively withdraw electron density through the sigma bond network, making the attached carbon significantly more electron-poor (more δ+) than if it were bonded to hydrogens instead.

electron-rich-poor.q: Between the carbon and the boron atom in a carbon-boron bond (as found in certain organoborane reagents), which atom is electron-rich?
options: Carbon, because boron is less electronegative than carbon
Boron, because it is a metalloid
Neither atom has partial charge in a C–B bond
electron-rich-poor.why: Boron's electronegativity is lower than carbon's, so the shared electrons in a C–B bond sit closer to carbon, making that carbon somewhat electron-rich, similar to the polarization seen in Grignard C–Mg bonds though less pronounced.

electron-rich-poor.q: Inductive electron withdrawal through sigma bonds (as from a nearby halogen) typically has its strongest effect on the immediately adjacent atom and weakens rapidly as you move further away through the chain.
electron-rich-poor.why: Inductive effects act through sigma bonds and fall off quickly with distance, so a halogen's electron-withdrawing influence is strongest on the carbon it's directly attached to and becomes much weaker two or three carbons away.

electron-rich-poor.q: Why does protonation of a carbonyl oxygen (under acid catalysis) make the attached carbonyl carbon even more electron-poor than it already was?
options: Protonation adds extra electron density to the whole system
The newly formed positive charge on oxygen further pulls electron density away from carbon through the sigma and pi framework, intensifying carbon's existing partial positive character
Protonation occurs on carbon, not oxygen, in this mechanism
Protonation has no effect on the carbon's electron density
electron-rich-poor.why: Adding a full positive charge directly onto the already electronegative oxygen dramatically increases its pull on the shared electrons, making the attached carbon even more electron-deficient and far more reactive to nucleophilic attack.

electron-rich-poor.q: Which species is more electron-rich at its reactive carbon: a simple alkene (C=C) or an enolate ion (C=C–O-)?
options: The simple alkene, because it has fewer atoms
The enolate, because the negative oxygen donates additional electron density into the pi system by resonance, making the alpha carbon even more electron-rich than in a neutral alkene
Enolates have no electron density on carbon at all
electron-rich-poor.why: The negatively charged oxygen of an enolate strongly donates its extra electron density through resonance into the adjacent carbon, making the enolate's nucleophilic carbon considerably more electron-rich (and thus more reactive) than a simple, unactivated alkene carbon.

electron-rich-poor.q: A sulfur atom in a thiol (R-SH) is generally considered more electron-rich and nucleophilic than the oxygen in a comparable alcohol (R-OH), even though oxygen is more electronegative.
electron-rich-poor.why: Although oxygen holds its own electrons more tightly (higher electronegativity, stronger base), sulfur's larger, more polarizable, more loosely held electron cloud makes it more willing to donate electron density in bond-forming reactions, so it behaves as more nucleophilic/electron-rich in a reactivity sense.

electron-rich-poor.q: In the molecule CH3-CH2-Cl, which carbon carries the greater partial positive charge (is more electron-poor)?
options: The terminal CH3 carbon, farther from chlorine
Both carbons carry identical partial charge
Neither carbon has any partial charge
The CH2 carbon directly bonded to chlorine
electron-rich-poor.why: The carbon directly bonded to the electronegative chlorine experiences the strongest inductive pull of electron density, making it the most electron-poor carbon in the molecule; the effect diminishes sharply at the next carbon over.

electron-rich-poor.q: Why is the oxygen of a carboxylic acid's hydroxyl group (the O–H oxygen, not the carbonyl oxygen) considered relatively electron-poor compared to the oxygen of a simple alcohol?
options: Its lone pairs are partially delocalized by resonance into the adjacent electron-withdrawing carbonyl group, reducing the electron density that remains localized on that oxygen
It is bonded to more hydrogens than an alcohol oxygen
Carboxylic acid oxygens have no lone pairs
There is no difference between the two oxygens
electron-rich-poor.why: One of the hydroxyl oxygen's lone pairs conjugates with the carbonyl pi system, pulling electron density toward the carbonyl oxygen; this depletion of electron density on the OH oxygen is part of why the O–H bond is more acidic (and the oxygen less basic) than in a simple alcohol.

electron-rich-poor.q: A carbon at the end of a polarized C≡N (nitrile) triple bond is generally electron-poor and can act as an electrophile toward strong nucleophiles like Grignard reagents.
electron-rich-poor.why: Nitrogen's higher electronegativity polarizes the triple bond, leaving the nitrile carbon partially positive and electrophilic, which is why Grignard and organolithium reagents can add to nitriles to eventually form ketones after hydrolysis.

electron-rich-poor.q: Which best explains why the alpha carbon of an alkyl halide (directly bonded to the halogen) is electron-poor, yet the beta carbon (one carbon further away) shows only a weak inductive effect?
options: The beta carbon is always more electron-poor than the alpha carbon

Inductive withdrawal operates through sigma bonds and weakens substantially with each additional bond traversed, so its effect is strong on the alpha carbon but much weaker by the time it reaches the beta carbon
Halogens only affect carbons they are not bonded to
Inductive effects have no distance dependence
electron-rich-poor.why: Inductive (sigma-bond) electron withdrawal falls off rapidly with each bond, so while the alpha carbon feels the halogen's pull strongly, the beta carbon experiences only a faint residual effect.

electron-rich-poor.q: Why can an enamine's beta carbon (the carbon two atoms from nitrogen, across the double bond) be considered especially electron-rich and strongly nucleophilic?
options: Nitrogen withdraws electron density from that carbon
Beta carbons are never affected by resonance

The nitrogen lone pair donates into the pi system by resonance, placing significant negative character (and thus high electron density) specifically at that beta carbon, similar to how an enolate's oxygen activates its alpha carbon
Enamines have no nitrogen lone pair available to donate
electron-rich-poor.why: Just as an enolate's oxygen lone pair activates the alpha carbon through resonance, an enamine's nitrogen lone pair conjugates through the C=C pi system to make the beta carbon unusually electron-rich and nucleophilic, a key feature exploited in many carbon-carbon bond-forming reactions.

electron-rich-poor.q: Both inductive and resonance (conjugative) effects can make a given atom more electron-poor or more electron-rich, and in some molecules these two effects can act in opposing directions on the same atom.
electron-rich-poor.why: A classic example is a halogen substituent on an aromatic ring: it withdraws electron density inductively (making the ring somewhat electron-poor overall) while donating electron density by resonance at the ortho/para positions (making those specific positions more electron-rich), so the two effects can genuinely pull in opposite directions.

electron-rich-poor.q: Which atom would you expect to be more electron-rich: the carbon of a terminal alkyne's triple bond carbon that bears the acidic hydrogen, or a typical sp3 alkane carbon?
options: The sp3 alkane carbon, because sp3 carbons are always more electron-rich
Neither is meaningfully different in electron density
The terminal alkyne carbon is always the most electron-rich carbon possible

This depends entirely on the specific substituents and cannot be generalized, though the acidic alkyne C–H bond reflects greater s-character holding electrons closer to carbon's nucleus, making that carbon less electron-rich and its hydrogen unusually acidic
electron-rich-poor.why: The sp-hybridized alkyne carbon has high s-character, holding its bonding electrons (including those in the C–H bond) closer to the nucleus; this makes the alkyne carbon itself relatively electron-poor in a way that acidifies its attached hydrogen, illustrating that hybridization also strongly influences electron richness/poorness, not just substituents.

electron-rich-poor.q: A bromonium ion intermediate (formed when Br2 adds to an alkene) carries its formal positive charge on bromine, so it is bromine itself, not either ring carbon, that an incoming nucleophile attacks.
electron-rich-poor.why: Although bromine formally bears the positive charge in the strained three-membered bromonium ring, the nucleophile actually attacks one of the electrophilic ring carbons from the backside, displacing bromine and opening the ring; formal charge location does not always mark the exact site of nucleophilic attack.

bronsted.q: A Brønsted-Lowry acid is defined as a species that:
bronsted.why: Brønsted-Lowry acids are proton donors; bases are proton acceptors.

bronsted.q: When an acid donates a proton, what is left behind called?
bronsted.why: After losing H⁺, the acid becomes its conjugate base (one less proton, one more negative/less positive charge).

bronsted.q: Water can act as both a Brønsted acid and a Brønsted base. What is this property called?
bronsted.why: A species that can donate or accept a proton depending on the reaction partner is called amphoteric (or amphiprotic).

bronsted.q: Which species is the Bronsted base in the reaction NH3 + H2O → NH4+ + OH-?
bronsted.why: NH3 accepts a proton from water to form NH4+, making it the Bronsted base while water acts as the acid.

bronsted.q: In a Bronsted acid-base reaction, a proton is transferred from the acid to the base.
bronsted.why: This is the core definition of Bronsted-Lowry theory: the acid donates H+ and the base accepts it.

bronsted.q: What is formed when a Bronsted base accepts a proton?
bronsted.why: Accepting H+ turns a base into its conjugate acid, which now carries one more proton.

bronsted.q: Which of the following best describes HCl dissolving in water?
options: HCl acts as a Bronsted base
HCl acts as a Bronsted acid, donating H+ to water
HCl acts as a Lewis base
bronsted.why: HCl donates a proton to water, forming H3O+ and Cl-, the defining Bronsted-Lowry acid behavior.

bronsted.q: A species must contain oxygen to act as a Bronsted acid.
bronsted.why: Any species with a removable proton, such as HCl or an alkyne C-H, can act as a Bronsted acid; oxygen is not required.

bronsted.q: In the reaction CH3COOH + NH3 → CH3COO- + NH4+, identify the Bronsted acid.
bronsted.why: Acetic acid donates a proton to ammonia, so it is the proton donor (acid) in this transfer.

bronsted.q: Which statement about amphoteric species is correct?
options: They can never accept a proton
They only exist in the gas phase
They can act as either a Bronsted acid or base depending on the reaction partner
bronsted.why: Amphoteric species like water or bicarbonate can donate a proton to a stronger base or accept one from a stronger acid.

bronsted.q: HSO4- (bisulfate) can act as both a Bronsted acid and a Bronsted base depending on what it reacts with.
bronsted.why: HSO4- can donate its remaining proton to become SO4^2- (acid) or accept a proton to become H2SO4 (base), making it amphoteric.

bronsted.q: Which pair does NOT represent an acid and its conjugate base?
bronsted.why: The conjugate base of HCl is Cl-, formed by loss of H+; OH- is not related to HCl by a single proton loss.

bronsted.q: When a carboxylic acid reacts with sodium bicarbonate, what role does bicarbonate play?
options: Bronsted base, accepting a proton to form carbonic acid
bronsted.why: Bicarbonate accepts the proton from the carboxylic acid, forming carbonic acid (which decomposes to CO2 and water), acting as a Bronsted base.

bronsted.q: Which of the following is the best Bronsted base among these conjugate bases of the hydrohalic acids: F-, Cl-, Br-, I-?
bronsted.why: F- is the conjugate base of the weakest acid (HF) among the hydrohalic acids, making it the strongest base of the group, though still weak in water.

bronsted.q: A Bronsted-Lowry acid-base reaction always requires an aqueous solvent.
bronsted.why: Proton transfer reactions occur in many settings, such as HCl gas reacting directly with NH3 gas to form solid NH4Cl smoke.

bronsted.q: In the reaction of two molecules of acetic acid, with one acting as acid and one as base, what species results from the molecule acting as the base?
bronsted.why: Even a weak acid like acetic acid has a small tendency to accept a proton from another acetic acid molecule, forming its protonated conjugate acid form.

bronsted.q: Consider HC triple-bond CH (acetylene) reacting with a very strong base like NaNH2. What role does acetylene play?
options: Bronsted acid, donating a terminal alkyne proton
None, alkynes have no acidic protons
bronsted.why: The sp-hybridized C-H of a terminal alkyne is weakly acidic (pKa about 25) and can be deprotonated by a sufficiently strong base like amide ion.

bronsted.q: Every Bronsted acid is automatically also classified as a Lewis acid in the usual sense.
bronsted.why: A Bronsted acid donates a proton, and it is really the proton itself that behaves as the electron-pair acceptor; the parent species (like HCl) is not typically classified as a Lewis acid.

bronsted.q: Why can methane (CH4) technically act as a Bronsted acid, even though it essentially never does in practice?
options: It has a C-H bond that could in principle lose a proton, but the resulting carbanion is so unstable that the reaction does not occur under normal conditions
Methane is a Lewis base only
Methane cannot dissolve in any solvent
bronsted.why: Any X-H bond can formally act as a Bronsted acid, but methane's conjugate base (CH3-) is extremely unstable, giving methane an extremely high pKa (about 50) and negligible real-world acidity.

bronsted.q: Which best explains why NH3 is a stronger Bronsted base than H2O?
options: Nitrogen has more lone pairs than oxygen
Ammonia is a liquid at room temperature
Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so it holds its lone pair less tightly and donates it more readily to a proton
Ammonia has a lower molecular weight
bronsted.why: Lower electronegativity means the lone pair on N is held less tightly, making it more available to bond with an incoming proton, so NH3 is the stronger base.

bronsted.q: Complete the analogy: a Bronsted acid is to a proton donor as a Bronsted base is to a ____.
bronsted.why: By definition, Bronsted-Lowry theory defines bases strictly as proton acceptors.

bronsted.q: Which of the following equations shows a classic Bronsted acid-base (proton transfer) reaction?
bronsted.why: HCl transfers a proton to hydroxide ion in a classic neutralization, a proton-transfer reaction; the other options are not proton transfers.

bronsted.q: In the self-ionization of water (2 H2O → H3O+ + OH-), how many water molecules act as the acid and how many as the base?
options: One acts as acid, one acts as base
Neither acts as acid or base
bronsted.why: One water molecule donates a proton (acid) to the other, which accepts it (base), producing hydronium and hydroxide.

bronsted.q: A student says phenol (C6H5OH) cannot be a Bronsted acid because it contains a benzene ring. What is wrong with this statement?
options: Benzene rings prevent all proton transfer
The O-H proton on phenol is still ionizable, and phenol is indeed a weak Bronsted acid with pKa around 10
Phenol is a Lewis base only
bronsted.why: The presence of an aromatic ring does not block the O-H proton from being donated; phenol is a well-known weak Bronsted acid.

bronsted.q: Amino acids exist predominantly as zwitterions in water. Regarding the carboxylic acid and amine groups, which statement is correct?
options: Only the amine group can ever be acidic
The carboxylic acid group is a Lewis base
The carboxylic acid group has already acted as a Bronsted acid, transferring its proton to the amine group, which acted as the Bronsted base
bronsted.why: In the zwitterion, -COOH has already given up its proton to -NH2 (forming -COO- and -NH3+), an internal proton transfer consistent with Bronsted theory.

bronsted.q: The stronger a Bronsted acid is, the weaker its conjugate base will be.
bronsted.why: There is an inverse relationship: a strong acid readily gives up its proton, leaving behind a conjugate base with little attraction for protons, i.e. a weak base.

bronsted.q: Which of these amine-type species acts purely as a Bronsted base and cannot donate an N-H proton at all?
bronsted.why: Trimethylamine has no N-H bond at all (every substituent is a methyl group), so unlike ammonia or primary and secondary amines, it cannot donate an N-H proton and behaves purely as a Bronsted base.

bronsted.q: Hydronium ion (H3O+) is the conjugate acid of water.
bronsted.why: H3O+ is formed when water accepts a proton, making it water's conjugate acid.

bronsted.q: Why is it often said that there is no such thing as a truly free, unattached proton in solution?
options: A bare H+ is so reactive that it immediately bonds to a lone pair on a nearby solvent molecule, such as water, forming a species like H3O+
Protons are too large to move in solution
Protons only exist in the gas phase
bronsted.why: A naked proton has an extremely high charge density and is instantly bound by an available electron-pair donor in solution, which is part of why Bronsted-Lowry reactions are really proton transfers rather than release of a free proton.

bronsted.q: Identify the conjugate acid-base pair among these four species: H2CO3, HCO3-, CO3^2-, H3O+.
bronsted.why: H2CO3 loses one proton to become HCO3-; they differ by exactly one H+ and are therefore a conjugate acid-base pair.

lewis-acids.q: A Lewis acid is defined as a species that:
lewis-acids.why: Lewis acids are electron pair acceptors — a broader definition than Brønsted acids, which must involve a proton.

lewis-acids.q: Which of these is a classic Lewis acid even though it has no protons to donate?
lewis-acids.why: BF₃ has an empty p orbital on boron and readily accepts an electron pair, making it a Lewis acid despite having no acidic protons.

lewis-acids.q: Metal cations like Al³⁺ or Zn²⁺ act as Lewis acids in organic reactions mainly by:
options: Acting as a leaving group themselves
Accepting an electron pair from a Lewis base (e.g., a carbonyl oxygen), activating it toward nucleophilic attack
lewis-acids.why: Metal cations have empty orbitals and coordinate to electron-rich atoms like carbonyl oxygen, pulling electron density away and making the carbon more electrophilic.

lewis-acids.q: Which of these is the best definition of a Lewis base?
lewis-acids.why: Lewis base theory defines a base strictly by its ability to donate an electron pair to form a new bond.

lewis-acids.q: Every Bronsted base is also a Lewis base.
lewis-acids.why: Accepting a proton requires donating an electron pair to form the new bond, so every Bronsted base (proton acceptor) is necessarily also a Lewis base.

lewis-acids.q: Which of the following is a classic example of a Lewis acid used as a catalyst in Friedel-Crafts reactions?
lewis-acids.why: AlCl3 has an incomplete octet on aluminum and readily accepts an electron pair, making it a powerful Lewis acid catalyst in Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation.

lewis-acids.q: BF3 acts as a strong Lewis acid primarily because:
options: fluorine is very electronegative and donates electrons
boron has an empty p orbital and an incomplete octet, making it electron-deficient
BF3 carries a formal negative charge
lewis-acids.why: Boron in BF3 has only six valence electrons around it, leaving an empty orbital that readily accepts an electron pair from a Lewis base.

lewis-acids.q: A Lewis acid must contain a hydrogen atom.
lewis-acids.why: Lewis acids are defined by their ability to accept an electron pair, not by containing hydrogen; BF3 and AlCl3 have no acidic protons at all.

lewis-acids.q: Which species below is a Lewis base that donates electron density through pi bond electrons rather than a lone pair?
lewis-acids.why: Ethylene has no lone pairs; it donates electron density from its pi bond to electrophiles such as Br2 or H+, a hallmark of alkene reactivity in organic chemistry.

lewis-acids.q: In the reaction of a carbonyl oxygen with a Lewis acid like BF3, forming a Lewis acid-base adduct, what is the role of the carbonyl oxygen?
options: Lewis base, donating a lone pair to boron
lewis-acids.why: The carbonyl oxygen's lone pair coordinates to the electron-deficient boron of BF3, activating the carbonyl toward nucleophilic attack, a common strategy in Lewis acid catalysis.

lewis-acids.q: A Lewis acid-base adduct always involves the transfer of a proton between the two species.
lewis-acids.why: Many Lewis acid-base adducts, such as BF3 binding NH3, form purely through electron-pair donation with no proton ever changing hands; proton transfer is a narrower, Bronsted-specific phenomenon.

lewis-acids.q: Which of the following best explains why carbocations are strong Lewis acids?
options: They have an empty p orbital on a positively charged carbon that readily accepts an electron pair from a nucleophile
lewis-acids.why: A carbocation's central carbon has only six valence electrons, leaving an empty p orbital that strongly attracts electron pairs from Lewis bases (nucleophiles).

lewis-acids.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes Lewis acid-base theory from Bronsted-Lowry theory?
options: Lewis theory applies only to gases
Lewis theory is broader and includes species that do not involve proton transfer at all, such as BF3 accepting electrons from NH3
Bronsted theory includes more species than Lewis theory
They are mutually exclusive theories with no overlap
lewis-acids.why: Lewis acid-base theory extends beyond proton transfer to any electron-pair donation or acceptance, so it encompasses Bronsted acid-base reactions plus additional reactions, like BF3 plus NH3, that involve no protons at all.

lewis-acids.q: Why does SnCl4 act as a Lewis acid in certain organic reactions?
options: Tin has a full valence shell and cannot accept electrons
SnCl4 is a strong Bronsted base
Tin can expand its coordination sphere and accept additional electron pairs from donor atoms
lewis-acids.why: Like other metal halides such as TiCl4 and AlCl3, SnCl4 can accommodate additional ligands by expanding its coordination number, accepting electron pairs from Lewis bases.

lewis-acids.q: In the Lewis acid-base adduct formed between NH3 and BF3 (H3N-BF3), what change occurs at boron's geometry?
options: Boron changes from trigonal planar (sp2) in BF3 to tetrahedral (sp3) in the adduct
lewis-acids.why: Forming the new B-N bond gives boron four bonding pairs instead of three, changing its hybridization from sp2 (trigonal planar) to sp3 (tetrahedral).

lewis-acids.q: A student claims that all Lewis acids are also Bronsted acids. Which example best refutes this claim?
options: BF3, which has no hydrogen to donate as a proton but readily accepts electron pairs
lewis-acids.why: BF3 cannot donate a proton since it has none, so it cannot be a Bronsted acid, yet it is a textbook strong Lewis acid, showing the two acid categories are not equivalent.

lewis-acids.q: Grignard reagents (RMgX) contain a carbon-metal bond. When a Grignard reagent attacks a carbonyl, which role does the carbonyl carbon play with respect to Lewis theory?
options: Lewis acid, accepting the electron pair from the nucleophilic carbon of the Grignard reagent
lewis-acids.why: The electrophilic carbonyl carbon accepts the electron pair donated by the carbanion-like carbon of the Grignard reagent, consistent with it acting as the Lewis acid in that bond-forming step.

lewis-acids.q: A species can simultaneously be a Lewis base toward one reagent and a Lewis acid toward a different reagent.
lewis-acids.why: Lewis acid or base character depends on the reaction partner, so the same species can play different roles with different partners depending on which one is electron-rich or electron-poor in that specific interaction.

lewis-acids.q: Which of these pairs correctly identifies the electron-pair donor and acceptor in the reaction H3N: + BF3 → H3N-BF3?
options: BF3 is the donor, NH3 is the acceptor
NH3 is the donor (Lewis base), BF3 is the acceptor (Lewis acid)
lewis-acids.why: Nitrogen's lone pair on NH3 is donated into the empty p orbital on boron, making ammonia the Lewis base and BF3 the Lewis acid.

lewis-acids.q: Which functional group commonly acts as a Lewis base due to its lone pairs, making it useful for coordinating to Lewis acid catalysts?
lewis-acids.why: The oxygen of a carbonyl group has lone pairs that readily coordinate to Lewis acids such as BF3 or AlCl3, a common activation strategy in synthesis.

lewis-acids.q: Lewis acids always carry a positive formal charge.
lewis-acids.why: Many neutral Lewis acids exist, such as BF3 and AlCl3, which are electron-deficient due to incomplete octets rather than formal positive charge.

lewis-acids.q: Which of the following is NOT typically classified as a Lewis acid?
lewis-acids.why: Chloride ion has a full octet and a lone pair to donate, making it a Lewis base, not a Lewis acid; the other three are classic electron-pair acceptors.

lewis-acids.q: TiCl4 is often used in organic synthesis, such as in Mukaiyama aldol reactions, because it:
options: acts as a Bronsted base deprotonating alcohols
acts as a Lewis acid that activates carbonyl groups toward nucleophilic attack by coordinating to the carbonyl oxygen
lewis-acids.why: TiCl4's electron-deficient titanium center coordinates to the carbonyl oxygen's lone pair, increasing the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon for the incoming nucleophile.

lewis-acids.q: Why can a proton (H+) itself be classified as the simplest possible Lewis acid?
options: It has a filled valence shell
It has a completely empty 1s orbital and accepts an electron pair from a base to form a new covalent bond
It always remains uncoordinated in solution
lewis-acids.why: A bare proton has no electrons at all, so when it bonds to a base, that bond forms entirely from the base's donated electron pair, the defining behavior of a Lewis acid.

lewis-acids.q: Consider a Lewis acid catalyst promoting ring-opening of an epoxide. What is its mechanistic role?
options: It acts as a nucleophile attacking the epoxide carbon directly
It reduces the epoxide to an alcohol directly
It coordinates to and polarizes the epoxide oxygen, making the adjacent carbons more electrophilic and activating the ring toward nucleophilic attack
lewis-acids.why: By accepting a lone pair from the epoxide oxygen, the Lewis acid withdraws electron density from the ring, weakening the C-O bonds and activating the epoxide carbons for nucleophilic ring-opening.

lewis-acids.q: Which best explains why carbenes, such as singlet :CH2, can act as Lewis acids?
options: The carbon has only six valence electrons and an empty orbital, making it electron-deficient and able to accept an electron pair
lewis-acids.why: Singlet carbenes have an empty p orbital on carbon in addition to a lone pair, giving them both electrophilic (Lewis acidic) and nucleophilic character.

lewis-acids.q: A coordinate covalent (dative) bond, as formed between a Lewis acid and Lewis base, is characterized by:
options: both bonding electrons coming from the Lewis acid
both bonding electrons coming from the Lewis base
one electron coming from each partner, as in a typical covalent bond
no electrons being shared at all
lewis-acids.why: In a Lewis acid-base adduct, the base supplies both electrons of the new bond while the acid simply provides the empty orbital to receive them.

lewis-acids.q: Steric bulk around a Lewis acid's empty orbital can reduce its practical effectiveness even if its electronic electron-deficiency is high.
lewis-acids.why: Bulky substituents can physically block a Lewis base from approaching the empty orbital, so steric hindrance, not just electronics, influences a Lewis acid's real-world reactivity.

lewis-acids.q: Why is SO3 (sulfur trioxide) considered a Lewis acid?
options: Sulfur has a complete octet and excess electrons
SO3 only acts as a base
Sulfur is highly electron-deficient and readily accepts an electron pair, such as from water to form sulfuric acid
lewis-acids.why: The electron-poor sulfur center in SO3 accepts a lone pair from a Lewis base like water, generating sulfuric acid via an addition reaction.

lewis-acids.q: A chemist uses a chiral Lewis acid catalyst in an asymmetric Diels-Alder reaction. What is the general purpose of the Lewis acid here?
options: To act as the diene itself
To coordinate to the dienophile's carbonyl, activating it electronically while also organizing the reacting partners spatially for enantioselective bond formation
lewis-acids.why: Chiral Lewis acids coordinate to an electrophile's lone-pair-bearing atom, such as a carbonyl oxygen, lowering the energy of the reactive orbital while imposing a chiral environment that biases which face reacts, enabling asymmetric induction.

pka.q: A lower pKa indicates:
pka.why: pKa and acid strength are inversely related — lower pKa means the acid dissociates more, so it’s stronger.

pka.q: If an acid has a pKa of 5 and a base’s conjugate acid has a pKa of 10, which side does the acid-base equilibrium favor?
options: The side with the stronger acid
The side with the weaker acid
Cannot be determined from pKa alone
pka.why: Proton transfer equilibria favor forming the weaker acid (higher pKa) — the reaction runs toward the more stable, less acidic species.

pka.q: Comparing HCl (pKa ≈ −7) and acetic acid (pKa ≈ 4.76), which is the stronger acid?
pka.why: A much lower (more negative) pKa means HCl dissociates far more completely — it is the much stronger acid.

pka.q: What does pKa represent mathematically?
pka.why: pKa is defined as the negative base-10 logarithm of the acid dissociation constant, Ka.

pka.q: A higher pKa value indicates a stronger acid.
pka.why: pKa and acid strength are inversely related; a lower pKa means a larger Ka and a stronger acid, while a higher pKa means a weaker acid.

pka.q: Which acid is stronger: one with pKa = 2 or one with pKa = 9?
pka.why: Lower pKa corresponds to a larger Ka, meaning greater dissociation, so the acid with pKa = 2 is significantly stronger.

pka.q: At what pH is a weak acid exactly 50 percent dissociated into its conjugate base, according to the Henderson-Hasselbalch relationship?
pka.why: When pH equals pKa, the concentrations of the acid and its conjugate base are equal, meaning the acid is 50 percent dissociated.

pka.q: Water has a pKa of about 15.7 (based on its autoionization), while ethanol's O-H has a pKa of about 16. What does this comparison show?
options: Ethanol is dramatically more acidic than water
Water is not acidic at all
Water and ethanol have very similar O-H acidity, with water very slightly more acidic
pka.why: Both O-H bonds sit in a similar electronic environment, so their pKa values are close, though water is very slightly more acidic since ethanol's alkyl group is weakly electron-donating and slightly destabilizes the alkoxide.

pka.q: A carboxylic acid has pKa around 4 to 5, while a simple alcohol has pKa around 16 to 18. Approximately how many orders of magnitude more acidic is the carboxylic acid?
pka.why: Since pKa is a log scale, a difference of about 12 pKa units corresponds to roughly 10^12 difference in Ka, reflecting the large stabilizing effect of resonance in the carboxylate compared to the alkoxide.

pka.q: To fully drive deprotonation of a carboxylic acid (pKa approximately 5) forward, the base used should form a conjugate acid whose pKa is:
options: significantly higher than 5, so the equilibrium favors the products
pka.why: For a favorable, forward-driven acid-base reaction, the base's conjugate acid should be a weaker acid (higher pKa) than the starting acid, ensuring the equilibrium lies toward products.

pka.q: pKa values can be negative for very strong acids, such as HCl or the first ionization of H2SO4.
pka.why: Since pKa = -log(Ka), an extremely large Ka for a very strong acid produces a negative pKa value.

pka.q: A terminal alkyne C-H has pKa around 25, while a simple alkane C-H has pKa around 50. What does this difference primarily reflect?
options: The greater s-character of the sp-hybridized carbon holds electrons closer to the nucleus, stabilizing the conjugate base far more than the sp3 alkane's conjugate base
Alkanes have resonance stabilization that alkynes lack
There is no real acidity difference between them
pka.why: Higher s-character (sp versus sp3) stabilizes the lone pair left behind in the conjugate base, making sp C-H bonds considerably more acidic than sp3 C-H bonds.

pka.q: Which solvent property most directly affects the experimentally measured pKa of an acid?
options: The solvent's ability to stabilize (solvate) the resulting ions, especially the conjugate base
pka.why: pKa values are measured in a specific solvent, commonly water, because the degree to which that solvent stabilizes the separated charges through solvation strongly affects the measured equilibrium constant.

pka.q: The pKa of the protonated carbonyl oxygen of a ketone is roughly -7, while the pKa of the same ketone's alpha C-H is roughly 20. What does this 27-unit gap tell you?
options: The alpha C-H is actually the more acidic of the two protons
Neither proton can ever be removed under any conditions
The protonated carbonyl oxygen is an enormously stronger acid, giving up its proton far more readily than the alpha C-H requires a base to remove its proton
pka.why: A pKa difference of 27 units corresponds to an enormous difference in Ka, showing the oxygen-protonated form is vastly more acidic than the alpha C-H, which needs a much stronger base to deprotonate.

pka.q: A compound has two acidic protons with pKa1 = 3 and pKa2 = 10. At a pH of 7, which species predominates?
options: The monoprotonated form, since pH is above pKa1 but below pKa2
All three forms are present in equal amounts
pka.why: When pH lies between pKa1 and pKa2, the species has lost the first, more acidic proton but retained the second, so the intermediate form dominates.

pka.q: The pKa of a compound is an intrinsic property that is completely independent of the solvent used.
pka.why: pKa values depend on the solvent because solvation stabilizes ions differently in different media; the same acid can show noticeably different pKa values in water versus a solvent like DMSO.

pka.q: Which range of pKa values is typical for a simple alcohol's O-H proton?
pka.why: Simple alcohols like ethanol have O-H pKa values around 16 to 18, close to but slightly less acidic than water.

pka.q: Which range of pKa values is typical for a simple carboxylic acid?
pka.why: Carboxylic acids like acetic acid typically have pKa values around 4 to 5, due to strong resonance stabilization of the carboxylate conjugate base.

pka.q: Protonated amines (ammonium ions, R-NH3+) typically have pKa values around:
pka.why: The conjugate acids of typical alkyl amines have pKa values in the range of about 9 to 11, reflecting amines' moderate basicity.

pka.q: If Ka for acid A is 1 times 10^-5 and Ka for acid B is 1 times 10^-3, what is the approximate difference in their pKa values, and which acid has the higher pKa?
options: 2 pKa units, with acid A having the higher pKa
2 pKa units, with acid B having the higher pKa
pka.why: pKa = -log(Ka), so a Ka of 10^-5 gives pKa = 5 and a Ka of 10^-3 gives pKa = 3; acid A, with the smaller Ka, has the higher pKa, a difference of 2 units.

pka.q: Why can it be misleading to directly compare a gas-phase acidity measurement to an aqueous-solution pKa for the same compound?
options: Gas-phase and solution pKa values are always identical
Solvation effects, especially stabilization of the conjugate base by hydrogen bonding or ion solvation, are absent in the gas phase, which can dramatically change the relative acidity order
pKa cannot be measured in the gas phase at all
Only inorganic acids have gas-phase pKa values
pka.why: In solution, polar solvents like water stabilize charged conjugate bases through solvation, which can significantly change or even reverse relative acidity trends compared to the gas phase, where no such stabilization exists.

pka.q: A pKa value can be used to predict which of two acids will protonate a common base more completely at equilibrium.
pka.why: Comparing the pKa values of two acids against a common base's conjugate acid lets you predict which acid-base pair favors products versus reactants at equilibrium.

pka.q: The pKa of hydronium ion (H3O+) is approximately -1.74. What does this illustrate about the leveling effect in water?
options: Water cannot have a pH below 7
Any acid stronger than H3O+ is essentially fully converted to H3O+ in dilute aqueous solution, since H3O+ is effectively the strongest persistent acid species in that solvent
The pKa of H3O+ has no bearing on acid strength in water
pka.why: Because H3O+ is the strongest acid species that persists in water, stronger acids added to dilute water are converted essentially completely to H3O+, a phenomenon known as the leveling effect.

pka.q: Which acid would you expect to have the lowest (most negative) pKa among methanol, acetic acid, HCl, and ethane?
pka.why: HCl is a strong mineral acid with pKa around -7, far lower than the weak O-H acids methanol and acetic acid, or the essentially non-acidic C-H of ethane.

pka.q: Phenol has pKa around 10, while cyclohexanol has pKa around 18. What is the primary reason phenol is more acidic?
options: The phenoxide conjugate base is stabilized by resonance delocalization of its negative charge into the aromatic ring
Phenol has more oxygen atoms than cyclohexanol
Cyclohexanol is aromatic while phenol is not
Phenol has a smaller molecular weight
pka.why: The negative charge on phenoxide can delocalize into the pi system of the benzene ring through resonance, stabilizing the conjugate base and making phenol more acidic than a non-resonance-stabilized alcohol like cyclohexanol.

pka.q: Trifluoroacetic acid (pKa approximately 0.5) is much more acidic than acetic acid (pKa approximately 4.76). This roughly 4.3-unit difference is mainly attributed to:
options: resonance differences between the two carboxylates
the strong inductive electron-withdrawing effect of the three fluorine atoms stabilizing the negative charge on the carboxylate oxygen
the larger atomic size of fluorine compared to hydrogen
trifluoroacetic acid having two acidic protons instead of one
pka.why: The highly electronegative fluorine atoms withdraw electron density through the sigma bonds (induction), stabilizing the adjacent carboxylate's negative charge and making the compound considerably more acidic than acetic acid.

pka.q: pKa is calculated using a base-10 logarithm of the acid dissociation constant.
pka.why: By definition, pKa equals the negative base-10 (common) logarithm of Ka.

pka.q: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) has a pKa around 4.2 for its first ionizable proton. Based on this value, how is it classified?
options: A strong acid that fully dissociates in water
A weak acid, since it does not fully dissociate in water and its pKa is well above typical strong-acid values near 0 or below
pka.why: A pKa of 4.2 means ascorbic acid only partially dissociates in water, placing it firmly in the weak acid category, similar in strength to acetic acid.

pka.q: A chemist measures an unusually low pKa, around 5, for an alcohol's O-H proton, much lower than the typical 16 to 18 range. What structural feature most likely explains this?
options: The molecule must contain no carbon atoms
This result is impossible and must be an experimental error
Strong electron-withdrawing groups nearby, such as multiple fluorines, stabilize the resulting alkoxide through induction
pka.why: Powerful inductive electron withdrawal from nearby electronegative groups can dramatically stabilize the conjugate base (alkoxide), lowering the pKa well below that of an ordinary alcohol, as seen in highly fluorinated alcohols.

pka.q: When comparing two acids, which quantity most directly and reliably predicts the extent to which an acid-base reaction will proceed toward completion?
options: Their Ka (or equivalently pKa) values, since these directly quantify the equilibrium position of proton transfer
pka.why: Ka, and its logarithmic form pKa, directly reflects the equilibrium constant for proton dissociation, making it the correct quantity for predicting whether an acid-base reaction favors products, unlike unrelated physical properties.

conjugate.q: The conjugate base of an acid has:
options: One fewer proton than the acid
One more proton than the acid
An extra electron pair donated externally
conjugate.why: Losing H⁺ from an acid gives its conjugate base — exactly one fewer proton.

conjugate.q: A strong acid has a conjugate base that is:
conjugate.why: Strong acids give up protons easily because their conjugate base is very stable (weak) once formed.

conjugate.q: The conjugate acid of ammonia (NH₃) is:
conjugate.why: Adding a proton (H⁺) to NH₃ gives NH₄⁺, its conjugate acid.

conjugate.q: The conjugate base of H2SO4, formed after losing one proton, is:
conjugate.why: Removing a single proton from H2SO4 gives the bisulfate ion, HSO4-, its conjugate base.

conjugate.q: The conjugate acid of OH- is:
conjugate.why: Adding one proton to hydroxide ion gives water, its conjugate acid.

conjugate.q: A conjugate acid-base pair differs by exactly one proton (H+).
conjugate.why: By definition, a conjugate acid and its conjugate base are related by the gain or loss of a single proton, with no other atoms changing.

conjugate.q: What is the conjugate base of HF?
conjugate.why: Removing the single proton from HF gives fluoride ion, F-, its conjugate base.

conjugate.q: Given that HCN has a pKa of approximately 9.2 and HF has a pKa of approximately 3.2, which conjugate base is the stronger base?
options: They are equal in base strength
Cannot be determined from pKa values
conjugate.why: Because HCN is a much weaker acid than HF (higher pKa), its conjugate base, cyanide, holds onto protons more strongly and is therefore the stronger base of the two.

conjugate.q: Which of the following conjugate bases would be expected to be the strongest (best proton acceptor)?
options: The conjugate base of acetic acid (acetate)
conjugate.why: Water is a much weaker acid than HCl or acetic acid, so its conjugate base, hydroxide, is a correspondingly much stronger base than chloride or acetate.

conjugate.q: Which conjugate acid-base pair is correctly matched?
conjugate.why: NH4+ loses a proton to become NH3, making them a properly matched conjugate acid and conjugate base pair, differing by exactly one H+.

conjugate.q: The conjugate base of a strong acid is generally a poor base in aqueous solution.
conjugate.why: Because a strong acid dissociates almost completely, its conjugate base has very little affinity for protons and is correspondingly a weak base, such as Cl- from HCl.

conjugate.q: Amide ion (NH2-) is the conjugate base of which species?
conjugate.why: Removing one proton from ammonia (NH3) gives amide ion, NH2-, a very strong base often used to deprotonate weak acids like terminal alkynes.

conjugate.q: Which of these is the conjugate acid of the carbonate ion, CO3^2-?
conjugate.why: Adding one proton to carbonate gives bicarbonate, HCO3-, its conjugate acid.

conjugate.q: An acid HA has pKa = 4. Using which relationship can you find the pKb of its conjugate base A- in water at 25 degrees C?
conjugate.why: In water at 25 degrees C, the pKa of an acid plus the pKb of its conjugate base always equals pKw (14), reflecting the relationship Ka times Kb equals Kw.

conjugate.q: Why does the acetate ion, the conjugate base of acetic acid, react with water far less extensively than the ethoxide ion, the conjugate base of ethanol?
options: Acetate is stabilized by resonance delocalization of its negative charge across two oxygens, making it a much weaker base than ethoxide, which lacks such delocalization
Acetic acid is itself a base, not an acid
conjugate.why: Resonance stabilization in acetate spreads the negative charge over two equivalent oxygens, making it a comparatively weak, stable base, whereas ethoxide's charge is localized on a single oxygen, making it a much stronger, more reactive base.

conjugate.q: Bicarbonate (HCO3-) is amphoteric. As the conjugate base of which species does it form by losing a proton, and as the conjugate acid of which species does it form by gaining a proton?
options: It is the conjugate base of CO3^2- and the conjugate acid of H2CO3
It is the conjugate base of H2CO3 and the conjugate acid of CO3^2-
It is only ever an acid, never a base
It is only ever a base, never an acid
conjugate.why: Bicarbonate forms when carbonic acid (H2CO3) loses a proton, making HCO3- its conjugate base, and also when carbonate (CO3^2-) gains a proton, making HCO3- its conjugate acid; this dual role is why it is amphoteric.

conjugate.q: The conjugate acid of a carboxylate ion (RCOO-) is:
conjugate.why: Adding one proton to a carboxylate ion regenerates the neutral carboxylic acid, its conjugate acid.

conjugate.q: Adding a proton to a conjugate base regenerates the original acid it came from.
conjugate.why: By definition, a conjugate base reacting with a proton reforms the acid it came from, since conjugate acid-base pairs differ by exactly one H+.

conjugate.q: Given the conjugate acids methane (pKa about 50), ammonia (pKa about 38), water (pKa about 15.7), and HF (pKa about 3.2), which of their conjugate bases, CH3-, NH2-, OH-, or F-, is the strongest base?
conjugate.why: The weaker the conjugate acid, the stronger the conjugate base; since methane is the weakest acid of the four (highest pKa), methyl anion is the strongest base.

conjugate.q: Which statement correctly relates acid strength and conjugate base strength within a conjugate pair?
options: A weak acid has a relatively strong conjugate base
A weak acid always has a weak conjugate base
Acid strength and conjugate base strength are unrelated
A weak acid has no conjugate base at all
conjugate.why: Because a weak acid holds onto its proton fairly well, its conjugate base, once formed, has a correspondingly stronger pull on protons, meaning it is a relatively strong base.

conjugate.q: In a buffer made of acetic acid and sodium acetate, which species is the conjugate base, and what role does it play when a strong acid is added?
options: Acetic acid is the conjugate base and neutralizes added OH-
Acetate ion is the conjugate base, and it neutralizes added H+ by accepting the proton to re-form acetic acid
Sodium ion is the conjugate base component
Acetate ion reacts with added acid by donating a proton
conjugate.why: In a buffer, the conjugate base component, acetate, absorbs any added strong acid's protons, converting back to the weak acid and resisting a large pH change.

conjugate.q: The conjugate base formed by removing the N-H proton from an amine (giving R-NH-) is a much stronger base than the conjugate base formed by removing the O-H proton from an alcohol (giving RO-).
conjugate.why: Because N-H, with pKa around 35 to 38, is far less acidic than O-H, with pKa around 16 to 18, the nitrogen-based conjugate base holds its electron pair much more tightly and is therefore a much stronger base than an alkoxide.

conjugate.q: Why is hydroxide (OH-) often called a strong base while water itself is called a weak base, even though both are conjugate bases of something?
options: The two statements are contradictory and cannot both be true
Base strength has nothing to do with conjugate relationships

OH- is the conjugate base of water, a weak acid (pKa about 15.7), making OH- a strong base, while water is the conjugate base of H3O+, a strong acid (pKa about -1.74), making water a comparatively weak base
OH- and H2O are not conjugate to anything
conjugate.why: Base strength depends on which acid is considered its conjugate partner; OH- is a strong base relative to water's acidity, while water is a weak base relative to the much stronger acid H3O+, showing that strength is tied to a specific conjugate pair.

conjugate.q: What is the conjugate acid of a chloride ion (Cl-)?
conjugate.why: Adding one proton to chloride ion gives HCl, its conjugate acid.

conjugate.q: A buffer requires a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid) present in significant amounts. Why can't a strong acid and its conjugate base form an effective buffer?
options: A strong acid's conjugate base is too weak to meaningfully react with added acid or hold onto protons, so it cannot resist pH changes the way a weak acid and conjugate base pair can
Strong acids cannot have conjugate bases
Buffers only ever work using bases, never acids
Strong acids always buffer better than weak acids
conjugate.why: Because a strong acid dissociates almost completely, its conjugate base is essentially non-basic and does not meaningfully re-associate with protons, so the pair cannot buffer against pH changes the way a weak acid and its conjugate base can.

conjugate.q: Sulfanilic acid has both an acidic -SO3H group and a basic -NH2 group in the same molecule and exists largely as a zwitterion. Which statement correctly uses conjugate acid-base terminology here?
options: Both groups are conjugate acids of one another
The -NH3+ form is the conjugate acid of the -NH2 group, while the -SO3- form is the conjugate base of the -SO3H group
The zwitterion has no conjugate acid-base relationships at all
conjugate.why: Each functional group has its own independent conjugate acid-base relationship: protonated amine (-NH3+) is the conjugate acid of the amine (-NH2), and sulfonate (-SO3-) is the conjugate base of sulfonic acid (-SO3H); they are not conjugates of each other.

conjugate.q: If an acid is written generically as A-H, which species represents its conjugate base after losing that proton?
conjugate.why: Removing the proton from A-H leaves behind A-, carrying one fewer proton and one additional unit of negative charge, its conjugate base.

conjugate.q: Given that HI has pKa around -10, H2O has pKa around 15.7, and NH3 has pKa around 38, how should their conjugate bases I-, OH-, and NH2- rank from weakest to strongest base?
options: NH2- less than OH- less than I-
OH- less than I- less than NH2-
All three bases are equal in strength
I- less than OH- less than NH2-
conjugate.why: The weaker the conjugate acid, the stronger the base; since HI is the strongest acid (most negative pKa) and NH3 is the weakest (highest pKa) of the three, their conjugate bases rank I- as weakest, then OH-, then NH2- as strongest.

conjugate.q: Two different acids can have conjugate bases of exactly equal base strength only if the two acids themselves have identical pKa values.
conjugate.why: Since acid strength and conjugate base strength are inversely linked through Ka and Kb, with Ka times Kb equal to Kw in water, two acids must share the same pKa for their conjugate bases to have identical base strength.

conjugate.q: Identify the two conjugate acid-base pairs in the reaction HCN + OH- → CN- + H2O.
options: HCN/CN- is one pair and H2O/OH- is the other pair
There are no conjugate pairs in this reaction
conjugate.why: HCN loses a proton to become CN-, forming one conjugate pair, while OH- gains that proton to become H2O, forming the other conjugate pair, illustrating the two pairs present in every proton-transfer reaction.

acidity-factors.q: Which factor makes an O–H more acidic: resonance stabilization of the conjugate base, or destabilization of the conjugate base?
options: Resonance has no effect on acidity
acidity-factors.why: A more stable (resonance-delocalized) conjugate base means the acid gives up its proton more readily — higher acidity.

acidity-factors.q: Across a period, as electronegativity of the atom bearing the negative charge increases, acidity of the H attached to it:
acidity-factors.why: More electronegative atoms stabilize the extra negative charge of the conjugate base better, increasing acidity (e.g., HF > CH₄ in acidity trend logic, comparing across a period).

acidity-factors.q: Which typically has the biggest effect on acidity when comparing O–H bonds across different molecules: atom size, hybridization, induction, and resonance all matter, but which factor dominates when a strongly electron-withdrawing group is nearby?
options: Resonance stabilization from the withdrawing group
Inductive electron withdrawal stabilizing the conjugate base
Hybridization of a distant, unrelated carbon
acidity-factors.why: A nearby electron-withdrawing group (like a halogen) inductively pulls electron density away, stabilizing the negative charge on the conjugate base and increasing acidity — this is why chloroacetic acid is more acidic than acetic acid.

acidity-factors.q: Which of the four classic factors affecting relative acidity refers to the identity of the element to which the acidic H is attached?
acidity-factors.why: Comparing acidity across a row or column of the periodic table by looking at the atom bearing the acidic proton is the atom effect, one of the four classic factors (often remembered as ARIO: atom, resonance, induction, orbital or hybridization).

acidity-factors.q: Down a column of the periodic table, such as F, Cl, Br, I, acidity of the corresponding H-X bond generally:
options: increases, due to increasing atom size and a weaker, more polarizable H-X bond
acidity-factors.why: Larger halogens form longer, weaker H-X bonds, and their larger conjugate base anions are more polarizable and better able to spread out the negative charge, both of which increase acidity going down the column, making HI more acidic than HF.

acidity-factors.q: Resonance stabilization of a conjugate base increases acidity only when the negative charge can be delocalized onto an atom actually capable of stabilizing it, such as an electronegative atom, not onto just any atom in the structure.
acidity-factors.why: Delocalization by itself is not automatically stabilizing; the atoms receiving the spread-out charge must be able to tolerate negative charge well, such as oxygen, otherwise resonance contributes little additional acid-strengthening effect.

acidity-factors.q: Inductive electron withdrawal by a nearby electronegative atom or group will generally:
options: increase acidity by helping stabilize the conjugate base's negative charge
acidity-factors.why: An electron-withdrawing group pulls electron density away through sigma bonds, which helps spread out and stabilize the negative charge on the conjugate base, increasing acidity.

acidity-factors.q: Comparing HF, H2O, and NH3, all with H attached to similarly sized second-period atoms, what is the correct acidity order from most to least acidic?
options: NH3 greater than H2O greater than HF
H2O greater than HF greater than NH3
HF greater than H2O greater than NH3
acidity-factors.why: Moving left to right across period 2, electronegativity increases, which better stabilizes the conjugate base's negative charge, so acidity increases in the order NH3 less than H2O less than HF.

acidity-factors.q: Why is cyclopentadiene, with pKa around 16, remarkably acidic for a simple hydrocarbon C-H bond?
options: The molecule contains a carbonyl group
The acidic C-H bond is sp hybridized
Induction from a nearby nitrogen atom stabilizes the anion
Deprotonation gives an aromatic cyclopentadienyl anion with its negative charge delocalized over five equivalent resonance structures, providing exceptional resonance and aromatic stabilization
acidity-factors.why: Removing that specific proton produces a fully conjugated, aromatic cyclopentadienyl anion, whose resonance and aromatic stabilization dramatically lowers the pKa compared to a typical alkane C-H, around 50.

acidity-factors.q: Which factor best explains why an alkyne C-H (sp carbon, pKa about 25) is more acidic than an alkene C-H (sp2 carbon, pKa about 44), which is in turn more acidic than an alkane C-H (sp3 carbon, pKa about 50)?
options: Increasing percent s-character holds the bonding and lone pair electrons closer to the nucleus, stabilizing the conjugate base progressively more from sp3 to sp2 to sp
Increasing resonance stabilization across the series
Increasing inductive withdrawal across the series
Decreasing bond length across the series alone explains it
acidity-factors.why: Orbitals with more s-character are lower in energy and hold electron density closer to the nucleus; since sp has the most s-character of the three, its conjugate base is the most stabilized, making the alkynyl C-H the most acidic.

acidity-factors.q: Placing an electron-withdrawing group closer to the acidic proton generally has a larger effect on acidity than placing the same group farther away along the chain.
acidity-factors.why: Inductive effects are transmitted through sigma bonds and weaken rapidly with distance, so a substituent closer to the site of deprotonation exerts a stronger acid-strengthening effect than the same group several bonds away.

acidity-factors.q: Chloroacetic acid (pKa about 2.87) is more acidic than acetic acid (pKa about 4.76). What is the dominant factor responsible for this difference?
options: Resonance differences between the two carboxylates
Inductive electron withdrawal by the electronegative chlorine stabilizes the carboxylate's negative charge
Chlorine changes the hybridization of the carbon it is attached to
Chlorine adds an extra acidic proton to the molecule
acidity-factors.why: Chlorine's high electronegativity withdraws electron density through the sigma bond framework, helping stabilize the adjacent carboxylate anion and thus increasing acidity relative to unsubstituted acetic acid.

acidity-factors.q: Trichloroacetic acid (pKa about 0.7) is dramatically more acidic than chloroacetic acid (pKa about 2.87), which is itself more acidic than acetic acid (pKa about 4.76). What does this trend best illustrate?
options: Only the first chlorine added has any effect, and additional ones do nothing further
Resonance is the dominant factor explaining this particular series
Inductive effects are roughly additive: each additional electron-withdrawing chlorine further stabilizes the conjugate base, progressively increasing acidity
Hybridization changes with each added chlorine in this series
acidity-factors.why: Each additional chlorine contributes further inductive electron withdrawal, and since these effects are roughly additive, going from zero to three chlorines produces a cumulative, substantial increase in acidity.

acidity-factors.q: Phenol (pKa about 10) is far more acidic than a simple alcohol like tert-butanol (pKa about 18), despite neither having a strong electron-withdrawing substituent like a halogen. What best explains this?
options: Phenol simply has a smaller atom attached to its oxygen
tert-Butanol actually has more resonance stabilization than phenol
The hybridization of oxygen differs fundamentally between the two compounds
Resonance delocalization of the negative charge from the phenoxide oxygen into the aromatic ring stabilizes the conjugate base far more than induction alone could explain
acidity-factors.why: The aromatic ring in phenoxide can accept electron density from the negatively charged oxygen through resonance, delocalizing it to the ortho and para ring positions, a stabilization pathway unavailable to a simple alkoxide like tert-butoxide.

acidity-factors.q: Para-nitrophenol (pKa about 7.2) is considerably more acidic than phenol itself (pKa about 10). Which combination of effects explains this?
options: The nitro group withdraws electron density both inductively through sigma bonds and by resonance, conjugating with the ring and the oxygen's negative charge through the para position, both stabilizing the phenoxide
The nitro group has no meaningful electronic effect, and the difference is due to molecular weight alone
The nitro group donates electrons by resonance, which destabilizes the acid form
This difference is due entirely to hybridization changes at the oxygen atom
acidity-factors.why: A para-nitro group can both inductively withdraw electron density and, through resonance reinforced by its para position, help delocalize and stabilize the phenoxide's negative charge, combining two acid-strengthening effects at once.

acidity-factors.q: Which of the following is generally considered one of the four classic factors affecting relative acidity of an X-H bond?
options: The hybridization of the atom bearing the negative charge in the conjugate base
The melting point of the acid
The optical rotation of the acid
acidity-factors.why: Hybridization of the atom holding the negative charge in the conjugate base is one of the four classic factors (atom, resonance, induction, orbital/hybridization) used to predict relative acidity.

acidity-factors.q: Formic acid (pKa about 3.75) is somewhat more acidic than acetic acid (pKa about 4.76). What is the best explanation for this difference?
options: Formic acid has resonance stabilization that acetic acid completely lacks
Acetic acid simply has a smaller molecular weight

The methyl group in acetic acid is weakly electron-donating by induction compared to the hydrogen in formic acid, slightly destabilizing the conjugate base's negative charge and making acetic acid a bit less acidic
Formic acid contains a carbon-carbon triple bond
acidity-factors.why: Alkyl groups are weakly electron-donating by induction compared to a hydrogen atom, which slightly destabilizes the negative charge on acetate's conjugate base relative to formate, making formic acid marginally more acidic.

acidity-factors.q: Larger atoms generally form weaker bonds to hydrogen, which tends to increase the acidity of that H-X bond.
acidity-factors.why: A larger atom forms a longer, weaker bond to hydrogen, making the proton easier to remove, which is part of why acidity increases going down a group, for example HI being more acidic than HF.

acidity-factors.q: Which of the following correctly ranks CH4, NH3, H2O, and HF by increasing acidity, based primarily on the atom (element) effect?
options: HF less than H2O less than NH3 less than CH4
NH3 less than CH4 less than HF less than H2O
All four are equal in acidity
CH4 less than NH3 less than H2O less than HF
acidity-factors.why: Moving left to right across period 2 (C, N, O, F), electronegativity increases, better stabilizing the conjugate base's negative charge, so acidity increases in the order CH4 less than NH3 less than H2O less than HF.

acidity-factors.q: A student argues that since fluorine is the most electronegative halogen, HF should always be the most acidic hydrogen halide. Why is this reasoning flawed?
options: Among the hydrogen halides, bond strength and atom size effects dominate over electronegativity, so HI, with the largest and weakest H-X bond, is actually the most acidic despite iodine being far less electronegative than fluorine
The reasoning is entirely correct, and HF is indeed the most acidic hydrogen halide
Electronegativity is irrelevant to every acidity trend
HF has no acidic proton at all
acidity-factors.why: While electronegativity dominates acidity trends across a period, down a group the increasing atom size and weaker, more polarizable H-X bond dominate instead, making HI far more acidic than HF even though fluorine is more electronegative.

acidity-factors.q: Protonated ketones are far more acidic than the same ketone's alpha C-H protons.
acidity-factors.why: The O-H formed by protonating a carbonyl oxygen has a pKa around -7, vastly lower than a typical alpha C-H, which has a pKa around 20, because oxygen stabilizes the resulting species far better than an unstabilized carbanion at carbon.

acidity-factors.q: Malonic acid, CH2(COOH)2, has a notably lower pKa1 (about 2.83) than acetic acid, despite having no halogen substituents. What effect explains this?
options: Resonance fully delocalizes the negative charge across both carboxyl groups equally
Inductive electron withdrawal by the second, electron-poor carbonyl-containing group nearby helps stabilize the conjugate base formed upon loss of the first proton
The two carboxyl groups change the hybridization of the central carbon to sp
There is no real acidity difference, and the pKa values are actually identical
acidity-factors.why: The second carbonyl-containing group, while not a halogen, is still electron-withdrawing by induction since carbonyl carbons are electron-poor, and its proximity to the first carboxylic acid group stabilizes the conjugate base, lowering pKa1 relative to acetic acid.

acidity-factors.q: Which acidity factor is most directly responsible for carboxylic acids (pKa about 4 to 5) being far more acidic than alcohols (pKa about 16 to 18), even though both have an O-H bond?
options: Differences in the hybridization of the oxygen atom itself
Differences in the size of the attached atom
Resonance stabilization of the carboxylate conjugate base across two equivalent oxygens, which is unavailable to a simple alkoxide
Differences in the length of the O-H bond itself
acidity-factors.why: A carboxylate's negative charge is delocalized equally over two oxygen atoms via resonance, a major stabilization unavailable to an alkoxide where the charge sits on a single oxygen, and this resonance effect is the dominant reason carboxylic acids are far more acidic than alcohols.

acidity-factors.q: Which statement about hybridization and acidity is correct?
options: Greater percent s-character always decreases acidity
Hybridization has no effect on acidity whatsoever
Greater p-character increases acidity more than greater s-character does
Greater percent s-character in the orbital holding the negative charge increases the stability of the conjugate base and increases acidity
acidity-factors.why: Orbitals with more s-character hold electron density closer to the nucleus, stabilizing a negative charge placed in that orbital, which is why sp-hybridized C-H bonds are more acidic than sp3-hybridized ones.

acidity-factors.q: Picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol) has a pKa of about 0.4, far more acidic than para-nitrophenol (pKa about 7.2) or plain phenol (pKa about 10). What best explains this extreme acidity?
options: Three nitro groups combine their inductive and resonance electron-withdrawing effects, cumulatively stabilizing the phenoxide far more than a single nitro group could alone
Only the nitro group at the 2-position matters, and the others are irrelevant
Picric acid's extreme acidity is due to its increased molecular weight
The three nitro groups act as electron donors, destabilizing the neutral acid form
acidity-factors.why: Each nitro group withdraws electron density both by induction and, when positioned ortho or para to the oxygen, by resonance; with three such groups stacking their effects, the phenoxide anion becomes extraordinarily stabilized, producing an acid nearly as strong as some mineral acids.
