sn2.q: In SN2, from which direction does the nucleophile attack the electrophilic carbon?
options: From the same side as the leaving group
From above the plane of the carbon
It attacks randomly from any direction
sn2.why: Backside attack lets the nucleophile's electron pair align with the antibonding orbital of the C-leaving group bond, which is what drives inversion.

sn2.q: Tertiary substrates readily undergo SN2 reactions because their transition state is well stabilized.
sn2.why: Tertiary carbons are surrounded by three alkyl groups that sterically block the nucleophile from approaching from the backside, so SN2 is essentially shut down.

sn2.q: What geometric shape describes the transition state of an SN2 reaction?
sn2.why: In the transition state the carbon is partially bonded to both the incoming nucleophile and the departing leaving group, giving five groups arranged around it.

sn2.q: Methyl halides (CH3X) react in SN2 reactions:
options: Exceptionally fast, since there is no steric hindrance
Exceptionally slow, since there is no nearby stabilization
Not at all, since there is no beta-hydrogen
sn2.why: With no substituents around the reacting carbon at all, the nucleophile has a completely open path for backside attack.

sn2.q: SN2 reactions occur in a single concerted step with no intermediate forming along the way.
sn2.why: Bond-breaking and bond-forming happen simultaneously in one transition state, unlike the two-step SN1 mechanism.

sn2.q: Ranking CH3Br, (CH3)2CHBr, and (CH3)3CBr by SN2 reaction rate, which order is correct?
options: All three react at the same rate
sn2.why: SN2 rate decreases as alkyl substitution increases because more groups crowd the backside approach path; methyl is fastest and tertiary essentially does not react.

sn2.q: Among F-, Cl-, Br-, and I- as leaving groups on the same carbon skeleton, which gives the fastest SN2 reaction?
sn2.why: Iodide is the weakest base of the four and the most stable once it leaves, making it the best leaving group and giving the fastest reaction.

sn2.q: Neopentyl bromide, (CH3)3CCH2Br, is technically a primary halide but reacts very slowly via SN2. Why?
options: It is secretly a tertiary halide
Bromide is a poor leaving group in this molecule
The bulky adjacent quaternary carbon blocks backside attack even though the reacting carbon itself is primary
sn2.why: Steric hindrance isn't limited to the reacting carbon itself; a bulky neighboring group can crowd the backside approach just as effectively.

sn2.q: For the same substrate, which nucleophile reacts faster in SN2: CH3O- or neutral CH3OH?
options: CH3O-, because it carries a full negative charge and is a stronger nucleophile
CH3OH, because it is less reactive and therefore more selective
They react at the same rate
CH3OH, because it is a better leaving group
sn2.why: Removing a proton from the nucleophile to generate its anion greatly increases its electron-donating ability, so the charged species attacks much faster.

sn2.q: Increasing the strength of the nucleophile speeds up SN2 reactions but has essentially no effect on SN1 reaction rates.
sn2.why: SN2 rate depends directly on nucleophile concentration and strength, while SN1 rate depends only on substrate ionization, which doesn't involve the nucleophile at all.

sn2.q: When a single enantiomer of a chiral secondary alkyl halide reacts with CN- via SN2, what is the stereochemical outcome at the reacting carbon?
options: The configuration is inverted relative to the starting material
sn2.why: Backside attack forces the three remaining groups to flip through the carbon like an umbrella turning inside out, inverting the spatial arrangement.

sn2.q: Why do SN2 reactions essentially never occur at vinyl (sp2, C=C) or aryl carbons?
options: Vinyl and aryl leaving groups are always too good
There are no nucleophiles strong enough
Backside approach is blocked by the pi system and the carbon's geometry
The C-H bonds are too strong
sn2.why: The trigonal planar geometry and the pi electron density around an sp2 carbon prevent the clean backside trajectory that SN2 requires.

sn2.q: SN2 reactions are known for proceeding with a single inversion of configuration, often called:
sn2.why: This classic term describes the clean flip in spatial arrangement caused by backside nucleophilic attack.

sn2.q: In SN2, what is the approximate bond angle between the incoming nucleophile, the central carbon, and the departing leaving group at the moment of the transition state?
sn2.why: Backside attack means the nucleophile approaches directly opposite the leaving group, so the two are roughly in a straight line through the central carbon at the transition state.

sn2.q: Which property makes a species a particularly good nucleophile for SN2, somewhat independent of how basic it is?
options: High polarizability (a soft, easily distorted electron cloud)
sn2.why: A polarizable nucleophile, like iodide, can more easily distort its electron cloud toward the electrophilic carbon during the approach, even if it is a comparatively weak base.

sn2.q: For a cyclohexane ring, SN2 backside attack on C1 proceeds fastest when the leaving group at C1 is positioned:
options: Equatorial, since the ring doesn't block the approach
It makes no difference in a chair conformation
Axial, since this leaves an open trajectory for backside attack
Neither position allows any SN2 reaction
sn2.why: When the leaving group is axial, the nucleophile can approach from the opposite axial direction without the ring itself blocking the path; an equatorial leaving group has its backside trajectory obstructed by the ring.

sn2.q: Compared to a simple secondary alkyl bromide, an allylic secondary bromide typically reacts faster in SN2. Why?
options: Allylic carbons are less hindered than ordinary secondary carbons
Allylic systems always form carbocations first
Allylic bromide is simply a better leaving group
The developing transition state gets extra stabilization from partial conjugation with the adjacent pi system
sn2.why: Even though no cation forms in SN2, the nearby double bond can partially delocalize electron density in the transition state, lowering its energy.

sn2.q: A secondary substrate is combined with a strong, very bulky base such as tert-butoxide. Why does this combination usually give mostly elimination rather than SN2?
options: The bulky base's steric bulk prevents it from approaching the backside of the carbon for substitution, so it instead removes a more accessible beta-hydrogen
Tert-butoxide is too weak a base to act as a nucleophile at all
Secondary substrates cannot undergo SN2 under any circumstances
Bulky bases always decompose before reacting
sn2.why: Steric bulk mainly interferes with the tight backside approach needed for substitution, while the base can still reach outward hydrogens for elimination.

sn2.q: An SN2 reaction between a negatively charged nucleophile and a neutral substrate is slowed in polar protic solvents because the solvent hydrogen-bonds to and stabilizes the nucleophile, raising the activation energy needed for it to attack.
sn2.why: Solvating (caging) the nucleophile with hydrogen bonds lowers its ground-state energy and effectively shields it, so more energy is needed to free it for attack.

sn2.q: Why does increasing the bulk of the alkyl substituents at the reacting carbon, from primary to tertiary, always slow SN2, regardless of any electronic stabilization those groups might otherwise provide?
options: More alkyl groups always destabilize the leaving group
Steric hindrance to backside attack dominates over any electronic effect, since the transition state physically cannot form if the nucleophile cannot reach the carbon
More alkyl groups make the carbon less electrophilic in a way that outweighs sterics
Bulkier substrates have weaker carbon-leaving group bonds
sn2.why: SN2's single transition state has an absolute geometric requirement (backside approach); no amount of favorable electronics can compensate if that pathway is physically blocked.

sn2.q: Which combination of conditions gives the fastest possible SN2 rate?
options: Tertiary substrate, weak bulky nucleophile, polar protic solvent, and a poor leaving group
Secondary substrate, weak nucleophile, nonpolar solvent, and a poor leaving group
Primary substrate, strong small nucleophile, polar aprotic solvent, and a good leaving group
Primary substrate, weak bulky nucleophile, polar protic solvent, and a good leaving group
sn2.why: Every one of these factors independently speeds up SN2: an open backside path, a reactive unshielded nucleophile, and a stable departing group.

sn2.q: Switching the solvent for an SN2 reaction with Cl- as the nucleophile from acetone (polar aprotic) to methanol (polar protic) typically has what effect on rate?
options: The rate increases, because methanol better stabilizes the transition state
There is no change, since solvent never affects SN2
The rate increases because methanol is more polar
The rate decreases, because methanol hydrogen-bonds to and cages the chloride nucleophile
sn2.why: Protic solvents solvate small anionic nucleophiles tightly through hydrogen bonding, tying up the electron density that would otherwise attack the substrate.

sn2.q: Treating (S)-2-bromopentane with NaN3 under SN2 conditions gives a product with which stereochemical relationship to the starting material at the reacting carbon?
options: Inverted spatial configuration at that carbon
A racemic mixture at that carbon
sn2.why: Azide attacks from the backside in a single concerted step, flipping the spatial arrangement at the carbon that held the leaving group.

sn1.q: SN1 reactions proceed through what kind of mechanism?
options: A stepwise mechanism via a carbocation intermediate
sn1.why: SN1 ("unimolecular") has two steps: ionization to form a carbocation, then nucleophilic attack on that cation.

sn1.q: SN1 reactions are favored at which type of carbon?
sn1.why: Tertiary carbocations are the most stable (hyperconjugation/inductive effects from 3 alkyl groups), so SN1 favors tertiary substrates.

sn1.q: Why does SN1 typically give a mixture of stereoisomers (racemization) at the reacting center?
options: The leaving group returns every time
The flat, planar carbocation intermediate can be attacked from either face
sn1.why: Once the carbocation forms, it is planar (sp²) and symmetric, so the nucleophile can attack from either face with roughly equal probability, giving racemization.

sn1.q: SN1 reaction rate depends on the concentration of which species?
sn1.why: SN1 is unimolecular in its rate-determining step, so only the substrate's concentration appears in the rate law.

sn1.q: SN1 is a two-step mechanism that passes through a carbocation intermediate.
sn1.why: The leaving group departs first to form a planar carbocation, and only then does the nucleophile attack in a separate second step.

sn1.q: Which step of SN1 is rate-determining?
options: Ionization of the substrate to form the carbocation
Attack of the nucleophile on the carbocation
Solvation of the leaving group after it departs
sn1.why: Breaking the C-leaving group bond without any assistance is the slow, high-energy step; capturing the cation afterward is fast.

sn1.q: SN1 reactions are favored by leaving groups that are:
options: Poor leaving groups that are strong bases
Good leaving groups (weak bases that form stable anions)
Leaving groups with a double bond character
Leaving groups that cannot be protonated
sn1.why: Since ionization is rate-determining, anything that stabilizes the departing group once it leaves speeds up the whole reaction.

sn1.q: SN1 reactions proceed with complete inversion of stereochemistry at the reacting carbon.
sn1.why: The flat carbocation intermediate can be attacked from either face, so the product is typically a racemic (or nearly racemic) mixture rather than cleanly inverted.

sn1.q: Which solvent type most favors SN1 reactions?
options: Solvent choice never matters for SN1
sn1.why: Polar protic solvents can hydrogen-bond to and stabilize both the developing carbocation and the departing anion, speeding up the ionization step.

sn1.q: Methyl and primary substrates essentially never react via SN1.
sn1.why: Methyl and primary carbocations are far too unstable to form at any appreciable rate, so ionization never gets going.

sn1.q: SN1 reaction rate is independent of the nucleophile's concentration.
sn1.why: Because the nucleophile only participates in the fast second step, changing its concentration does not change the overall observed rate.

sn1.q: What is the overall reaction order typically observed for an SN1 reaction?
sn1.why: Since the rate-determining step involves only the substrate breaking apart, the overall rate law is first order in substrate.

sn1.q: Rank the following carbocations from most to least stable: methyl, primary, secondary, tertiary.
sn1.why: More alkyl substituents donate electron density and provide hyperconjugation to the empty p-orbital, stabilizing the positive charge; tertiary cations are stabilized the most.

sn1.q: Which phenomenon can accompany SN1 reactions but essentially never occurs in SN2?
sn1.why: Because SN1 generates a real, freestanding carbocation intermediate, that intermediate has time to rearrange to a more stable cation before being trapped.

sn1.q: A 1,2-hydride shift can convert a less stable secondary carbocation into a more stable tertiary carbocation during an SN1 reaction.
sn1.why: A neighboring hydrogen can migrate with its bonding electrons to the cationic carbon, shifting the positive charge to a position where it is better stabilized.

sn1.q: Allylic and benzylic halides react readily via SN1 even though they are often only secondary or primary. Why?
options: They have unusually good leaving groups
They cannot undergo any other mechanism
Resonance delocalizes and stabilizes the resulting carbocation
Their carbocations are tertiary in disguise
sn1.why: The adjacent pi system spreads the positive charge over multiple atoms through resonance, which lowers the cation's energy similarly to extra alkyl substitution.

sn1.q: Comparing a tertiary alkyl chloride to the otherwise identical tertiary alkyl iodide under SN1 conditions, which reacts faster, and why?
options: The chloride, because chlorine is more electronegative
The chloride, because it ionizes in a different mechanism entirely
The iodide, because the C-I bond is weaker and iodide is a more stable, better leaving group
sn1.why: A weaker carbon-halogen bond combined with a more stable leaving anion makes ionization easier and faster for the iodide.

sn1.q: Weak nucleophiles such as water or alcohols are well suited as the nucleophile in SN1 reactions because the overall rate does not depend on nucleophile strength.
sn1.why: Since the slow step only involves the substrate ionizing, even a weak nucleophile can still efficiently capture the carbocation once it forms.

sn1.q: Starting from a single pure enantiomer, what is the typical stereochemical outcome of the product mixture from an SN1 reaction at that center?
options: Mostly racemic, sometimes with a slight excess of the inverted product
Perfectly and completely racemic with no exceptions
Fully inverted configuration, just like SN2
sn1.why: The planar carbocation can in principle be attacked equally from both faces, giving near-racemization, though ion pairing can sometimes partially shield one face and skew the ratio slightly.

sn1.q: What kind of solvent effect accelerates the rate-determining step of an SN1 reaction?
sn1.why: A more polar, ionizing solvent stabilizes the separating charges (the carbocation and the departing anion) as the bond breaks, lowering the activation energy.

sn1.q: Why do vinyl and aryl halides essentially never undergo SN1?
options: Vinyl and aryl halides have unusually strong carbon-halogen bonds
There is no possible nucleophile that could trap such a cation
The resulting vinylic or aryl cation would be extremely unstable, since the empty orbital is sp2 and poorly stabilized
SN1 requires a double bond to already be present
sn1.why: Vinylic and aryl cations place the positive charge in an sp2 orbital that is not well stabilized by the adjacent pi system, making ionization prohibitively unfavorable.

sn1.q: For a tertiary substrate, which solvent type gives a faster SN1 rate: polar protic or polar aprotic?
options: Polar aprotic, since it leaves the nucleophile unshielded
Neither solvent type affects SN1 rate
Polar protic, since it can hydrogen-bond to stabilize the developing cation and the leaving anion
sn1.why: SN1's rate-determining step is ionization, which benefits specifically from a solvent that can stabilize charged species through hydrogen bonding.

sn1.q: Tert-butyl bromide is hydrolyzed faster in pure water than in a 50:50 water-ethanol mixture. Why?
options: Pure water has higher polarity and ionizing power, so adding ethanol lowers the rate by diluting that polarity
Ethanol is a stronger nucleophile that outcompetes water
Water cannot dissolve tert-butyl bromide at all
Ethanol reacts with the bromide ion before it can leave
sn1.why: Since the rate-determining step is ionization, anything that lowers the solvent's overall polarity and ability to stabilize charge slows the reaction, even if both solvents are polar protic.

sn1.q: A secondary carbocation can undergo a methyl shift to a more stable cation before being trapped by a nucleophile. Why does this rearrangement happen?
options: The nucleophile forces the shift to occur
Migration to a more stable cation lowers the overall energy of the system before the nucleophile captures it
Methyl shifts only occur in SN2 reactions
The leaving group pulls the methyl group away
sn1.why: A carbocation intermediate has a finite lifetime in which nearby groups can migrate with their bonding electrons if doing so reaches a more stable, lower-energy structure.

sn1.q: The common ion effect can suppress SN1 rate when excess of the leaving group's conjugate anion is added, because it shifts the reversible ionization step backward.
sn1.why: Ionization is an equilibrium; adding more of the product anion pushes that equilibrium back toward the un-ionized substrate, slowing the forward (productive) rate.

sn1.q: Why does SN1 at a chiral tertiary center rarely give exactly 100% racemization in practice?
options: The carbocation is never actually planar
Nucleophiles always attack from the same side as the leaving group
Ion pairing can let the departing leaving group briefly shield one face of the flat carbocation, giving a slight excess of the inverted product
SN1 always proceeds with complete inversion, never racemization
sn1.why: Before it fully diffuses away, the leaving group can linger near one face of the cation as a tight ion pair, partially blocking nucleophilic attack from that side.

sn1.q: Which cation is more stable, and why: a simple tertiary alkyl cation, or a tertiary benzylic cation?
options: The simple tertiary cation, since aromatic rings destabilize adjacent cations
Benzylic cations cannot form at all
The benzylic cation, due to additional resonance delocalization into the aromatic ring
sn1.why: A benzylic cation can spread its positive charge into the ring through resonance in addition to any alkyl hyperconjugation, adding extra stabilization beyond a purely alkyl-substituted cation.

sn1.q: Ranking 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, 2-chlorobutane, and chloroethane by SN1 reactivity, which order is correct?
options: All three react at similar rates
sn1.why: SN1 rate tracks carbocation stability, and stability increases from primary to secondary to tertiary, so the tertiary chloride ionizes fastest and the primary essentially does not react.

sn1.q: Why is SN1 solvolysis of an alkyl halide often accompanied by E1 elimination byproducts?
options: E1 and SN1 are actually the same mechanism with different names
The same carbocation intermediate can either be captured by a nucleophile (substitution) or lose a beta-hydrogen to a base (elimination), so both pathways compete
Elimination only happens after substitution is already complete
The leaving group itself acts as a base after it departs
sn1.why: Once the carbocation forms, nothing commits it to one specific fate; it is simply captured by whichever available species reacts with it first.

sn1.q: A tertiary alkyl halide is dissolved in pure formic acid, a highly polar, strongly ionizing, but weakly nucleophilic protic solvent. What is the expected SN1 rate?
options: Very slow, because a weak nucleophile cannot drive SN1 at all
Unpredictable, since nucleophile strength is the only factor that matters for SN1
Very fast, because the solvent's strong ionizing power stabilizes the cation and leaving group even though it is a weak nucleophile
Identical to a nonpolar solvent, since nucleophilicity controls SN1 rate
sn1.why: Because the nucleophile isn't involved in the rate-determining step, a solvent's ionizing power (not its nucleophilicity) is what controls SN1 rate.

e1.q: E1 elimination shares its first step with which substitution mechanism?
e1.why: E1 and SN1 both begin by ionizing the leaving group to form a carbocation; E1 then loses a proton instead of being attacked by a nucleophile.

e1.q: In E1, which alkene product is usually favored?
e1.why: E1 goes through a carbocation and loses a proton to give the most stable (most substituted) alkene — the Zaitsev product.

e1.q: E1 reactions are often seen competing with which other mechanism, since both start from the same carbocation intermediate?
e1.why: E1 and SN1 share the same first step (ionization to a carbocation); from there the cation either loses a proton (E1, elimination) or is attacked by a nucleophile (SN1, substitution).

e1.q: E1 is a two-step mechanism; which step is rate-determining?
options: Removal of the beta-hydrogen by a base
Formation of the carbocation (loss of the leaving group)
e1.why: Just like SN1, the slow step is ionization to form the carbocation; deprotonation afterward is fast.

e1.q: E1 reactions, like SN1, are unimolecular in their rate-determining step.
e1.why: Both mechanisms share the same first step, the unassisted departure of the leaving group to generate a carbocation, which depends only on substrate concentration.

e1.q: What is removed in the second step of E1, once the carbocation has already formed?
options: A proton (H+) from a carbon adjacent to the cation
The leaving group a second time
A hydride ion from the cationic carbon itself
An electron pair from the solvent
e1.why: A base plucks off a hydrogen from a neighboring (beta) carbon, and the electrons from that C-H bond form the new pi bond.

e1.q: E1 requires a strong, bulky base to proceed, in the same way that achieving good selectivity in E2 does.
e1.why: Because deprotonation in E1 happens fast and isn't rate-limiting, even a weak base can remove the proton once the cation has formed; strict base strength or geometry is not required.

e1.q: E1 is favored by which type of substrate?
options: Tertiary (and to a lesser extent secondary) substrates that can form stable carbocations
e1.why: Since the first step is identical to SN1, E1 needs a substrate capable of forming a reasonably stable carbocation.

e1.q: E1 reactions typically occur under conditions of heat with a weak base/nucleophile present.
e1.why: Heat favors elimination pathways generally, and since the rate-determining step doesn't need a strong base, a weak one is often sufficient to pull off the final proton.

e1.q: What determines the overall rate of an E1 reaction?
options: The concentration of both substrate and base
The concentration of the base alone
The concentration of the substrate alone
e1.why: E1 is first order overall because its rate-determining step, ionization, only involves the substrate.

e1.q: Which side phenomenon, common to SN1, can also occur during E1 and scramble the carbon skeleton before elimination finishes?
e1.why: Because E1 shares the same carbocation intermediate as SN1, that cation can rearrange to a more stable structure before a proton is ever removed.

e1.q: Immediately after the leaving group departs in E1, what is the hybridization of the carbon that held it?
e1.why: Losing the leaving group leaves behind an empty p-orbital on a planar, trigonal carbon, exactly as in SN1's carbocation intermediate.

e1.q: Among several possible alkenes from E1 dehydrohalogenation of a secondary carbocation, why is the more substituted (Zaitsev) alkene usually favored?
options: Less substituted alkenes cannot form from a carbocation
A more substituted double bond is stabilized by greater alkyl hyperconjugation, making it lower in energy
The more substituted alkene always forms first kinetically
Base strength alone determines which alkene forms
e1.why: More alkyl groups attached to the double bond carbons donate electron density into the pi system, lowering its overall energy and making that alkene more stable and, usually, more abundant.

e1.q: What effect does raising the temperature typically have on the E1 versus SN1 product ratio from the same substrate and solvent?
options: Higher temperature favors substitution (SN1) over elimination (E1)
Temperature has no effect on the E1/SN1 ratio
Higher temperature favors elimination (E1) over substitution (SN1)
Higher temperature stops the reaction entirely
e1.why: Elimination pathways generally have a more favorable entropy of activation, so heating a reaction mixture tends to push the product distribution toward more alkene.

e1.q: An E1 reaction can proceed through a carbocation rearrangement before the final proton is lost, giving an alkene skeleton different from simple dehydrohalogenation.
e1.why: If the initially formed cation rearranges to a more stable one, the final elimination step occurs from that rearranged structure, changing the product's carbon skeleton.

e1.q: 3-chloro-3-methylpentane undergoes E1 solvolysis with heat. Which alkene is the expected major product?
options: No alkene forms; only substitution occurs
e1.why: E1 deprotonation under Zaitsev control favors loss of the hydrogen that produces the most stable, most substituted double bond.

e1.q: Which change best increases the E1-to-SN1 product ratio for a given tertiary substrate's solvolysis?
options: Raising the temperature or introducing a base rather than just a weak nucleophile/solvent
Switching to a worse leaving group
e1.why: Heat favors the entropically-preferred elimination pathway, and having an actual base present (rather than just a weak nucleophilic solvent) makes proton removal more competitive with nucleophilic capture.

e1.q: Unlike E2, E1 has no strict geometric requirement, such as anti-periplanar alignment, between the leaving group and the hydrogen being removed.
e1.why: Since the leaving group and the beta-hydrogen depart in two separate steps through a freely rotating carbocation, there's no need for them to have been aligned in any particular way beforehand.

e1.q: Why do polar protic solvents favor E1 (and SN1) over E2?
options: They make the beta-hydrogens more acidic
They stabilize the cationic intermediate, promoting the ionization step that both E1 and SN1 depend on
They prevent the formation of any pi bond
They increase the concentration of the base
e1.why: E1's rate-determining step is identical to SN1's, so any solvent effect that helps stabilize a developing carbocation speeds up E1 specifically.

e1.q: How does the nucleophile/base concentration affect the overall rate law of E1?
options: It appears squared in the rate law
It appears linearly, just as in E2
It doesn't appear in the rate law at all, since it only acts in the fast second step
It determines the rate but not which alkene forms
e1.why: Because the second (deprotonation) step is fast and not rate-limiting, the concentration of the base influences product selectivity far more than it influences overall reaction rate.

e1.q: A secondary carbocation in an E1 reaction can lose either of two different beta-hydrogens, giving alkene A (more substituted) or alkene B (less substituted). Which is the expected major product?
options: Alkene B, since less substituted alkenes are always kinetically preferred
Both alkenes form in exactly equal amounts in every case
Neither forms; the carbocation is trapped by the leaving group instead
Alkene A, following Zaitsev's rule that the more stable, more substituted alkene predominates
e1.why: With no strict geometric constraint like E2's anti-periplanar requirement, E1 product selection is governed mainly by the relative stability of the possible alkenes.

e1.q: A secondary carbocation in an E1 reaction undergoes a hydride shift to a more stable tertiary cation before elimination occurs. What is the likely result?
options: A rearranged alkene, different in skeleton from the product expected from simple, unrearranged dehydrohalogenation
Exactly the same alkene that simple dehydrohalogenation would predict
No alkene at all, since rearranged cations cannot eliminate
A mixture of the starting alkyl halide's two enantiomers
e1.why: Elimination proceeds from whichever cation is actually present at that moment, so if rearrangement occurs first, the final alkene reflects the new, rearranged carbon skeleton.

e1.q: Why can E1 and SN1 give a surprisingly complex product mixture when a carbocation rearranges partway through the reaction?
options: Rearrangement always stops the reaction completely
Both the original and the rearranged cation can independently be captured by a nucleophile or lose a proton, multiplying the number of possible product pathways
Only the rearranged cation can ever react further
e1.why: Each distinct carbocation present in solution, whether original or rearranged, has its own competing fates (substitution or elimination), so the overall outcome can be a mixture of several structurally different products.

e1.q: Because E1 proceeds through a planar carbocation, the E/Z geometry of the resulting alkene is determined mainly by which beta-hydrogen is removed and the relative thermodynamic stability of the resulting alkenes, rather than by a fixed stereochemical requirement from the starting material.
e1.why: Since the cation can rotate freely before deprotonation, there is no anti-periplanar-style constraint linking starting material stereochemistry to product alkene geometry; stability considerations dominate instead.

e1.q: Comparing tert-butyl chloride and tert-butyl iodide in the same solvent, which undergoes E1 faster, and why?
options: Tert-butyl chloride, because chlorine is more electronegative
They react at the same rate since both are tertiary
Tert-butyl iodide, because the weaker C-I bond and more stable iodide ion make ionization easier
Tert-butyl iodide reacts slower because iodide is too large
e1.why: Since E1's rate-determining step is the same ionization step as SN1's, a better leaving group accelerates E1 in exactly the same way it accelerates SN1.

e1.q: In a mixed water/ethanol solvolysis of a tertiary alkyl halide, what happens to E1 rate as ethanol content is increased (lowering overall solvent polarity)?
options: The rate increases, since ethanol is a stronger base than water
The rate is unaffected by solvent composition
The mechanism switches entirely to E2
The rate decreases, since lower polarity and ionizing power slow the carbocation-forming step
e1.why: E1's rate-determining ionization step is highly sensitive to how well the solvent can stabilize developing charge, so diluting the more polar water with less polar ethanol slows that step.

e1.q: Why might E1 show greater selectivity for the thermodynamically most stable (Zaitsev) alkene than E2 does on the same substrate?
options: The long-lived carbocation intermediate in E1 allows the system to favor whichever elimination pathway leads to the most stable alkene, giving the reaction more thermodynamic character than E2's single concerted transition state
E2 never produces the Zaitsev product under any conditions
E1 cannot produce the Hofmann product under any conditions
Carbocations are always more stable than alkenes
e1.why: Because the cation exists as a discrete intermediate, there is more opportunity for the more stable transition state (leading to the more stable alkene) to be favored, compared to E2's single, more geometry-constrained step.

e1.q: Adding excess of the leaving group's conjugate anion (for example, extra Cl- during solvolysis of an alkyl chloride) to an E1 reaction has what effect on rate?
options: It increases the rate, since it stabilizes the transition state
It decreases the rate, since it pushes the reversible ionization equilibrium back toward the starting substrate
It has no effect, since the leaving group anion cannot influence ionization
It converts the mechanism to E2
e1.why: Ionization is an equilibrium step; adding more of the anion product (common ion effect) shifts that equilibrium backward and slows the overall forward reaction.

e1.q: Why can very weak or sterically hindered bases still readily bring about E1 elimination, even though they would be poor at driving E2?
options: Weak bases cannot remove protons at all, so E1 never actually needs step two
E1 does not actually require any base
Because deprotonation in E1 isn't rate-limiting, even a weak or hindered base can remove the proton once the carbocation has already formed, without needing strict geometry or great basicity
Hindered bases are always stronger than small bases
e1.why: Unlike E2, where the base must be strong and well-positioned to drive a single slow concerted step, E1's second step is inherently fast and forgiving of a less capable base.

e1.q: 2-bromo-2-methylbutane undergoes E1 elimination with heat in aqueous ethanol. What is the expected major alkene product?
options: No alkene forms, only the substitution alcohol product
e1.why: Following Zaitsev's rule, E1 favors loss of the beta-hydrogen that generates the more stable, more highly substituted double bond.

e2.q: E2 elimination occurs in how many mechanistic steps?
options: It has no defined number of steps
e2.why: E2 ("bimolecular elimination") is concerted: base removes a proton as the leaving group departs, all in one step.

e2.q: E2 requires the leaving group and the departing H to be in what relationship for the best geometry?
e2.why: Anti-periplanar alignment lets the breaking C–H bond’s electrons align with the empty orbital forming as the leaving group departs — the best orbital overlap.

e2.q: Why do bulky bases (like tert-butoxide) favor E2 over SN2?
options: Bulky bases are never strong bases
Steric bulk hinders backside attack on carbon (poor SN2) but doesn’t hinder removing an exposed proton (good E2)
There is no relationship between base size and mechanism
e2.why: A bulky base struggles to approach the crowded carbon for SN2 backside attack, but has no trouble reaching an exposed, less hindered proton for E2.

e2.q: What is the rate law for a typical E2 reaction?
options: Rate = k[substrate]^2, second order in substrate
e2.why: Since the base participates directly in the single concerted step, both the substrate and the base concentrations appear in the rate law.

e2.q: E2 is a concerted, one-step mechanism with no intermediate forming.
e2.why: Proton removal, pi bond formation, and loss of the leaving group all happen at the same time in a single transition state.

e2.q: Which bonds break and form simultaneously during the single step of E2?
options: The beta C-H bond and the C-leaving group bond break, while a new C=C pi bond forms
Only the C-leaving group bond breaks
Only the beta C-H bond breaks
A new sigma bond forms between the base and the leaving group
e2.why: All of this bond reorganization occurs in one coordinated transition state, which is what makes E2 concerted rather than stepwise.

e2.q: Efficient E2 elimination generally requires what kind of base?
options: A strong base, often one that is also a relatively poor nucleophile
No base is actually needed for E2
e2.why: A strong base is needed to remove the relatively unreactive beta-hydrogen in a single concerted step, and bases that are poor nucleophiles help elimination compete successfully against substitution.

e2.q: What does the base remove during an E2 reaction?
options: A hydrogen on the same carbon as the leaving group
A hydrogen on the carbon adjacent (beta) to the one bearing the leaving group
An electron from the pi bond
e2.why: Removing a beta-hydrogen, rather than the leaving group's carbon itself, is what allows the new double bond to form between those two adjacent carbons.

e2.q: Increasing the concentration of the base in an E2 reaction has what effect on rate?
options: It has no effect on rate
It only affects which alkene forms, not the rate
It increases the rate proportionally, since E2 is first order in base
e2.why: Since base concentration appears directly in the E2 rate law, doubling it doubles the reaction rate (all else equal).

e2.q: E2 reactions can occur on primary, secondary, and tertiary substrates.
e2.why: Unlike SN2 (blocked at tertiary carbons) or SN1/E1 (essentially unavailable at primary carbons), E2 doesn't require carbocation formation or backside attack at the leaving-group carbon, so it tolerates all substitution levels.

e2.q: Why are tertiary substrates often the substrate of choice for E2 with a strong base, rather than for SN2?
options: Steric hindrance at the tertiary carbon blocks backside SN2 attack, while the strong base can still remove a nearby beta-hydrogen
Tertiary carbons have no beta-hydrogens at all
E2 only works on tertiary substrates
Tertiary carbons form the least stable alkenes
e2.why: E2 doesn't need to approach the crowded leaving-group carbon directly; the base simply needs access to a hydrogen on an adjacent carbon, which is much less hindered.

e2.q: A substrate that has only one type of beta-hydrogen available typically gives how many distinct alkene connectivity products from E2 (ignoring E/Z isomerism)?
options: Zero, since elimination requires multiple beta-hydrogen types
e2.why: If there's only a single position from which a beta-hydrogen can be removed, there is only one possible carbon-skeleton outcome for the alkene, though E and Z isomers may still both form.

e2.q: With a small, non-bulky strong base like ethoxide, which alkene is typically the major E2 product, according to Zaitsev's rule?
options: Whichever alkene has the lowest molecular weight
Only the terminal alkene, regardless of stability
e2.why: Small bases can reach any available beta-hydrogen, so the more stable transition state leading to the more substituted alkene is generally favored.

e2.q: Switching from a small strong base to a bulky base like tert-butoxide on the same substrate typically shifts the major E2 product toward:
options: A mixture of substitution products only
No change in alkene distribution at all
e2.why: A bulky base has trouble reaching the more crowded, more substituted hydrogens, so it preferentially grabs a more exposed, less hindered hydrogen, giving the less substituted alkene.

e2.q: In most acyclic and many cyclic substrates, efficient E2 elimination requires the leaving group and the beta-hydrogen being removed to be in what geometric relationship?
e2.why: This geometry lets the orbitals that are breaking and forming align properly in a single transition state, minimizing torsional strain as the pi bond develops.

e2.q: In a cyclohexane ring, why must the leaving group and the beta-hydrogen both be axial for efficient E2 elimination?
options: Axial positions are always more accessible to the base
Only diaxial substituents on adjacent ring carbons are anti-periplanar in the chair conformation, aligning the orbitals needed for the concerted step
Equatorial substituents cannot leave the ring under any conditions
Axial hydrogens are always more acidic
e2.why: The chair conformation's geometry means only two adjacent axial groups are oriented 180 degrees apart from each other, which is the alignment E2 needs.

e2.q: 2-bromobutane is treated with NaOEt, a strong, non-bulky base. What is the expected major E2 alkene product?
options: A 50:50 mixture of 1-butene and 2-butene with no preference
2-butene (the more substituted, Zaitsev product), with the E isomer usually predominating
No alkene forms under these conditions
e2.why: A small strong base reaches the internal beta-hydrogens easily, so the more stable, more substituted double bond is favored, and the less sterically strained E geometry is typically the major stereoisomer.

e2.q: When E2 with a small base produces both E and Z alkene isomers, which one tends to predominate?
options: The Z (cis) isomer, since it forms faster kinetically
Both form in exactly equal amounts every time
Neither forms; only the less substituted alkene forms
The E (trans) isomer, since its transition state has less steric strain
e2.why: The transition state leading to the E alkene generally has larger groups positioned farther apart, lowering steric strain and making it the lower-energy, more commonly favored pathway.

e2.q: E2 reactions are generally less sensitive to changes in solvent polarity than SN1 or E1 reactions are.
e2.why: Because E2 is concerted and doesn't generate a free ionic intermediate, it doesn't depend as strongly on a solvent's ability to stabilize charge the way the ionization step of SN1/E1 does.

e2.q: Why does a secondary substrate reacting with a small, strong base/nucleophile like NaOH often give a mixture of SN2 and E2 products?
options: The same species can act as both a strong nucleophile (attacking for substitution) and a strong base (removing a proton for elimination), so the two pathways compete
NaOH cannot act as a nucleophile under any conditions
Secondary substrates can never undergo SN2
E2 never competes with SN2 on secondary substrates
e2.why: Hydroxide is simultaneously a good nucleophile and a good base, so on a substrate that is accessible enough for backside attack, both substitution and elimination pathways remain viable and compete.

e2.q: How does leaving group quality affect E2 rate, compared to its effect on SN2?
options: Leaving group quality has no effect on E2 rate, unlike SN2
Better leaving groups (e.g., I- > Br- > Cl- > F-) speed up E2, just as they do SN2
Worse leaving groups speed up E2 while better ones speed up SN2
Leaving group quality only matters for E1, not E2
e2.why: Since the leaving group departs in the same single step as proton removal, a more stable, easier-to-lose leaving group lowers the activation energy for E2 just as it does for SN2.

e2.q: In a disubstituted cyclohexane where the only beta-hydrogen on one side happens to be equatorial (not anti-periplanar to an axial leaving group), what happens to E2 elimination toward that side?
options: It proceeds normally regardless of the hydrogen's orientation
E2 switches automatically to E1 in that situation
It cannot occur toward that side; elimination is forced toward a different available anti-periplanar hydrogen, or the ring must flip if possible
The leaving group becomes equatorial instead to compensate
e2.why: Without a hydrogen positioned anti-periplanar to the leaving group on that side, the required transition-state geometry simply cannot be reached, so that elimination pathway is blocked.

e2.q: Menthyl chloride has only one beta-hydrogen that is trans-diaxial (anti-periplanar) to its chlorine. Why does its E2 reaction often give the less substituted (anti-Zaitsev) alkene as the major product?
options: Menthyl chloride has no accessible beta-hydrogens at all
Less substituted alkenes are always favored in E2, regardless of geometry
The chlorine in menthyl chloride is a poor leaving group
Only that one specific hydrogen is geometrically accessible for anti-periplanar elimination, regardless of whether it leads to the more or less stable alkene
e2.why: E2's strict geometric requirement can override simple product-stability preferences; if the only anti-periplanar hydrogen happens to give the less stable alkene, that's still the product that forms.

e2.q: The strict anti-periplanar requirement of E2 means that the stereochemistry of a specific diastereomer of starting material can determine which alkene stereoisomer (E or Z) actually forms.
e2.why: Because only certain conformations place a given hydrogen anti-periplanar to the leaving group, the starting material's three-dimensional arrangement directly dictates which hydrogen is removed and therefore the resulting double bond geometry.

e2.q: Why are deuterium kinetic isotope effects observed when comparing C-H versus C-D cleavage in E2, but not typically in SN2?
options: In E2, breaking the beta C-H (or C-D) bond occurs in the single rate-determining step, so replacing H with heavier D measurably slows the reaction; in SN2 no C-H bond breaks in the rate-determining step
Deuterium always reacts faster than hydrogen in every mechanism
SN2 never involves any hydrogen atoms
E2 does not actually involve breaking any C-H bond
e2.why: A kinetic isotope effect appears specifically when the bond to the isotope is broken in the rate-determining step; since E2's only step breaks the beta C-H bond, while SN2's step does not touch that bond at all, only E2 shows this effect.

e2.q: Switching the base on a secondary substrate from hydroxide to much bulkier tert-butoxide typically has what combined effect on E2?
options: The rate always increases dramatically with no change in selectivity

Overall elimination rate may drop somewhat due to steric hindrance reaching a beta-hydrogen, but selectivity shifts strongly toward the Hofmann (less substituted) alkene, and E2 is favored more heavily over SN2
Selectivity shifts toward the Zaitsev alkene instead
Both rate and product distribution remain completely unchanged
e2.why: Steric bulk in the base both hinders its approach somewhat and redirects it toward whichever hydrogen is least crowded, which usually leads to the less substituted alkene and less competing SN2.

e2.q: Why can E2 occur at primary carbons even though SN1 and E1 essentially cannot?
options: Primary carbons are always more electrophilic than secondary or tertiary carbons
E2 actually proceeds through a primary carbocation intermediate
E2 is concerted and doesn't require carbocation formation, so it doesn't depend on the substrate's ability to stabilize positive charge, only on accessible beta-hydrogens and proper geometry
Primary substrates have no beta-hydrogens, which makes E2 easier
e2.why: Since no cationic intermediate ever forms in E2, the usual instability of a primary carbocation is simply irrelevant to whether E2 can proceed.

e2.q: In a stereochemically defined diastereomer where only one specific beta-hydrogen happens to be anti-periplanar to the leaving group, what primarily determines the regiochemistry of the E2 product?
options: The relative thermodynamic stability of the possible alkenes alone
The identity of the leaving group alone
The polarity of the solvent alone
The conformational requirement for anti-periplanar elimination, not simple Zaitsev-type stability preference
e2.why: When geometry restricts the reaction to only one accessible hydrogen, that constraint, not which alkene would otherwise be most stable, controls which product actually forms.

e2.q: Comparing a tosylate (OTs) leaving group to a chloride on the same substrate with the same base, how does E2 rate typically compare?
options: The tosylate reacts faster, since it is an excellent, very stable leaving group that accelerates E2 just as it would SN2
The chloride reacts faster, since chlorine is smaller
Both react at identical rates, since leaving group identity never affects E2
Neither leaving group allows E2 to occur
e2.why: Because the leaving group departs in the same concerted step as proton removal, a more stable, weaker-base leaving group like tosylate lowers the activation energy for elimination just as it does for substitution.

e2.q: Switching the base from weakly basic acetate to the very strongly basic amide ion (NH2-) can push an otherwise unhindered secondary substrate's reaction from predominantly SN2 toward predominantly E2. Why?
options: Amide ion cannot act as a nucleophile at all
A much stronger, more basic species increasingly favors proton removal relative to substitution, and strong bases generally promote elimination pathways
Acetate is actually a stronger base than amide ion
Stronger bases always slow down every reaction
e2.why: As basicity increases sharply, a reagent's tendency to grab a proton (driving elimination) increasingly outcompetes its tendency to attack the carbon directly (driving substitution), even without added steric bulk.

substrate-effects.q: A strong, bulky base (like tert-butoxide) with a secondary substrate tends to favor:
substrate-effects.why: Bulky strong bases have trouble doing backside attack (poor SN2) but easily deprotonate, favoring E2.

substrate-effects.q: Polar protic solvents (like water or alcohols) favor which mechanism type by stabilizing cationic intermediates?
substrate-effects.why: Polar protic solvents solvate (stabilize) carbocations and leaving groups well, favoring the ionization step in SN1/E1.

substrate-effects.q: A primary substrate with a strong, non-bulky nucleophile/base (like NaOCH₃ in a small amount) and good backside access typically favors:
substrate-effects.why: Primary carbons have minimal steric hindrance for backside attack and cannot stabilize a carbocation well, so SN2 dominates with a decent nucleophile.

substrate-effects.q: Methyl and primary substrates, when paired with a non-bulky nucleophile, react almost exclusively via which mechanism?
substrate-effects.why: With essentially no steric hindrance at the carbon and no ability to form a stable carbocation, backside attack (SN2) dominates.

substrate-effects.q: A tertiary substrate with a weak nucleophile/base in a polar protic solvent typically reacts mainly via which mechanism(s)?
substrate-effects.why: Tertiary carbons can form stable carbocations, polar protic solvent stabilizes that ionization, and a weak base/nucleophile can't force a bimolecular pathway, so unimolecular substitution and elimination dominate.

substrate-effects.q: Tertiary substrates cannot undergo SN2 because three alkyl groups sterically block backside attack.
substrate-effects.why: No matter how strong or small the nucleophile, the geometric backside approach is physically obstructed at a tertiary carbon.

substrate-effects.q: Primary substrates essentially cannot undergo SN1 or E1 because the primary carbocation is too unstable to form.
substrate-effects.why: With minimal alkyl substitution to stabilize the positive charge, a primary cation's energy is too high to form at a useful rate under normal conditions.

substrate-effects.q: Which single mechanism is essentially unavailable to a tertiary substrate, regardless of solvent, nucleophile strength, or temperature?
substrate-effects.why: SN2's requirement for a clear backside approach is a geometric barrier that no change in reagent or solvent can overcome at a tertiary carbon.

substrate-effects.q: Secondary substrates are often described as the mechanistic borderline case. Why?
options: They cannot undergo any substitution or elimination reactions
They only ever react via SN1
They can undergo all four mechanisms (SN1, SN2, E1, E2) depending on the specific nucleophile/base strength and solvent used
They are always less reactive than primary substrates
substrate-effects.why: Secondary carbons are sterically open enough for some backside attack yet can also form a moderately stable carbocation, so the outcome hinges heavily on the specific reagents and solvent chosen.

substrate-effects.q: Polar aprotic solvents generally favor which family of mechanisms?
options: The unimolecular pathways, SN1 and E1
The bimolecular pathways, SN2 and E2
substrate-effects.why: Polar aprotic solvents dissolve ionic reagents without caging the nucleophile/base through hydrogen bonding, keeping it highly reactive for a bimolecular attack.

substrate-effects.q: A strong, bulky base always favors E2 over SN2, even on an unhindered primary substrate where the reacting carbon itself has little steric hindrance.
substrate-effects.why: Bulk mainly matters where it blocks backside attack; on a primary carbon, which is already quite open, a bulky base can still give substantial SN2 unless it is extremely hindered or other factors intervene.

substrate-effects.q: Which single factor generally has the largest influence on whether SN2 or SN1/E1 is even feasible at all for a given substrate?
options: Substrate structure (the degree of alkyl substitution at the reacting carbon)
The color of the leaving group
substrate-effects.why: Substrate substitution pattern determines both whether backside attack is geometrically possible and whether a stable carbocation can form, which are the two gateway requirements for these mechanisms.

substrate-effects.q: 1-bromobutane (primary) is treated with NaSH (a strong, small nucleophile) in DMSO (polar aprotic). Which mechanism dominates?
substrate-effects.why: A primary substrate with an open backside path, a strong unhindered nucleophile, and a polar aprotic solvent that doesn't shield the nucleophile is the textbook setup for SN2.

substrate-effects.q: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (tertiary) is stirred in water (a weak nucleophile) at room temperature. Which mechanism(s) dominate?
substrate-effects.why: A tertiary substrate in an ionizing polar protic solvent with only a weak nucleophile present is set up to ionize on its own, giving substitution and elimination from the resulting carbocation.

substrate-effects.q: Cyclohexyl bromide (secondary) is treated with NaOEt (a moderately bulky, strong base) in ethanol. Which mechanism is the expected major pathway?
substrate-effects.why: A strong base on a secondary substrate tends to favor elimination, especially with a base that is reasonably hindered, though some competing substitution is still possible.

substrate-effects.q: Cyclohexyl bromide (secondary) is treated with NaI (a strong nucleophile that is a comparatively weak base) in acetone. Which mechanism dominates?
substrate-effects.why: A strong, minimally basic nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent favors attacking the carbon directly rather than removing a proton, pushing the reaction toward substitution.

substrate-effects.q: A secondary substrate reacting with a strong nucleophile that is a weak base, like NaN3, in a polar aprotic solvent gives predominantly substitution (SN2) rather than elimination.
substrate-effects.why: Because azide is a much better nucleophile than base, and the solvent keeps it highly reactive, the reaction favors attacking the carbon over removing a proton.

substrate-effects.q: Why does increasing temperature generally shift product distribution toward elimination products (E1 or E2) over substitution, for a given substrate and reagent combination?
options: Heat always destroys the substrate before it can react
Elimination pathways tend to have a more favorable entropy of activation, so heat increasingly favors them relative to substitution
Substitution products are never thermodynamically stable
Elimination never depends on temperature at all
substrate-effects.why: Forming two separate, more freely moving product pieces (the alkene and, e.g., water) from one substrate is entropically favorable, and that advantage becomes more significant as temperature rises.

substrate-effects.q: A tertiary substrate is treated with a strong, bulky base like potassium tert-butoxide in a polar aprotic solvent. What is the expected major outcome?
options: SN2, since bulky bases are always good nucleophiles
SN1, since bulky bases promote ionization
E2, typically giving the Hofmann (less substituted) alkene as the major product
No reaction, since bulky bases cannot react with tertiary substrates
substrate-effects.why: SN2 is blocked by the tertiary carbon's sterics, so a strong base reaching an available beta-hydrogen drives E2, and its bulk biases the outcome toward the less hindered, less substituted alkene.

substrate-effects.q: Methyl iodide is treated with a strong, bulky base like potassium tert-butoxide. What is the expected outcome?
options: E2 elimination dominates, just as it would with a tertiary substrate
SN1 dominates, since strong bases always promote ionization
SN2 substitution still occurs, since a methyl carbon has no beta-carbon at all and therefore cannot undergo elimination
substrate-effects.why: Elimination requires a beta-hydrogen on an adjacent carbon, and methyl carbons have no adjacent carbon whatsoever, so substitution is the only mechanistic option available regardless of base bulk.

substrate-effects.q: Even with a very strong, bulky base, a primary substrate bearing beta-hydrogens can sometimes give significant E2 product if steric hindrance near the leaving group (not just the base) also gets in the way of substitution.
substrate-effects.why: Steric crowding doesn't have to come from the reacting carbon alone; a hindered neighboring group plus a bulky base together can tip the balance toward elimination even at a formally primary carbon.

substrate-effects.q: Neopentyl bromide, (CH3)3CCH2Br, is treated with NaOEt (a strong base/nucleophile). Despite the reacting carbon being primary, which pathway dominates, and why?
options: E2, because the bulky adjacent quaternary carbon blocks backside attack almost as effectively as a more substituted carbon would, while a distant beta-hydrogen is still removable
SN2, because primary carbons always favor substitution regardless of neighboring groups
SN1, because the leaving group departs spontaneously
No reaction occurs, since neopentyl systems are completely unreactive
substrate-effects.why: Steric hindrance for SN2 purposes depends on what's crowding the approach path, not strictly on the formal classification of the reacting carbon; a bulky neighbor can make substitution difficult even at a primary center.

substrate-effects.q: A secondary substrate is placed in pure water (a highly ionizing polar protic solvent) along with a moderately strong nucleophile such as bromide ion. Why might SN1/E1 still dominate despite the decent nucleophile present?
options: Bromide ion cannot act as a nucleophile in water under any conditions

Since the rate-determining ionization step doesn't depend on nucleophile concentration or strength, strongly ionizing conditions can let unimolecular pathways compete effectively even with a reasonable nucleophile around, especially since protic solvents also solvate and slow that nucleophile's bimolecular attack
SN1/E1 always dominates over SN2/E2 for any secondary substrate
Water prevents all substitution reactions from occurring
substrate-effects.why: Ionizing power and nucleophile/base reactivity are somewhat independent levers; a solvent that strongly favors ionization can tip the balance toward unimolecular pathways even when a competent bimolecular reagent is technically present, partly because that same solvent also dampens the nucleophile's effective reactivity.

substrate-effects.q: Raising the concentration of a strong nucleophile/base for a given substrate can shift the overall mechanism from largely unimolecular toward bimolecular, because increasing [Nu or base] increases the rate of SN2/E2 while the unimolecular (substrate-only) rate stays the same.
substrate-effects.why: Since the bimolecular rate laws depend directly on reagent concentration while the unimolecular ones do not, pushing up reagent concentration makes the bimolecular pathway increasingly competitive, even on a substrate that might otherwise favor ionization.

substrate-effects.q: A tertiary substrate sits in a nonpolar, non-nucleophilic, non-basic solvent (such as an inert hydrocarbon) with no added nucleophile or base. What happens, and why?
options: SN2 proceeds readily, since tertiary substrates favor substitution in nonpolar solvents
SN1/E1 proceed rapidly, since nonpolar solvents always favor ionization
Essentially no useful reaction occurs, since there is no polar solvent to stabilize ionization and no nucleophile/base to drive a bimolecular pathway
E2 proceeds rapidly even with no base present
substrate-effects.why: Both families of mechanism have a hard requirement that this solvent and reagent combination fails to meet: no ionizing power for SN1/E1, and no reactive species at all for SN2/E2.

substrate-effects.q: 3-bromo-3-ethylpentane (tertiary) is solvolyzed separately in (a) pure water and (b) an 80:20 water:ethanol mixture. Which solvent gives the faster SN1/E1 rate, and why?
options: The water-ethanol mixture, because ethanol is a better nucleophile
Both give identical rates, since both are polar protic solvents
The water-ethanol mixture, because it has a lower boiling point
Pure water, because its higher overall polarity and ionizing power stabilize the developing cation more than the diluted water-ethanol mixture
substrate-effects.why: Even among polar protic solvents, overall polarity/ionizing power can vary; diluting water with a less polar component lowers that ionizing power and slows the rate-determining ionization step.

substrate-effects.q: Why does substrate structure often override solvent and nucleophile choice when it comes to whether SN2 is even possible, rather than just how fast it goes?
options: The steric blocking of the backside trajectory by three bulky alkyl groups on a tertiary carbon is a geometric barrier that no choice of nucleophile or solvent can overcome; the required transition state simply cannot form
Solvent polarity always matters more than substrate structure for SN2 feasibility
Nucleophile strength can always compensate for any amount of steric hindrance
Tertiary substrates can undergo SN2 if the solvent is sufficiently polar
substrate-effects.why: Some barriers are about rate (how fast something happens) while others are about feasibility (whether it can happen at all); the tertiary SN2 backside-attack problem is of the second, more absolute kind.

substrate-effects.q: A primary substrate with available beta-hydrogens reacts with a weak, non-bulky, non-basic nucleophile such as I- in acetone. Why does SN2 dominate with essentially no elimination?
options: Primary substrates cannot undergo elimination under any circumstances
Iodide, while a good nucleophile, is a very weak base, so it has little tendency to remove a proton, leaving substitution as the dominant pathway
Acetone actively prevents elimination from occurring
Iodide cannot act as a nucleophile in acetone
substrate-effects.why: Elimination requires the reagent to act as a base, and a species can be an excellent nucleophile while still being a poor base, which is exactly the combination that shuts down the elimination pathway here.

substrate-effects.q: A secondary alkyl halide's solvent is switched from polar aprotic (acetone) to polar protic (ethanol), while the same moderately strong nucleophile/base is used throughout. How does this shift the overall mechanistic balance?
options: It has no effect on the mechanistic balance at all
It shifts the balance toward more SN2/E2 character, since protic solvents always favor bimolecular pathways
It shifts the balance toward more SN1/E1 character, since the protic solvent both solvates and slows the nucleophile/base while also stabilizing the cationic intermediate
It shifts the balance toward SN2 only, with no change to elimination
substrate-effects.why: Protic solvents work against bimolecular pathways by caging the nucleophile/base through hydrogen bonding, and simultaneously work in favor of unimolecular pathways by stabilizing developing charge, so both effects push the balance the same direction.

substrate-effects.q: Of the four mechanisms, E2 is comparatively unique in that it can occur efficiently across primary, secondary, and tertiary substrates given a sufficiently strong base, making substrate structure the least restrictive variable for E2 relative to the other three mechanisms.
substrate-effects.why: SN2 is blocked at tertiary carbons and SN1/E1 are essentially blocked at primary carbons, but E2 needs neither backside access at the reacting carbon nor carbocation stability, so it tolerates the widest range of substrate types.

alkene-structure.q: The carbons of a simple alkene C=C are hybridized as:
alkene-structure.why: Each alkene carbon has 3 regions of electron density (2 sigma bonds + 1 pi bond counted as part of the double bond group) — sp², trigonal planar, ~120°.

alkene-structure.q: Degree of unsaturation counts how many rings and π bonds are in a molecule. One ring plus one double bond equals a degree of unsaturation of:
alkene-structure.why: Each ring and each pi bond (in a double bond or triple bond counts twice) contributes one degree of unsaturation — 1 ring + 1 double bond = 2.

alkene-structure.q: Why can’t the two carbons of a C=C double bond freely rotate relative to each other?
options: The pi bond’s parallel p-orbital overlap would break upon rotation
Rotation around double bonds is actually free
alkene-structure.why: Rotating one carbon relative to the other would misalign the parallel p orbitals forming the pi bond, breaking that overlap — this restricted rotation is what gives rise to cis/trans alkene isomers.

alkene-structure.q: What is the hybridization of each carbon in a simple C=C double bond?
alkene-structure.why: Each alkene carbon forms three sigma bonds (to two substituents and the other alkene carbon) plus one pi bond from an unhybridized p orbital, which requires sp2 hybridization with 120° bond angles.

alkene-structure.q: What is the general molecular formula for an acyclic (non-cyclic) alkene with one double bond and n carbons?
alkene-structure.why: Each pi bond or ring removes two hydrogens relative to the saturated alkane formula CnH2n+2, so one double bond gives CnH2n.

alkene-structure.q: Alkenes have the general molecular formula CnH2n+2, the same as alkanes.
alkene-structure.why: CnH2n+2 is the alkane (fully saturated) formula. Alkenes have one fewer degree of saturation, so they follow CnH2n.

alkene-structure.q: In ethylene (H2C=CH2), the C=C bond is made up of:
options: one sigma bond and one pi bond
alkene-structure.why: A double bond always consists of one sigma bond (head-on overlap) and one pi bond (side-by-side overlap of p orbitals); you cannot have two sigma bonds between the same two atoms.

alkene-structure.q: A carbon-carbon double bond is shorter than a carbon-carbon single bond between the same two types of carbons.
alkene-structure.why: The additional pi bond in a double bond pulls the two carbons closer together, shortening the bond compared to a single (sigma-only) bond.

alkene-structure.q: How many sigma bonds are present in ethylene, H2C=CH2 (including the C-C sigma bond)?
alkene-structure.why: Ethylene has one C-C sigma bond and four C-H sigma bonds (5 total), plus one pi bond that is not counted as a sigma bond.

alkene-structure.q: Cis and trans isomers of an alkene exist because rotation around the C=C bond is restricted.
alkene-structure.why: Rotating one carbon relative to the other would require breaking the pi bond's side-by-side p-orbital overlap, so geometric (cis/trans) isomers are locked in place at room temperature.

alkene-structure.q: A compound with the molecular formula C5H10 and no rings has a degree of unsaturation of:
alkene-structure.why: Degree of unsaturation = (2(5)+2-10)/2 = (12-10)/2 = 1, consistent with one double bond and no ring.

alkene-structure.q: Which suffix in IUPAC nomenclature indicates the presence of a carbon-carbon double bond?
alkene-structure.why: The suffix -ene specifically designates a double bond in the parent chain, as in propene or 2-butene.

alkene-structure.q: According to general alkene stability trends, which alkene is typically the most stable?
alkene-structure.why: More substituted alkenes are stabilized by additional alkyl groups donating electron density (hyperconjugation) into the pi system, so tetrasubstituted alkenes are typically the most stable.

alkene-structure.q: E/Z nomenclature (rather than simple cis/trans) is needed when:
options: the alkene has a plane of symmetry
each carbon of the double bond has two different groups attached, so CIP priority rules are needed to rank them
the alkene is part of a ring
alkene-structure.why: Cis/trans only works cleanly when it's obvious which groups are 'similar'; when each carbon carries two different substituents, CIP priority rules assign E (opposite, higher priorities) or Z (same side, higher priorities) unambiguously.

alkene-structure.q: What is the degree of unsaturation of a compound with molecular formula C6H10?
alkene-structure.why: DoU = (2×6+2-10)/2 = 2, which could correspond to two double bonds, one ring plus one double bond, or one triple bond.

alkene-structure.q: A compound with a degree of unsaturation of 2 could contain one triple bond instead of two double bonds or a ring plus a double bond.
alkene-structure.why: A triple bond itself counts as two degrees of unsaturation (two pi bonds), so DoU=2 is consistent with one triple bond, two double bonds, two rings, or one ring plus one double bond.

alkene-structure.q: For CIP priority at an alkene carbon bearing both a chlorine atom and a methyl group, which substituent receives higher priority?
options: it depends on the rest of the molecule only
alkene-structure.why: CIP priority is assigned first by atomic number at the point of attachment; chlorine (Z=17) outranks a carbon-based methyl group (Z=6) regardless of what else is in the molecule.

alkene-structure.q: Geometric (cis/trans) isomerism is possible for an alkene only when:
options: each double-bond carbon bears two different substituents
there are at least three carbons total
alkene-structure.why: If either alkene carbon has two identical substituents, there is no distinct 'other side' to compare, so no cis/trans isomerism exists; each carbon needs two different groups.

alkene-structure.q: The pi bond of an alkene forms from the side-by-side overlap of:
options: an s orbital and a p orbital
two unhybridized p orbitals perpendicular to the sp2 plane
alkene-structure.why: Each sp2 carbon retains one unhybridized p orbital oriented perpendicular to the plane of the three sp2 orbitals; side-by-side overlap of these two p orbitals creates the pi bond.

alkene-structure.q: Alkenes are generally more chemically reactive than alkanes because the pi electrons are held less tightly and are more exposed than sigma electrons.
alkene-structure.why: Pi electrons sit above and below the molecular plane, farther from the nuclei and more accessible to electrophiles, making the C=C pi bond a reactive site compared to the strong, low-energy C-C and C-H sigma bonds in alkanes.

alkene-structure.q: For the same number of carbons, how does the molecular formula of an alkyne compare to that of an alkene?
options: alkyne has two more hydrogens than the alkene
alkyne and alkane have the same formula
alkyne has two fewer hydrogens than the alkene, CnH2n-2
alkene-structure.why: A triple bond contributes two degrees of unsaturation versus one for a double bond, removing two additional hydrogens, so alkynes follow CnH2n-2 while alkenes follow CnH2n.

alkene-structure.q: Why is trans-2-butene more stable (lower in energy) than cis-2-butene?
options: in cis-2-butene the two methyl groups are forced closer together on the same side, creating steric (van der Waals) strain that trans avoids
cis has a longer bond length
trans has more degrees of unsaturation
alkene-structure.why: In the cis isomer, the two methyl groups point to the same side of the double bond and crowd each other, raising the molecule's energy; in trans they point to opposite sides, minimizing steric clash.

alkene-structure.q: What is the degree of unsaturation of a monoterpene with molecular formula C10H16?
alkene-structure.why: DoU = (2×10+2-16)/2 = 3, consistent with, for example, one ring and two double bonds, a common pattern in monoterpenes.

alkene-structure.q: A six-membered ring containing three double bonds (like benzene) has a degree of unsaturation of 4.
alkene-structure.why: One ring contributes 1 and each of the three pi bonds contributes 1, for a total DoU of 1+3=4, matching benzene's formula C6H6: (2×6+2-6)/2=4.

alkene-structure.q: A double bond positioned at the bridgehead carbon of a small bicyclic ring system is typically extremely unstable or impossible to form because:
options: bridgehead carbons cannot bond to hydrogen
the rigid ring geometry prevents the bridgehead carbon and its substituents from achieving the planar, 120° sp2 arrangement a double bond requires
pi bonds cannot exist in rings
alkene-structure.why: An sp2 alkene carbon needs its three attached groups and itself to lie in one plane; in small fused or bridged ring systems the bridgehead geometry can't twist into that planar arrangement without severe strain (this limitation is summarized by Bredt's rule).

alkene-structure.q: Why can a small ring like cyclohexene easily be cis but trans-cyclohexene is essentially impossible to isolate?
options: a small ring isn't large enough to span a trans double bond without extreme angle strain forcing the ring apart
alkene-structure.why: Placing the ring's two connecting chains on opposite faces of the double bond (trans) in a small ring requires bond angles far from ideal, introducing enormous strain; only larger rings (roughly 8+ membered) can accommodate a stable trans-cycloalkene.

alkene-structure.q: Free rotation around a C=C double bond does not occur at room temperature because doing so would require:
options: breaking the pi bond (roughly 260 kJ/mol), since rotation would take the p orbitals out of the alignment needed for their side-by-side overlap
breaking a sigma bond, which needs very little energy
alkene-structure.why: Rotating one carbon 90° relative to the other misaligns the two p orbitals so they can no longer overlap, effectively breaking the pi bond; this costs far more energy (~260 kJ/mol) than is available from ordinary thermal motion.

alkene-structure.q: In an alkene, the two double-bond carbons and the four atoms directly attached to them all lie approximately in a single plane.
alkene-structure.why: Because each alkene carbon is sp2 hybridized, its three sigma-bonded groups (including the other alkene carbon) are arranged trigonally in one plane, making the whole six-atom C=C unit planar.

alkene-structure.q: A smaller magnitude (less exothermic) heat of hydrogenation for an alkene indicates that alkene is:
options: less stable, higher in energy to begin with
more stable, lower in energy to begin with
alkene-structure.why: Hydrogenation converts all alkene isomers to the same alkane product, so the isomer that starts out lower in energy (more stable) releases less heat upon hydrogenation.

alkene-structure.q: Ranking by stability, which alkene substitution pattern is generally most stable?
alkene-structure.why: Alkene stability generally increases with the number of alkyl substituents directly attached to the double-bond carbons, due to increased hyperconjugative and inductive electron donation into the pi system; tetrasubstituted alkenes are the most stable of these options.

addition-reactions.q: In an addition reaction across a C=C double bond, the pi bond is:
options: Broken, and two new sigma bonds form
addition-reactions.why: Addition reactions break the reactive pi bond and add two new groups, one to each former alkene carbon.

addition-reactions.q: Which step typically starts an electrophilic addition to an alkene?
options: The alkene acts as an electrophile
The alkene’s pi electrons act as a nucleophile, attacking an electrophile
A proton is removed from the alkene
addition-reactions.why: Alkenes are electron-rich at the pi bond and act as nucleophiles toward an incoming electrophile, forming a carbocation (or similar) intermediate.

addition-reactions.q: Which of these is a classic electrophile added across an alkene in a halogenation (addition) reaction?
addition-reactions.why: Br₂ is polarized by the approaching alkene and forms a bromonium ion intermediate, a classic electrophilic addition across the double bond.

addition-reactions.q: In a general addition reaction, what happens to the alkene's degree of unsaturation?
addition-reactions.why: Addition reactions convert the pi bond into two new sigma bonds to the added atoms, removing one degree of unsaturation from the starting alkene.

addition-reactions.q: Addition reactions to alkenes increase the molecule's degree of unsaturation.
addition-reactions.why: Addition reactions consume the pi bond, converting an alkene (or alkyne) into a more saturated product, which decreases the degree of unsaturation, not increases it.

addition-reactions.q: Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene (addition of H2) typically requires a catalyst such as:
addition-reactions.why: H2 doesn't react with alkenes on its own at a useful rate; a transition metal catalyst (commonly Pt, Pd, or Ni) adsorbs H2 and the alkene on its surface, allowing the addition to occur.

addition-reactions.q: What is the product of adding Br2 across ethylene (H2C=CH2)?
addition-reactions.why: Br2 adds across the double bond, putting one bromine on each former alkene carbon, giving the vicinal dihalide 1,2-dibromoethane.

addition-reactions.q: Acid-catalyzed hydration of an alkene adds an H atom and an OH group across the former double bond.
addition-reactions.why: Hydration is the addition of water (formally H and OH) across the pi bond, converting the alkene into an alcohol.

addition-reactions.q: Addition of Br2 or Cl2 to an alkene is an example of what general reaction category?
addition-reactions.why: The electron-rich pi bond of the alkene attacks the electrophilic halogen, and both halogen atoms end up added to the former double-bond carbons, making this an electrophilic addition.

addition-reactions.q: The gradual disappearance of the orange-brown color when Br2 is added to an unknown compound is commonly used as a qualitative test for the presence of:
options: a halogen already in the molecule
a carbon-carbon pi bond (alkene or alkyne)
addition-reactions.why: Colored Br2 is consumed as it adds across a reactive pi bond, turning colorless; alkanes lack this reactive pi bond and don't decolorize Br2 without light or heat.

addition-reactions.q: The addition of H2 across a carbon-carbon double bond is called hydrogenation.
addition-reactions.why: Hydrogenation specifically refers to the addition of molecular hydrogen (H2) across a multiple bond, typically with a metal catalyst.

addition-reactions.q: Addition of a hydrogen halide (HX) across an alkene's double bond produces:
addition-reactions.why: HX adds H to one carbon and the halogen X to the other, converting the alkene directly into an alkyl halide.

addition-reactions.q: The electrophilic addition of Br2 to an alkene proceeds through which key intermediate?
addition-reactions.why: The alkene's pi electrons attack one bromine of Br2, displacing bromide and forming a three-membered ring bromonium ion in which bromine bridges both former alkene carbons, before bromide attacks from the opposite face.

addition-reactions.q: Hydroboration-oxidation (BH3 then H2O2/NaOH) converts an alkene into an alcohol with what regiochemistry?
options: always on a ring carbon only
addition-reactions.why: Boron, the less electronegative, bulkier atom, adds preferentially to the less hindered (less substituted) carbon, and after oxidation that carbon ends up bearing the OH, giving the anti-Markovnikov alcohol.
