addition-reactions.q: Oxymercuration-demercuration gives the Markovnikov alcohol without the carbocation rearrangements sometimes seen in acid-catalyzed hydration because the mechanism proceeds through:
options: direct SN2 attack by water on the alkene carbon
a bridged mercurinium ion that spreads out the positive charge, avoiding a discrete carbocation
addition-reactions.why: Mercury bridges both alkene carbons in a cyclic mercurinium ion; the positive character is delocalized rather than concentrated on one carbon, so water attacks the more substituted carbon (Markovnikov) without a true carbocation able to rearrange.

addition-reactions.q: Addition of Br2 to an alkene gives anti (opposite-face) stereochemistry because the bridged bromonium ion is attacked by bromide from the face opposite the bromonium ring.
addition-reactions.why: Since the first bromine already blocks one face as part of the bromonium ion, the incoming bromide ion must attack from the backside, giving net anti addition of the two bromines.

addition-reactions.q: Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene over a metal surface delivers the two hydrogen atoms with what stereochemistry?
addition-reactions.why: Both the alkene and H2 adsorb onto the same flat metal surface, so both hydrogen atoms are transferred to the same face of the double bond, giving syn addition.

addition-reactions.q: Why does bromine water (or Br2/CCl4) turn from colored to colorless when shaken with an alkene?
options: the alkene dissolves the bromine without reacting
the alkene's pi electrons attack Br2, forming a bromonium ion and consuming the colored Br2 as it's incorporated into a colorless dibromide product
the alkene reduces Br2 to HBr gas
addition-reactions.why: The addition reaction chemically consumes Br2, converting it into a colorless vicinal dibromide, which is why the test solution loses its color as the reaction proceeds.

addition-reactions.q: Hydroboration-oxidation follows Markovnikov's rule, placing OH on the more substituted carbon.
addition-reactions.why: Hydroboration-oxidation is anti-Markovnikov: boron adds to the less substituted, less hindered carbon due to steric factors (not carbocation stability), and OH ends up there after oxidation.

addition-reactions.q: The acid-catalyzed addition of water across an alkene's double bond is called:
addition-reactions.why: Acid catalysis protonates the alkene to form a carbocation, which water then attacks, adding H and OH across the former double bond in a process called acid-catalyzed hydration.

addition-reactions.q: Which reagent adds H and Br across a double bond with Markovnikov selectivity via a carbocation intermediate?
options: HBr in the absence of peroxides or light
addition-reactions.why: Without peroxides, HBr adds through a polar (ionic) mechanism: the alkene is protonated to form the more stable carbocation, which is then captured by bromide, giving the Markovnikov product.

addition-reactions.q: Why doesn't hydroboration-oxidation give the carbocation-rearrangement products sometimes seen with acid-catalyzed hydration?
options: the B-H addition is a single concerted (syn) step across the pi bond, so no free carbocation ever forms that could rearrange
Boron is too unreactive to add to alkenes at all
hydroboration only works on alkynes, not alkenes
oxidation always occurs before boron can add
addition-reactions.why: In hydroboration, boron and hydrogen add to the same face of the double bond simultaneously in one transition state, so there's no discrete carbocation intermediate available to undergo a hydride or alkyl shift.

addition-reactions.q: What is the overall stereochemical outcome when an alkene undergoes catalytic hydrogenation, and why?
options: anti addition, because the two hydrogens approach from opposite faces of the metal surface
syn addition, because both hydrogen atoms are delivered from the same catalyst surface to the same face of the alkene
no defined stereochemistry, because the mechanism is radical-based
anti addition, because a bridged intermediate forms like in halogenation
addition-reactions.why: Since the alkene binds flat against the catalyst surface and both hydrogens are transferred from that same surface, they must end up added to the same face, producing syn addition.

addition-reactions.q: Bromine addition can be used to chemically distinguish alkenes from alkanes because alkanes do not readily react with Br2 in the dark at room temperature, while alkenes do.
addition-reactions.why: Alkanes require light or heat to undergo a slow radical halogenation, whereas alkenes rapidly and visibly decolorize Br2 at room temperature via fast electrophilic addition, making the color change a useful diagnostic test.

addition-reactions.q: What is the correct order of key mechanistic steps in the ionic (non-radical) addition of HX to an alkene?
options: nucleophile attacks first, then protonation occurs
halide ion attacks the alkene directly in one step with no intermediate
the alkene's pi electrons are protonated by HX first, generating a carbocation, and then the halide ion attacks that carbocation
the alkene is first oxidized, then protonated
addition-reactions.why: In the standard two-step mechanism, the pi bond acts as a nucleophile toward the acidic H of HX, forming the more stable carbocation in the rate-determining first step, after which halide ion rapidly captures that carbocation.

addition-reactions.q: In the ionic addition of HX to an alkene, what determines the rate-determining step?
options: the final product stability has no bearing on rate at all
halide attack on the carbocation is always rate-determining
the reaction has no discernible rate-determining step
formation of the carbocation intermediate (protonation of the alkene) is rate-determining, since it is the higher-energy, slower step
addition-reactions.why: Generating the carbocation requires breaking the pi bond and is the higher-activation-energy step; the subsequent capture of that carbocation by halide ion is fast, so the first step controls the overall rate.

addition-reactions.q: Acid-catalyzed hydration of an alkene can give rearranged (unexpected) products because the reaction proceeds through a carbocation intermediate that can undergo hydride or alkyl shifts.
addition-reactions.why: Because a genuine carbocation forms during acid-catalyzed hydration, it is free to rearrange to a more stable carbocation (via a 1,2-hydride or alkyl shift) before water attacks, sometimes giving a product with the OH in an unexpected position.

addition-reactions.q: Oxymercuration-demercuration avoids the rearranged products possible in simple acid-catalyzed hydration because the mechanism proceeds through:
options: a bridged mercurinium ion, in which positive charge is shared between mercury and carbon rather than concentrated on one fully formed carbocation
a fully localized, long-lived carbocation just like acid hydration
direct nucleophilic substitution with no intermediate at all
addition-reactions.why: Because the mercurinium ion delocalizes the positive charge across a three-membered ring rather than placing it entirely on one carbon, there's no free carbocation available to rearrange before water attacks the more substituted carbon.

addition-reactions.q: How does the degree of alkyl substitution on an alkene generally affect its rate of electrophilic addition (e.g., with HX or Br2)?
options: more substituted alkenes react more slowly because they are more stable and less reactive
more substituted alkenes generally react faster because their pi bond is more electron-rich and stabilizes the developing positive charge
substitution has no effect on the rate of addition
only terminal alkenes undergo electrophilic addition at a useful rate
addition-reactions.why: Additional alkyl groups donate electron density into the pi system (making it a better nucleophile toward electrophiles) and stabilize the developing positive charge in the transition state, so more substituted alkenes typically react faster in electrophilic additions.

addition-reactions.q: Halogenation of an alkene gives anti addition, while catalytic hydrogenation gives syn addition. What accounts for this mechanistic difference?
options: halogenation and hydrogenation actually proceed through the identical intermediate
hydrogenation always occurs in two completely separate, unrelated steps years apart

halogenation proceeds through a bridged halonium ion that forces the second group to attack from the opposite face, while hydrogenation delivers both hydrogens from the same metal surface to the same face
anti addition only happens with gases, and syn addition only happens with liquids
addition-reactions.why: The bromonium/chloronium ion intermediate in halogenation blocks one face, forcing backside (anti) attack by the halide, whereas in hydrogenation both H atoms come from the same catalyst surface onto the same (syn) face — different intermediates give different stereochemical outcomes.

markovnikov.q: Markovnikov addition places the new H (or nucleophile, depending on convention) on the carbon that is:
options: Already least substituted (more H’s), so the new group ends up on the more substituted carbon
markovnikov.why: Markovnikov’s rule: the electrophile (often H⁺) adds to the carbon with more hydrogens already, placing the nucleophile on the more substituted (more stable-cation) carbon.

markovnikov.q: Anti-Markovnikov addition (e.g., via radical HBr addition) places Br on the:
options: Same carbon as in Markovnikov addition
markovnikov.why: Radical mechanisms form the more stable radical at the more substituted carbon, so Br ends up on the less substituted carbon — opposite of the ionic Markovnikov outcome.

markovnikov.q: Markovnikov’s rule is best explained mechanistically by:
options: The more stable (more substituted) carbocation forming preferentially during ionic addition
Steric hindrance of the nucleophile alone
markovnikov.why: In ionic (non-radical) addition, the proton adds to give whichever carbon leads to the more stable carbocation — i.e., the more substituted one — and the nucleophile then attacks that cation.

markovnikov.q: Markovnikov's rule states that when HX adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the hydrogen atom adds preferentially to the carbon that:
options: already has the fewest hydrogens attached
already has the most hydrogens attached
markovnikov.why: Markovnikov's original empirical rule: the H of HX ends up on the carbon that already bears more hydrogens, while X ends up on the more substituted carbon.

markovnikov.q: Markovnikov's rule was originally formulated as an empirical observation about reaction outcomes before the carbocation mechanism was understood.
markovnikov.why: Vladimir Markovnikov proposed the rule in 1865 based on observed patterns in addition reactions, decades before carbocation intermediates and their stability were used to explain why the rule holds.

markovnikov.q: What is the major product when HCl adds to propene (CH3-CH=CH2)?
markovnikov.why: Protonation occurs at the terminal CH2 carbon to generate the more stable secondary carbocation, which chloride then captures, giving 2-chloropropane as the Markovnikov product.

markovnikov.q: Anti-Markovnikov addition of HBr to an alkene is observed specifically under which condition?
options: in the presence of peroxides (radical chain mechanism)
with excess HBr and no catalyst
markovnikov.why: Peroxides generate bromine radicals that initiate a radical chain addition mechanism, which adds Br first and gives the opposite (anti-Markovnikov) regiochemistry compared to the normal ionic pathway.

markovnikov.q: When HBr adds to propene in the presence of peroxides, the major product is 1-bromopropane rather than 2-bromopropane.
markovnikov.why: Under radical (peroxide) conditions, bromine adds first to the terminal carbon to generate the more stable secondary radical, placing Br at the end of the chain — the anti-Markovnikov product, 1-bromopropane.

markovnikov.q: Acid-catalyzed (Markovnikov) hydration of 2-methylpropene (isobutylene) gives which alcohol as the major product?
markovnikov.why: Protonation generates the more stable tertiary carbocation at the central carbon, which water then attacks, giving tert-butanol as the Markovnikov product.

markovnikov.q: In determining the Markovnikov product, which carbocation is more stable and therefore favored as the reaction intermediate?
options: it doesn't matter, they're equally stable
secondary carbocation (compared to a primary option)
markovnikov.why: Carbocation stability increases with substitution (methyl less than primary less than secondary less than tertiary) due to hyperconjugation and inductive donation from neighboring alkyl groups, so the reaction favors forming the more substituted, more stable carbocation.

markovnikov.q: Anti-Markovnikov selectivity with peroxides works equally well for HCl, HBr, and HI.
markovnikov.why: Only HBr undergoes an efficient radical chain addition; the bond energetics for HCl and HI make the necessary radical propagation steps unfavorable, so anti-Markovnikov addition is essentially unique to HBr among the hydrogen halides.

markovnikov.q: The term 'Markovnikov addition' is named after:
markovnikov.why: Vladimir Markovnikov, a 19th-century Russian chemist, first described the regiochemical pattern now named after him.

markovnikov.q: What is the major product of HBr addition (no peroxides) to 1-methylcyclohexene?
options: Br ends up on C2, away from the methyl group
Br ends up on C1, the carbon already bearing the methyl group (tertiary carbocation)
Br adds to both carbons equally
No reaction occurs because the alkene is in a ring
markovnikov.why: Protonation of the ring double bond occurs at C2 to place the positive charge on C1 (already bearing a methyl group), forming the more stable tertiary carbocation; bromide then attacks C1, so Br and the methyl end up on the same carbon.

markovnikov.q: What is the major product of HI addition to 2-methyl-2-butene, (CH3)2C=CHCH3?
options: 2-iodo-2-methylbutane (I on the more substituted, tertiary carbon)
markovnikov.why: Protonating the less substituted alkene carbon generates the more stable tertiary carbocation at the other carbon; iodide then attacks that tertiary center, giving 2-iodo-2-methylbutane as the Markovnikov product.

markovnikov.q: Markovnikov's rule can be restated in mechanistic terms as: the electrophile's positively polarized atom adds to whichever carbon generates the more stable carbocation intermediate.
markovnikov.why: This mechanistic restatement explains the empirical rule: reaction proceeds through the lower-energy transition state, which is the pathway that forms the more stable (typically more substituted) carbocation.

markovnikov.q: For a terminal alkene CH2=CHR reacting with HX under normal ionic conditions, the halogen X ends up mainly on:
options: neither carbon; X leaves as HX unreacted
the internal carbon bearing R (the more substituted carbon)
markovnikov.why: Protonation at the terminal CH2 carbon generates the more stable carbocation at the internal, more substituted carbon, which halide then attacks, placing X on that more substituted carbon.

markovnikov.q: How does the regiochemistry of hydroboration-oxidation compare to Markovnikov's rule?
options: it is anti-Markovnikov: OH ends up on the less substituted carbon
it gives a random mixture with no preference
it only works on alkynes, not alkenes
markovnikov.why: Because hydroboration proceeds through steric control (boron adding to the less hindered carbon) rather than carbocation stability, the resulting alcohol has OH on the less substituted carbon — the opposite of the typical Markovnikov outcome.

markovnikov.q: Oxymercuration-demercuration of an alkene installs the new OH group following which regiochemical pattern?
options: anti-Markovnikov orientation (OH on the less substituted carbon)
Markovnikov orientation (OH on the more substituted carbon)
OH always ends up on a terminal carbon regardless of substitution
no defined pattern; products are random
markovnikov.why: Water attacks the more substituted carbon of the bridged mercurinium ion, where positive character is greater, giving the same overall Markovnikov regiochemistry as acid-catalyzed hydration, but without carbocation rearrangement.

markovnikov.q: In the anti-Markovnikov radical addition of HBr, a bromine radical (not a hydrogen atom) is the species that adds first, attaching to the terminal carbon.
markovnikov.why: The radical chain begins when a bromine radical adds to the less hindered terminal carbon, generating the more stable internal (secondary or tertiary) carbon radical, which then abstracts H from HBr — this order is why Br ends up terminal.

markovnikov.q: What intermediate determines the regiochemistry of anti-Markovnikov radical addition of HBr?
options: the more stable free radical (e.g., secondary or tertiary carbon radical)
markovnikov.why: Radical addition proceeds by bromine radical adding to generate the most stable carbon radical (paralleling how ionic mechanisms favor the most stable carbocation), which dictates where Br ultimately attaches.

markovnikov.q: Why does ordinary HBr addition (no peroxides present) give the Markovnikov product rather than the anti-Markovnikov one?
options: HBr is simply incapable of anti-Markovnikov addition under any conditions
anti-Markovnikov addition requires light, which is always present
HBr only reacts with alkynes, not alkenes, without peroxides
without a radical initiator like peroxide, the reaction proceeds by the standard ionic (carbocation) mechanism, which favors the more stable carbocation and thus the Markovnikov product
markovnikov.why: The radical chain mechanism needs peroxides (or similar initiators) to generate the initial bromine radical; absent that, the alkene reacts through the conventional polar mechanism, which is governed by carbocation stability and gives the Markovnikov outcome.

markovnikov.q: Addition of HCl to 3,3-dimethyl-1-butene, (CH3)3C-CH=CH2, can give a rearranged product in addition to the expected one because:
options: the initially formed secondary carbocation can undergo a 1,2-methyl shift to form a more stable tertiary carbocation before chloride attacks
HCl never reacts with this alkene
the methyl groups block all possible addition
the secondary carbocation is already the most stable possible intermediate here
markovnikov.why: Protonation gives a secondary carbocation adjacent to a carbon bearing three methyl groups; a methyl group can shift over (1,2-shift) to generate a more stable tertiary carbocation, leading to a rearranged chloride product alongside the 'simple' Markovnikov product.

markovnikov.q: Why does a tertiary carbocation intermediate lead to the Markovnikov product being favored over one from a secondary carbocation?
options: tertiary carbocations are actually less stable, so they form more slowly but give better yields
tertiary carbocations are more stabilized by hyperconjugation and inductive electron donation from three alkyl groups, lowering the activation energy for that pathway
tertiary carbocations are not real intermediates, just a convenient theoretical tool
secondary and tertiary carbocations are always equally stable
markovnikov.why: More alkyl groups attached to the cationic carbon donate electron density through hyperconjugation and induction, lowering the energy of the carbocation and the transition state leading to it, which channels the reaction toward the product derived from the more stable intermediate.

markovnikov.q: Radical (anti-Markovnikov) addition of HBr proceeds via the more stable free radical intermediate, in direct analogy to how the ionic mechanism proceeds via the more stable carbocation.
markovnikov.why: Both mechanisms are governed by the same underlying principle — the reaction pathway that generates the lower-energy reactive intermediate (radical or cation) is favored — they just differ in which species (radical vs. cation) and which atom (Br vs. H) adds first.

markovnikov.q: In peroxide-mediated (anti-Markovnikov) HBr addition, what species initiates the radical chain?
options: a bromide anion formed by simple ionization of HBr
a proton (H+) generated from the peroxide
a bromine radical generated when peroxide-derived radicals react with HBr
a carbocation formed directly from the peroxide
markovnikov.why: Peroxides undergo weak O-O bond homolysis to generate alkoxy radicals, which abstract a hydrogen atom from HBr to generate a bromine radical; this bromine radical is what adds to the alkene to begin the chain.

markovnikov.q: Markovnikov's original rule (H goes to the carbon with more H's already) becomes ambiguous or insufficient in which situation, revealing why the carbocation-stability explanation is actually needed?
options: never; the simple rule always works perfectly for every alkene
only for symmetrical alkenes, which have no regiochemistry question at all
only when no acid catalyst is present
for more complex or highly substituted alkenes, simply counting H atoms doesn't clearly predict which carbocation is more stable
markovnikov.why: The simple 'more H's' heuristic can fail to clearly distinguish outcomes for more complex or highly substituted alkenes; the mechanistic version — protonate to form the more stable carbocation — is the general and reliable explanation underlying the empirical rule.

markovnikov.q: Why is anti-Markovnikov addition essentially unique to HBr among the hydrogen halides (HF, HCl, HBr, HI), rather than occurring readily with HCl or HI too?
options: the radical chain's steps are reasonably exothermic and selective for Br, but too exothermic/unselective for Cl or endothermic for I
HCl and HI simply don't exist as reagents
HCl and HI are too unreactive to add to alkenes by any mechanism
anti-Markovnikov addition actually works equally well for all four halides
markovnikov.why: The bond dissociation energies involved make each step of the HBr radical chain reasonably exothermic and selective, while the analogous steps for HCl are too exothermic and unselective and for HI are endothermic, so a clean radical chain mechanism practically only works for HBr.

markovnikov.q: Anti-Markovnikov regiochemistry from a radical mechanism is a special case associated with HBr addition; it does not apply to ordinary acid-catalyzed hydration or to halogenation (Br2/Cl2 addition) reactions under typical conditions.
markovnikov.why: Hydration and halogenation (Br2/Cl2 addition) proceed through cationic or bridged-ion intermediates that follow normal Markovnikov-type (most stable intermediate) selectivity; the radical chain pathway that flips the regiochemistry is essentially unique to peroxide-mediated HBr addition.

markovnikov.q: Comparing HBr addition to 2-methyl-1-butene with and without peroxides, what regiochemical difference is expected?
options: no difference; both conditions give the identical major product
without peroxides, Br ends up on the more substituted C2 carbon (Markovnikov); with peroxides, Br ends up on the less substituted terminal C1 carbon (anti-Markovnikov)
without peroxides, Br ends up on C1; with peroxides, Br ends up on C2
peroxides prevent the reaction from occurring at all
markovnikov.why: The ionic pathway is governed by carbocation stability, favoring Br at the more substituted carbon (C2); the radical pathway is governed by radical stability formed by Br adding first to the terminal carbon (C1), flipping the regiochemistry.

markovnikov.q: Rank the following carbocations from least to most stable, which underlies the reasoning behind Markovnikov's rule:
options: tertiary less than secondary less than primary less than methyl
secondary less than methyl less than tertiary less than primary
methyl less than primary less than secondary less than tertiary
all carbocations are equally stable regardless of substitution
markovnikov.why: Carbocation stability increases with the number of alkyl groups attached to the cationic carbon because each alkyl group donates electron density via hyperconjugation and the inductive effect, giving the order methyl less than primary less than secondary less than tertiary.

alkynes.q: A terminal alkyne’s C–H is unusually acidic (pKa ~25) because:
options: sp carbons hold electron density closer to the nucleus (more s-character), stabilizing the resulting anion
There is no acidity difference from alkanes
alkynes.why: sp hybrid orbitals have 50% s-character (vs. 25% for sp³), holding the lone pair closer to the nucleus and stabilizing the conjugate base — more s-character, more acidic.

alkynes.q: How many pi bonds are in a carbon-carbon triple bond?
alkynes.why: A triple bond is 1 sigma bond plus 2 pi bonds.

alkynes.q: Compared to an alkene, an alkyne undergoing addition of 2 equivalents of HX can ultimately give what kind of product?
options: Only a single addition is ever possible
A geminal dihalide (both halogens on the same carbon) after two additions
alkynes.why: The first HX addition (following Markovnikov) gives a vinyl halide; a second addition of HX to that alkene gives a geminal dihalide, both halogens on the same, more substituted carbon.

alkynes.q: What is the hybridization of each carbon in a carbon-carbon triple bond?
alkynes.why: Each alkyne carbon forms two sigma bonds (linear, 180°) using sp hybrid orbitals, leaving two unhybridized p orbitals to form the two pi bonds of the triple bond.

alkynes.q: What is the approximate bond angle around each carbon of a terminal or internal alkyne?
alkynes.why: sp-hybridized carbons arrange their two sigma bonds linearly, 180° apart, giving alkynes their characteristic straight, rod-like geometry at the triple bond.

alkynes.q: Alkynes are generally somewhat less reactive than alkenes toward many electrophilic addition reactions because the sp carbons hold their pi electrons more tightly.
alkynes.why: Alkyne pi electrons are held closer to the carbon nuclei due to the higher s-character (more electronegative character) of sp carbons, making the alkyne pi bond somewhat less available to electrophiles compared to the more loosely held pi electrons of an alkene.

alkynes.q: What is the general molecular formula for an acyclic alkyne with one triple bond and n carbons?
alkynes.why: A triple bond counts as two degrees of unsaturation, removing four hydrogens relative to the saturated alkane (CnH2n+2), giving CnH2n-2.

alkynes.q: A terminal alkyne is defined by having the triple bond:
options: in the middle of a long carbon chain
at the end of the chain, with one triple-bond carbon bonded directly to a hydrogen
alkynes.why: In a terminal alkyne, such as HC≡C-CH3 (propyne), one sp carbon of the triple bond is bonded to a hydrogen atom rather than to another carbon, placing the triple bond at the very end of the chain.

alkynes.q: In an internal alkyne, both triple-bond carbons are bonded to other carbons rather than to hydrogen.
alkynes.why: An internal alkyne, like 2-butyne (CH3-C≡C-CH3), has the triple bond flanked on both sides by carbon substituents, distinguishing it from a terminal alkyne, which has a triple-bond C-H.

alkynes.q: Addition of exactly 1 equivalent of Br2 to an internal alkyne gives what kind of product?
options: a saturated alkane with four bromines
a tetrahalide with no unsaturation remaining
a dihaloalkene, with one degree of unsaturation still remaining
alkynes.why: Just as with alkenes, Br2 adds across one of the two pi bonds of the triple bond first, converting the alkyne into a dihalogenated alkene; a second equivalent of Br2 would be needed to fully saturate it into a tetrahalide.

alkynes.q: Which IUPAC suffix indicates a carbon-carbon triple bond?
alkynes.why: The suffix -yne is used specifically to denote a triple bond in the parent chain, as in ethyne (acetylene) or 2-butyne.

alkynes.q: How many sigma bonds exist directly between the two carbon atoms of a carbon-carbon triple bond?
alkynes.why: A triple bond is composed of exactly one sigma bond (from head-on sp-sp orbital overlap) plus two pi bonds (from two pairs of unhybridized p orbitals); there is never more than one sigma bond between any two directly bonded atoms.

alkynes.q: Why is the C-H bond of a terminal alkyne (pKa ~25) considerably more acidic than a similar C-H bond in an alkene or alkane?
options: the alkyne C-H bond is longer and weaker
alkynes have more hydrogens overall, diluting the charge
the lone pair left on the sp carbon after deprotonation sits in an orbital with more s-character, holding electron density closer to the nucleus and stabilizing the negative charge
terminal alkynes contain an oxygen atom that withdraws electron density
alkynes.why: An sp orbital has 50% s character, versus 33% for sp2 and 25% for sp3; more s character means the lone pair sits closer to and is better stabilized by the positively charged nucleus, making the conjugate base (acetylide ion) more stable and the C-H more acidic.

alkynes.q: Given the approximate pKa values: alkane C-H ~50, alkene C-H ~44, alkyne C-H ~25, water ~15.7, which of these four is the most acidic?
alkynes.why: A lower pKa means a stronger acid; water at pKa ~15.7 is far more acidic than even a terminal alkyne C-H (pKa ~25), even though the alkyne C-H is unusually acidic compared to other hydrocarbon C-H bonds.

alkynes.q: Which of the following bases is commonly strong enough to fully deprotonate a terminal alkyne C-H?
alkynes.why: Since the conjugate acid of amide ion, ammonia (pKa ~38), is a much weaker acid than a terminal alkyne (pKa ~25), sodium amide is a strong enough base to completely deprotonate terminal alkynes to form acetylide ions; hydroxide (conjugate acid water, pKa ~15.7) is not strong enough.

alkynes.q: The acetylide ion formed by deprotonating a terminal alkyne is a good nucleophile that can be used in SN2 reactions with primary alkyl halides to form a new carbon-carbon bond.
alkynes.why: Acetylide ions are strong, relatively unhindered carbanion-like nucleophiles that readily displace halide from primary (unhindered) alkyl halides via SN2, a classic method for extending carbon chains and building larger alkynes.

alkynes.q: Acid/Hg2+-catalyzed (Markovnikov) hydration of a terminal alkyne proceeds through an unstable enol intermediate that then converts into what final functional group?
alkynes.why: Markovnikov addition of water places OH on the more substituted alkyne carbon, generating an enol, which rapidly tautomerizes (favoring the more stable keto form) into a ketone.

alkynes.q: Anti-Markovnikov hydration of a terminal alkyne via hydroboration-oxidation ultimately yields what functional group?
alkynes.why: Boron adds to the less substituted terminal carbon; oxidation replaces boron with OH there, giving an enol with OH on the terminal carbon, which tautomerizes to an aldehyde rather than a ketone.

alkynes.q: Treating an alkyne with excess H2 and a Pt (or Pd/Ni) catalyst results in complete reduction to the corresponding alkane.
alkynes.why: With an unrestricted (non-poisoned) metal catalyst and excess H2, both pi bonds of the triple bond are hydrogenated in sequence, first to the alkene and then fully to the alkane.

alkynes.q: Partial hydrogenation of an internal alkyne using Lindlar's catalyst (Pd poisoned with lead and quinoline) gives predominantly which product?
alkynes.why: Lindlar's catalyst delivers both hydrogens to the same face of the triple bond (syn addition) and is deliberately poisoned to stop after adding just one equivalent of H2, giving the cis alkene selectively.

alkynes.q: Reduction of an internal alkyne with sodium metal in liquid ammonia (Na/NH3, a dissolving-metal reduction) gives predominantly which product?
options: no reaction; Na/NH3 does not reduce alkynes
alkynes.why: The Na/NH3 dissolving-metal mechanism proceeds through a vinyl radical/anion intermediate that equilibrates to the more stable, less crowded trans geometry before picking up a second electron and proton, giving the trans alkene selectively — complementary to Lindlar's cis selectivity.

alkynes.q: Mechanistically, why does Lindlar's catalyst stop at the cis-alkene stage rather than continuing on to the fully saturated alkane?
options: the cis-alkene is simply the only possible product from any hydrogenation of a triple bond
the catalyst is poisoned (partially deactivated) so it can still add H2 across the triple bond but is far less active toward further hydrogenating the resulting alkene
Lindlar's catalyst only works on terminal alkynes
the reaction is run with insufficient H2 gas to go any further
alkynes.why: Lead and quinoline additives reduce the catalytic activity of Pd just enough that it can still deliver H2 syn across a triple bond but is much less effective at further adsorbing and reducing the resulting alkene, letting the reaction be stopped cleanly at the cis-alkene stage.

alkynes.q: Mechanistically, why does dissolving-metal (Na/NH3) reduction of an internal alkyne favor the trans alkene rather than the cis?
options: the mechanism is identical to catalytic hydrogenation, which also favors trans products
trans alkenes are formed because Na/NH3 is a poor reducing agent that barely reacts
an electron adds to the alkyne forming a vinyl radical anion that adopts the more stable, less strained trans-like geometry before a proton and second electron complete the reduction
the alkyne first converts to a cis alkene, which then isomerizes under basic conditions
alkynes.why: Unlike the concerted syn delivery on a catalyst surface, the dissolving-metal mechanism proceeds stepwise through a radical anion intermediate that has time to adopt the thermodynamically preferred, less strained trans-like arrangement before being fully reduced, giving the trans alkene as the major product.

alkynes.q: Acid-catalyzed hydration of an unsymmetrical internal alkyne can give a mixture of two different ketones, because water can add with its oxygen ending up on either of the two different triple-bond carbons.
alkynes.why: Unless the internal alkyne is symmetrical, Markovnikov addition of water is not perfectly selective for one carbon over the other when both are similarly substituted, so both possible enol/ketone regiochemistries can form, giving a mixture of ketone products.

alkynes.q: When a terminal alkyne reacts with 2 equivalents of HBr (no peroxides), Markovnikov addition occurs in both steps. What is the final product?
options: a 1,2-dibromide with one Br on each of the original terminal alkyne carbons
a vicinal dihalide alkene still containing a double bond
an alkane with no halogens at all
a geminal dihalide, with both bromine atoms ending up on the same (internal, more substituted) carbon
alkynes.why: The first HBr addition follows Markovnikov's rule, putting Br on the more substituted carbon to form a bromoalkene; the second HBr addition again follows Markovnikov's rule on that bromoalkene, placing the second Br on the very same carbon, yielding a geminal dihalide.

alkynes.q: Why does the initial product of acid-catalyzed alkyne hydration (an enol) not survive as the final isolated product?
options: the enol rapidly tautomerizes because the carbonyl (keto) form is thermodynamically more stable, and this keto-enol equilibrium strongly favors the ketone
the enol is actually more stable than the corresponding ketone and is isolated unchanged
enols are never formed in alkyne hydration in the first place
the enol immediately polymerizes into a completely different product class
alkynes.why: Keto-enol tautomerization is a fast, acid- or base-catalyzed equilibrium that overwhelmingly favors the keto form because a C=O pi bond is significantly more stable than a C=C-OH arrangement, so the enol formed transiently from alkyne hydration converts essentially completely to the ketone.

alkynes.q: Terminal alkynes, but not internal alkynes, give an aldehyde product from hydroboration-oxidation, because boron selectively adds to the less hindered, terminal carbon of the triple bond.
alkynes.why: Only a terminal alkyne has a CH-bearing end carbon available for boron's steric preference to place OH there after oxidation, generating a terminal enol that tautomerizes to an aldehyde; internal alkynes lack a terminal position and instead give ketones.

alkynes.q: Ranking carbon-carbon bond lengths and relative bond strengths from a single bond to a triple bond, which statement is correct?
options: triple bonds are the longest and weakest of the three
triple bonds are the shortest and strongest of the three, due to more shared electron pairs and the highest s-character of the hybrid orbitals
all three bond types have essentially identical length and strength
double bonds are shorter than triple bonds
alkynes.why: More shared electron pairs (three bonding pairs in a triple bond) pull the bonded atoms closer together and require more energy to break, and the increased s-character of sp orbitals further shortens the sigma bond, making triple bonds the shortest and strongest, followed by double, then single bonds.

alkynes.q: Why does a carbon-carbon triple bond contain two mutually perpendicular pi bonds rather than one larger pi bond?
options: because triple bonds actually only have one pi bond, just like double bonds
because the two pi bonds merge into a single circular orbital around the bond axis

because each sp carbon retains two unhybridized p orbitals oriented 90° to each other, and each p orbital pair overlaps side-by-side independently with its counterpart on the other carbon, forming two separate, perpendicular pi bonds
because nitrogen atoms are required to form the second pi bond
alkynes.why: sp hybridization uses only one s and one p orbital, leaving two p orbitals unhybridized and oriented perpendicular to each other; each of these forms its own independent pi bond with the matching p orbital on the other sp carbon, giving two distinct, perpendicular pi bonds plus the one sigma bond.

alkynes.q: Treating a symmetrical internal alkyne, such as 2-butyne (CH3-C≡C-CH3), with H2O/H2SO4/HgSO4 gives what outcome, and why?
options: a mixture of two different ketones, because the molecule isn't symmetrical enough to favor one over the other
no reaction at all, because symmetrical alkynes cannot undergo hydration
an alcohol with no carbonyl group formed
a single ketone product (2-butanone) cleanly, because the molecule's symmetry means water adds equally well to either carbon and gives the identical ketone either way
alkynes.why: Because both triple-bond carbons of 2-butyne carry identical methyl substituents, it doesn't matter which carbon water's oxygen ends up on — both regiochemical outcomes converge on the same single ketone product (2-butanone), avoiding the mixture problem seen with unsymmetrical internal alkynes.

alcohol-reactions.q: Why can’t OH⁻ typically leave directly from an alcohol in a substitution reaction?
options: OH⁻ is a strong base and therefore a poor leaving group
alcohol-reactions.why: Hydroxide is a strong base (poor leaving group); alcohols are typically first protonated (or converted to a better leaving group like a tosylate) before substitution/elimination.

alcohol-reactions.q: Protonating an alcohol with strong acid converts –OH into:
options: –OH₂⁺, which leaves as neutral water — a good leaving group
alcohol-reactions.why: Protonation turns the leaving group into neutral H₂O, which is a much weaker base (and thus a far better leaving group) than OH⁻.

alcohol-reactions.q: Which reagent is commonly used to convert an alcohol into a good leaving group (a tosylate) without disturbing its stereochemistry?
options: Tosyl chloride (TsCl) with a mild base
alcohol-reactions.why: TsCl converts the OH into OTs, a weak-base, excellent leaving group, via a mechanism that doesn’t touch the stereocenter’s configuration (unlike acid-catalyzed substitution, which can invert or racemize it).

alcohol-reactions.q: Which mechanism does tert-butanol follow when it reacts with concentrated HCl to form tert-butyl chloride?
alcohol-reactions.why: Tertiary carbocations are stable enough to form, so the reaction proceeds through ionization (loss of water) followed by chloride capture, a classic SN1 pathway.

alcohol-reactions.q: Primary alcohols react with HBr via an SN1 mechanism because primary carbocations form easily.
alcohol-reactions.why: Primary carbocations are highly unstable, so primary alcohols instead react with HX through SN2, with the protonated alcohol acting as the leaving group while bromide attacks from the backside.

alcohol-reactions.q: Which reagent converts a primary alcohol to the corresponding alkyl chloride with the least risk of carbocation rearrangement?
alcohol-reactions.why: SOCl2 reacts through a chlorosulfite intermediate without generating a free carbocation, avoiding the hydride or alkyl shifts that can occur in purely acid-catalyzed routes.

alcohol-reactions.q: Treating a primary alcohol with PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate) in dichloromethane gives:
alcohol-reactions.why: PCC is an anhydrous, mild oxidant that stops at the aldehyde stage because there is no water present to hydrate the aldehyde into the gem-diol needed for further oxidation.

alcohol-reactions.q: To oxidize a primary alcohol all the way to a carboxylic acid, the best choice is:
alcohol-reactions.why: Strong aqueous Cr(VI) oxidants hydrate the intermediate aldehyde into a gem-diol, which is then readily oxidized further to the carboxylic acid; PCC and Swern conditions are anhydrous and stop at the aldehyde.

alcohol-reactions.q: Oxidizing a secondary alcohol with any chromium(VI) reagent (PCC, Jones, etc.) produces:
options: No reaction; secondary alcohols resist oxidation
alcohol-reactions.why: Secondary alcohols have only one hydrogen on the carbinol carbon; removing it gives a ketone, which has no further C-H bond to remove, so oxidation stops there regardless of the specific Cr(VI) reagent.

alcohol-reactions.q: Tertiary alcohols can be oxidized to ketones using PCC.
alcohol-reactions.why: Oxidation by these reagents requires removing a C-H bond from the carbinol carbon; a tertiary carbinol carbon has no such hydrogen, so tertiary alcohols resist this kind of oxidation entirely.

alcohol-reactions.q: Acid-catalyzed dehydration of 2-butanol gives mainly:
alcohol-reactions.why: Zaitsev's rule favors the more stable, more substituted alkene; in the E1 mechanism the carbocation loses a proton preferentially toward the more substituted side, forming the more stable double bond.

alcohol-reactions.q: Put the steps of acid-catalyzed (E1) dehydration of an alcohol in the correct order.
options: Loss of a proton, protonation of OH, loss of water
Protonation of OH, loss of water to form a carbocation, loss of a proton to form the alkene
Loss of water, loss of a proton, protonation of OH
Protonation of OH, loss of a proton, loss of water
alcohol-reactions.why: The OH must first be protonated to become a good leaving group (water), which then departs to generate a carbocation; a base finally removes a beta-proton to form the alkene.

alcohol-reactions.q: Dehydration rates for alcohols under acid catalysis follow the order 3 degrees > 2 degrees > 1 degree primarily because:
options: Primary alcohols have stronger O-H bonds
More substituted carbocations are more stable and form faster
Steric hindrance speeds up primary alcohol dehydration
alcohol-reactions.why: The rate-limiting step is carbocation formation; hyperconjugation and inductive electron donation from additional alkyl groups stabilize more substituted carbocations, lowering the activation energy for their formation.

alcohol-reactions.q: Acid-catalyzed dehydration of a secondary alcohol can give a rearranged alkene product that would not be predicted from simply removing a proton adjacent to the original carbinol carbon.
alcohol-reactions.why: Because the mechanism passes through a carbocation intermediate, a hydride or alkyl shift can occur before the proton is lost, shifting the position of the resulting double bond or even the carbon skeleton.

alcohol-reactions.q: Adding sodium metal to ethanol produces:
options: No reaction; alcohols do not react with Na
alcohol-reactions.why: Alcohols are weak acids; the reactive Na metal reduces the O-H proton, releasing H2 gas and leaving behind the sodium alkoxide salt.

alcohol-reactions.q: In a Williamson ether synthesis starting from an alcohol, the first step is usually to:
options: Deprotonate the alcohol with a strong base like NaH
Oxidize the alcohol to a ketone
alcohol-reactions.why: The alkoxide, not the neutral alcohol, is the nucleophile needed to perform SN2 displacement on the alkyl halide partner, so a strong, non-nucleophilic base like NaH is used first to form it.

alcohol-reactions.q: Fischer esterification combines an alcohol with a carboxylic acid under acid catalysis to form:
alcohol-reactions.why: Acid catalyzes nucleophilic attack of the alcohol on the protonated carbonyl; after loss of water from the resulting tetrahedral intermediate, the ester is formed. The overall process is reversible.

alcohol-reactions.q: A vicinal diol treated with acid can undergo a pinacol rearrangement, which proceeds by:
options: A simple SN2 substitution of one OH by the other
Direct elimination with no carbocation intermediate at all
Loss of water to form a carbocation, followed by a 1,2-shift of an alkyl or hydride group to give a more stable cation that then loses a proton to form a ketone
Radical coupling of the two oxygens
alcohol-reactions.why: One OH is protonated and leaves as water to form a carbocation; a neighboring alkyl or hydride group migrates to stabilize the positive charge, and loss of a proton from the resulting species gives the ketone product.

alcohol-reactions.q: Treating a vicinal (1,2-) diol with periodic acid (HIO4) results in:
options: No reaction; HIO4 only cleaves alkenes
Oxidative cleavage of the C-C bond to give two carbonyl compounds
alcohol-reactions.why: Periodic acid selectively cleaves the carbon-carbon bond between two adjacent hydroxyl groups, converting each carbinol carbon into a carbonyl (an aldehyde or ketone depending on substitution).

alcohol-reactions.q: Alcohols are generally slightly weaker acids than water.
alcohol-reactions.why: The alkyl group attached to the oxygen is electron-donating relative to hydrogen, which destabilizes the alkoxide conjugate base somewhat compared to hydroxide, making most simple alcohols a bit less acidic than water.

alcohol-reactions.q: Compared to methanol, tert-butanol is:
options: Less acidic (higher pKa), because the three methyl groups destabilize the alkoxide by electron donation
More acidic (lower pKa), because of steric relief on ionization
Equally acidic; alkyl substitution does not affect alcohol pKa
More acidic because tertiary carbons stabilize negative charge better
alcohol-reactions.why: The added alkyl groups push electron density onto the already-negative alkoxide oxygen, destabilizing the anion (and hindering its solvation), which raises the pKa relative to methanol.

alcohol-reactions.q: Adding a Grignard reagent (R-MgBr) to an alcohol results in:
options: Nucleophilic addition to give a new, larger alcohol
Simple acid-base protonation that destroys the Grignard reagent
An SN2 substitution that gives an ether
No reaction, since Grignards do not react with alcohols
alcohol-reactions.why: The O-H of an alcohol is acidic enough to protonate the strongly basic, carbanion-like Grignard reagent, quenching it as an alkane before it can perform any useful addition chemistry.

alcohol-reactions.q: Swern oxidation (DMSO and oxalyl chloride, then base) converts a primary alcohol to an aldehyde while avoiding:
options: Any stereochemical change at the carbinol carbon
Over-oxidation to the carboxylic acid, since the conditions are anhydrous and mild
The need for a final aqueous work-up
alcohol-reactions.why: Like PCC, Swern conditions contain no water, so the aldehyde product cannot be hydrated into the gem-diol that aqueous Cr(VI) systems go on to oxidize; it also avoids toxic chromium reagents.

alcohol-reactions.q: The Lucas test (HCl/ZnCl2) distinguishes primary, secondary, and tertiary alcohols based on how quickly a cloudy alkyl chloride layer forms.
alcohol-reactions.why: Tertiary alcohols react almost instantly because their carbocation is highly stabilized, secondary alcohols take several minutes, and primary alcohols show little change at room temperature, so the reaction rate reveals the alcohol's class.

alcohol-reactions.q: In the Lucas test, a tertiary alcohol shows:
options: No visible change even after heating
Cloudiness only after five to ten minutes
A color change from orange to green
Immediate cloudiness or a separate layer
alcohol-reactions.why: Tertiary alcohols ionize very quickly under these acidic conditions because the resulting carbocation is highly stabilized, so the insoluble alkyl chloride forms almost immediately.

alcohol-reactions.q: Converting an alcohol to a TMS (trimethylsilyl) ether before carrying out a reaction elsewhere in the molecule is done primarily to:
options: Temporarily mask the OH so it cannot act as a nucleophile or acidic proton during other steps
Make the molecule more acidic overall
Oxidize the alcohol in a controlled, reversible way
alcohol-reactions.why: Protecting groups like TMS ethers are easily installed and later removed (for example with mild acid or fluoride), letting chemists carry out reactions elsewhere in a molecule without interference from a free -OH.

alcohol-reactions.q: The reaction of a secondary alcohol with PBr3 proceeds through:
options: An SN1 mechanism with a free carbocation, racemizing the product
An SN2-like mechanism with backside attack by bromide, inverting configuration
Simple proton transfer with no bond-breaking at carbon
alcohol-reactions.why: PBr3 first converts the OH into a good leaving group, and bromide then displaces it in a single concerted backside attack, giving clean inversion rather than the racemization seen with carbocation intermediates.

alcohol-reactions.q: Treating a chiral secondary alcohol with PBr3 gives the alkyl bromide with inverted stereochemistry at that carbon.
alcohol-reactions.why: Because PBr3 operates through a concerted SN2-type displacement without a free carbocation, bromide must attack from the side opposite the leaving group, inverting the configuration.

alcohol-reactions.q: Treating that same chiral secondary alcohol with concentrated HBr alone (simple acid-catalyzed substitution) tends to give a racemized, or partially racemized, product.
alcohol-reactions.why: Protonation of the OH followed by loss of water generates a planar carbocation that can be attacked by bromide from either face, scrambling the stereochemistry relative to the clean inversion seen with PBr3.

alcohol-reactions.q: Among methanol, isopropanol, and tert-butanol, which dehydrates fastest when heated with strong acid?
options: They all dehydrate at the same rate
alcohol-reactions.why: Acid-catalyzed dehydration proceeds through a carbocation intermediate; tert-butanol forms the most stable (tertiary) carbocation most readily, so it reacts fastest, while methanol has no adjacent carbon to form a double bond with at all.

ether-chemistry.q: Why are ethers generally unreactive under basic conditions?
options: There is no good leaving group (RO⁻ is a strong base) until acid activates it
The C–O bond is too strong to ever break
Ethers react only with other ethers
ether-chemistry.why: Like alcohols, ethers need protonation (acidic conditions) to turn the alkoxide oxygen into a viable leaving group (neutral alcohol) before cleavage.

ether-chemistry.q: Strong acid cleavage of an ether (e.g., with HI) proceeds through what kind of mechanism for a secondary/tertiary carbon?
ether-chemistry.why: Protonated ethers at secondary/tertiary centers tend to cleave via SN1 (carbocation pathway), while primary centers favor SN2.

ether-chemistry.q: Why are ethers often used as solvents for reactions involving strong nucleophiles/bases (like Grignard reagents)?
options: They are highly reactive and participate directly
They are relatively unreactive (no acidic O-H, no easy leaving group) yet can coordinate to stabilize reactive intermediates
Ethers decompose readily under these conditions
ether-chemistry.why: Ethers lack an acidic proton and don’t have a good leaving group under neutral/basic conditions, so they tolerate strongly basic/nucleophilic reagents while still solvating them through the oxygen’s lone pairs.

ether-chemistry.q: Why do ethers generally have lower boiling points than alcohols of similar molecular weight?
options: Ethers are always smaller molecules than alcohols
Ethers have stronger London dispersion forces
Ether molecules cannot hydrogen-bond to each other, unlike alcohols
ether-chemistry.why: Alcohols can hydrogen-bond to one another through their O-H groups, which raises their boiling points substantially; ethers lack an O-H bond, so they only experience weaker dipole-dipole and dispersion forces between molecules.

ether-chemistry.q: Ethers can act as hydrogen bond acceptors (through their oxygen lone pairs) but not as hydrogen bond donors.
ether-chemistry.why: An ether oxygen has lone pairs that can accept a hydrogen bond from an O-H or N-H elsewhere, but since ethers have no O-H or N-H of their own, they cannot donate a hydrogen bond.

ether-chemistry.q: Heating methyl propyl ether with excess concentrated HI cleaves the ether to give propanol plus which alkyl halide?
options: A mixture of both in equal amounts
No cleavage occurs; ethers are inert to HI
ether-chemistry.why: Once the ether oxygen is protonated, iodide attacks via SN2 at the less hindered, less sterically crowded methyl carbon rather than the propyl carbon, giving methyl iodide and propanol (which can react further with excess acid).

ether-chemistry.q: Treating tert-butyl methyl ether with excess HI gives:
options: A mixture of tert-butyl and methyl iodide in equal amounts
No reaction, since tertiary ethers resist acidic cleavage
ether-chemistry.why: The tertiary carbon can ionize readily to form a stable carbocation (SN1-like pathway), so iodide captures that carbocation, leaving methanol as the other fragment rather than forming a methyl cation.

ether-chemistry.q: An unsymmetrical ether with one primary alkyl group and one tertiary alkyl group is treated with HBr. The major products are expected to be:
options: The primary bromide and the tertiary alcohol
Both carbons are substituted with equal probability
The tertiary bromide and the primary alcohol
Neither C-O bond breaks under these conditions
ether-chemistry.why: The tertiary carbon can ionize to a stable carbocation far more easily than the primary carbon can undergo a slow SN2 displacement, so cleavage occurs preferentially at the tertiary center, releasing the primary alcohol intact.

ether-chemistry.q: Treating anisole (methyl phenyl ether) with HI cleaves it to give phenol and methyl iodide, with the aryl-oxygen bond remaining completely intact.
ether-chemistry.why: Breaking the aryl-oxygen bond would require either an unstable aryl cation (no SN1 pathway) or backside attack on a planar, sp2 aromatic carbon (no SN2 pathway), so cleavage instead occurs exclusively at the methyl carbon.

ether-chemistry.q: Why is the Williamson ether synthesis generally a poor method for making an ether from a tertiary alkyl halide?
options: Tertiary alkyl halides are never soluble in the reaction solvent
Alkoxides cannot act as nucleophiles toward tertiary carbons
Tertiary halides spontaneously hydrolyze before the alkoxide can react
The strongly basic alkoxide promotes E2 elimination instead of SN2 substitution on the tertiary halide
ether-chemistry.why: A bulky, basic alkoxide approaching a hindered tertiary carbon strongly favors removing a beta-hydrogen (E2) over performing a backside SN2 attack, so elimination products dominate instead of the desired ether.

ether-chemistry.q: To cleanly synthesize an unsymmetrical ether via the Williamson method, you should generally:
options: Use the alkoxide from the more hindered alcohol paired with the less hindered (often primary) alkyl halide
Use the alkoxide from the less hindered alcohol paired with a tertiary alkyl halide
It never matters which partner is the alkoxide versus the halide
Always use two different tertiary components for best yield
ether-chemistry.why: Because the alkyl halide is the electrophile undergoing SN2 attack, choosing one that is primary (or otherwise unhindered) avoids competing elimination, regardless of how bulky the alkoxide nucleophile itself is.

ether-chemistry.q: Crown ethers such as 18-crown-6 are useful in organic synthesis mainly because they:
options: React covalently with alkyl halides to form new ethers
Selectively bind and solubilize specific metal cations, even in nonpolar organic solvents
ether-chemistry.why: The ring of oxygen atoms in a crown ether can wrap around a metal cation of the right size, effectively dissolving otherwise poorly soluble ionic salts in nonpolar solvents.

ether-chemistry.q: 18-Crown-6 binds K+ more selectively than it binds Na+ because its cavity size is a better match for the potassium ion.
ether-chemistry.why: Crown ethers show size selectivity: 18-crown-6's ring cavity closely matches the ionic radius of K+, giving tighter binding than with the smaller Na+ ion, which fits less snugly.

ether-chemistry.q: Dissolving KF with 18-crown-6 in a nonpolar organic solvent makes fluoride a much more effective nucleophile because:
options: The crown ether reduces the overall negative charge on fluoride
Crown ethers convert fluoride into a stronger base but weaker nucleophile
The crown ether sequesters the potassium cation, leaving a more 'naked,' poorly ion-paired fluoride anion
The crown ether reacts with fluoride to form a more reactive complex
ether-chemistry.why: Normally F- is tightly ion-paired with its counter-cation and poorly solvated in nonpolar media, dampening its reactivity; encapsulating K+ inside the crown ether frees the anion to act as a much more potent, less hindered nucleophile.

ether-chemistry.q: Diethyl ether was historically used as a general anesthetic in surgery.
ether-chemistry.why: Diethyl ether was one of the earliest general anesthetics used in medicine, though it was eventually replaced by safer, less flammable agents.

ether-chemistry.q: Tetrahydrofuran (THF) is a commonly used ether solvent mainly because it:
options: Is a strong acid that activates electrophiles
Reacts readily with Grignard reagents to improve yields
Dissolves both polar and nonpolar reagents and coordinates well to metal centers like Mg2+ or Li+ while staying largely unreactive
ether-chemistry.why: THF's oxygen lone pairs coordinate to metal cations (helping stabilize organometallic reagents in solution) while its ring is chemically unreactive toward most nucleophiles and bases, making it a versatile, widely used solvent.

ether-chemistry.q: Old bottles of diethyl ether that have been stored for a long time can become dangerous to distill because they slowly form explosive peroxides through reaction with atmospheric oxygen.
ether-chemistry.why: Autoxidation at the carbon next to the ether oxygen slowly generates peroxide and hydroperoxide species that can concentrate and detonate, especially when the ether is evaporated or distilled, which is why old ether stocks are handled with caution.

ether-chemistry.q: Why does peroxide formation (autoxidation) occur preferentially at the carbon directly attached to the ether oxygen?
options: The C-H bond there is weakened because the resulting radical is stabilized by the adjacent oxygen's lone pair
That carbon has the most hydrogens available statistically
The oxygen atom itself is directly oxidized first
Ether oxygens catalyze peroxide formation only at the far end of the chain
ether-chemistry.why: Removing a hydrogen from the carbon next to the ether oxygen gives a radical that is stabilized by overlap with a lone pair on oxygen, making that particular C-H bond especially susceptible to slow radical autoxidation by atmospheric O2.

ether-chemistry.q: Which characteristic infrared absorption is commonly used to help identify an ether functional group?
options: A broad O-H stretch around 3300 cm-1
A strong C-O stretch around 1050-1150 cm-1
A sharp C=O stretch around 1715 cm-1
ether-chemistry.why: Ethers lack the O-H and C=O groups that dominate alcohol and carbonyl spectra, so their most diagnostic IR feature is the strong C-O single bond stretch in the 1050-1150 cm-1 region.

ether-chemistry.q: Heating diethyl ether with a large excess of concentrated HI eventually gives, as the final organic products:
options: One equivalent of ethyl iodide and one of ethanol
Diethyl ether is unreactive toward HI even in excess
ether-chemistry.why: With excess strong acid and heat, both C-O bonds of the symmetrical ether are eventually cleaved by iodide via SN2, first releasing ethanol (which itself then reacts further with HI) and ultimately converting both ethyl groups into ethyl iodide.

ether-chemistry.q: Protonation of an ether's oxygen atom by a strong acid forms:
ether-chemistry.why: Adding a proton to the ether oxygen gives it three bonds plus a formal positive charge, a species called an oxonium ion, which makes the adjacent C-O bonds much easier to break.

ether-chemistry.q: Unlike alcohols, simple ethers have no O-H bond and therefore cannot be oxidized to aldehydes, ketones, or carboxylic acids under standard laboratory oxidation conditions.
ether-chemistry.why: Reagents like PCC or Jones reagent oxidize by removing the O-H hydrogen along with a C-H hydrogen from the carbinol carbon; since ethers have no O-H to begin with, this pathway simply is not available to them.

ether-chemistry.q: Grignard reagents generally fail to form well, or are ineffective, when prepared in purely hydrocarbon solvents like hexane mainly because:
options: Without ether oxygen lone pairs to coordinate and stabilize the organomagnesium species, it does not form or stay usefully in solution
Hydrocarbons react violently with magnesium metal
Hydrocarbon solvents are too polar for Grignard chemistry
Grignard reagents require an acidic solvent to initiate
ether-chemistry.why: Ether solvents donate electron density from their oxygen lone pairs to the electrophilic magnesium center, which helps stabilize and solubilize the highly reactive organomagnesium species; nonpolar hydrocarbons cannot offer this coordination.

ether-chemistry.q: Vinyl (enol) ethers are hydrolyzed much more readily under mild aqueous acid than ordinary dialkyl ethers because:
options: Vinyl ethers contain an extra oxygen atom that dialkyl ethers lack
Protonation of the double bond generates a resonance-stabilized oxocarbenium ion that water can attack easily, ultimately giving a carbonyl compound
The C-O bond in a vinyl ether is a double bond, which is intrinsically weaker
Vinyl ethers are actually esters in disguise
ether-chemistry.why: Protonating the alkene carbon of a vinyl ether produces a cation stabilized by resonance donation from the adjacent oxygen (an oxocarbenium ion); water then adds and loss of the alcohol gives a carbonyl compound, a much faster pathway than the harsh conditions needed to cleave a saturated dialkyl ether.

ether-chemistry.q: Tetrahydrofuran (THF) is best classified as a:
ether-chemistry.why: THF is a five-membered ring containing one oxygen atom and four carbons, making it a saturated cyclic ether rather than an open-chain one.

ether-chemistry.q: IUPAC nomenclature typically names simple ethers as alkoxy-substituted alkanes, such as calling CH3-O-CH2CH3 'methoxyethane.'
ether-chemistry.why: Rather than using a standalone 'ether' suffix, the preferred IUPAC approach treats the shorter alkyl-oxygen unit as an alkoxy substituent on the longer parent chain, giving names like methoxyethane for ethyl methyl ether.

ether-chemistry.q: Ethers are generally poor nucleophiles themselves in most reactions, but their oxygen lone pairs make them good Lewis bases, able to form a stable complex with a Lewis acid such as BF3.
options: False, ethers cannot interact with Lewis acids at all
False, only alcohols can coordinate to Lewis acids
True, but only aromatic ethers can do this
True, an ether-BF3 complex (an 'etherate') is a well-known, stable adduct
ether-chemistry.why: The ether oxygen's lone pair can donate into the empty orbital of a Lewis acid like BF3, forming a stable donor-acceptor (Lewis acid-base) adduct, such as the BF3 etherate commonly used as a mild Lewis acid catalyst.

ether-chemistry.q: Small ethers like diethyl ether show modest but real solubility in water, higher than a comparably sized pure hydrocarbon would have.
ether-chemistry.why: Although ethers cannot donate hydrogen bonds, their oxygen lone pairs can accept hydrogen bonds from water molecules, giving small ethers noticeably greater water solubility than alkanes of similar size.

ether-chemistry.q: Ether cleavage reactions are typically carried out with HI or HBr rather than HCl mainly because:
options: Iodide and bromide are much better nucleophiles than chloride, making the SN2/SN1 displacement step faster
HCl cannot protonate an ether oxygen at all
HI and HBr are weaker acids, which favors cleavage
Chloride ions are too large to attack the ether carbon
ether-chemistry.why: After the ether oxygen is protonated, the halide ion must still act as the nucleophile (or cation-trapping species) that displaces the alcohol; iodide and bromide are considerably more nucleophilic than chloride, making the overall cleavage much faster and more practical.

ether-chemistry.q: Why do simple dialkyl ethers typically require a strong acid and prolonged heating to be cleaved, while esters hydrolyze readily with just dilute aqueous base at room temperature?
options: Esters contain more carbon atoms, making them inherently more reactive
Esters have an electrophilic carbonyl carbon that forms a stabilized tetrahedral intermediate, while a neutral ether oxygen offers no comparable site for attack until it is first protonated
Ethers are aromatic and therefore unreactive
Esters are ionic compounds, unlike ethers
ether-chemistry.why: A base can attack an ester's carbonyl carbon directly because the resulting tetrahedral intermediate is stabilized by the carbonyl oxygen and can expel a leaving group; an ether has no such electrophilic carbon, so it must first be protonated by strong acid before any C-O bond becomes breakable.

epoxides.q: Epoxides are much more reactive than regular ethers because:
options: The three-membered ring has significant ring strain, which is relieved on opening
epoxides.why: The ~60° bond angles in the three-membered ring are far from ideal, so opening the ring relieves substantial strain, driving reactivity.

epoxides.q: Under basic conditions, a nucleophile opens an epoxide by attacking:
options: The less substituted carbon (SN2-like, backside attack)
epoxides.why: Basic/neutral conditions favor an SN2-like mechanism — backside attack at the less hindered carbon.

epoxides.q: Under acidic conditions, a nucleophile opens an epoxide preferentially at the:
options: Less substituted carbon only, same as base
More substituted carbon, since protonation gives it more carbocation-like character
The oxygen atom itself is attacked
epoxides.why: Protonating the epoxide oxygen makes the ring-opening more SN1-like, so the nucleophile attacks the carbon that better stabilizes positive charge — the more substituted one — unlike the SN2-like base-catalyzed case.

epoxides.q: Epoxides are most commonly synthesized in the laboratory from alkenes using:
options: A peroxyacid such as mCPBA (meta-chloroperoxybenzoic acid)
epoxides.why: Peroxyacids like mCPBA deliver an oxygen atom directly across the carbon-carbon double bond in a single concerted step, converting the alkene into an epoxide.

epoxides.q: Epoxidation of an alkene with a peroxyacid proceeds with syn (same-face) addition of the oxygen atom.
epoxides.why: The peroxyacid transfers its oxygen to both alkene carbons simultaneously from one face in a single concerted step (often pictured as a 'butterfly' transition state), so the new C-O bonds form on the same side of the original double bond.

epoxides.q: Epoxidizing cis-2-butene with mCPBA gives, as the major (and only) product:
options: A single meso epoxide, since syn addition to the cis alkene places both methyl groups on the same relative side
A racemic mixture of two chiral epoxides
A mixture of cis and trans epoxide diastereomers
No epoxide forms from cis alkenes
epoxides.why: Syn addition preserves the original cis relationship of the two methyl groups, and the resulting epoxide has an internal mirror plane, making it a single achiral meso compound rather than a mixture of enantiomers.

epoxides.q: Epoxidizing trans-2-butene with mCPBA gives, as the product:
options: A racemic mixture of the two chiral (2R,3R) and (2S,3S) epoxide enantiomers
A mixture of four different diastereomers
epoxides.why: Syn addition to the trans alkene produces a chiral epoxide (no internal mirror plane); because the peroxyacid can approach either face of the planar alkene with equal likelihood, both enantiomers form in equal amounts, giving a racemic mixture.

epoxides.q: Regardless of whether the conditions are acidic or basic, nucleophilic ring-opening of an epoxide occurs through:
options: A radical mechanism with no stereochemical preference
Backside (SN2-type) attack that inverts the configuration at the carbon being attacked
Attack that always occurs with complete racemization
epoxides.why: In both the basic and acidic mechanisms, the nucleophile approaches from the side opposite the breaking C-O bond, so the carbon under attack is inverted even though the overall regiochemistry (which carbon is attacked) differs between the two conditions.

epoxides.q: Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis of cyclohexene oxide gives predominantly trans-1,2-cyclohexanediol rather than the cis diastereomer.
epoxides.why: Water attacks the protonated epoxide from the face opposite the ring oxygen (backside attack), so the two new OH groups end up anti to each other, giving the trans diol rather than the cis one.

epoxides.q: Reducing an unsymmetrical epoxide with excess LiAlH4 places the new hydrogen mainly on:
options: The more hindered carbon regardless of sterics
Neither carbon; LiAlH4 does not reduce epoxides
The less hindered carbon, leaving the new OH on the more substituted carbon
epoxides.why: Hydride is a strong nucleophile that reacts via an SN2-like pathway, so like other strong nucleophiles it attacks the less sterically hindered carbon, which ends up bonded to the delivered hydrogen while the OH remains on the more substituted carbon.

epoxides.q: Treating an unsymmetrical epoxide with a Grignard reagent (RMgX) opens the ring with the carbon nucleophile attacking:
options: The less hindered carbon, consistent with an SN2-like strong-nucleophile mechanism
The more substituted carbon, as in acid-catalyzed opening
Whichever carbon is closer to the oxygen's lone pairs, which is both equally
Neither carbon; Grignards do not react with epoxides
epoxides.why: Grignard reagents are strong, basic carbon nucleophiles that react with epoxides under essentially basic-type conditions, favoring backside SN2 attack at the more accessible, less hindered carbon.

epoxides.q: Treating a simple epoxide with HBr produces, as the initial product:
options: A vicinal halohydrin, with a bromine on one carbon and an OH on the adjacent carbon
epoxides.why: Under acidic conditions the protonated epoxide is opened by bromide acting as the nucleophile at one carbon, while the oxygen (now an OH after losing its proton) remains on the adjacent carbon, giving a halohydrin.

epoxides.q: In the acid-catalyzed ring-opening of 2-methyl-2,3-epoxybutane with methanol, the methanol oxygen attacks mainly at:
options: The less substituted carbon, exactly as it would under basic conditions
The more substituted carbon, because that transition state carries significant positive (carbocation-like) character
Neither carbon; methanol is too weak a nucleophile to react
epoxides.why: Protonation of the epoxide oxygen gives the C-O bonds partial cationic character, concentrated at the carbon that would form the more stable carbocation; even a weak nucleophile like methanol is then directed to that more substituted carbon.

epoxides.q: In the basic ring-opening of 2-methyl-2,3-epoxybutane with sodium methoxide, methoxide attacks mainly at:
options: The more substituted carbon, exactly as under acidic conditions
Whichever carbon bears the oxygen lone pairs
The reaction does not proceed under basic conditions
epoxides.why: Under basic or neutral conditions the epoxide is not protonated, so the strong methoxide nucleophile simply performs a straightforward SN2 attack at the more sterically accessible, less hindered carbon.

epoxides.q: The oxirane (epoxide) ring consists of one oxygen atom and two carbon atoms joined in a three-membered ring.
epoxides.why: An epoxide, or oxirane, is defined by this specific three-membered ring of two carbons and one oxygen, which is what gives it its characteristic angle strain and heightened reactivity.

epoxides.q: Compared to a typical acyclic dialkyl ether, an epoxide reacts with nucleophiles much faster mainly because of:
options: Relief of significant ring strain upon opening the three-membered ring
Epoxides having a much more electronegative oxygen atom
Epoxides containing an extra oxygen atom
epoxides.why: The epoxide's three-membered ring has bond angles far smaller than the ideal tetrahedral angle, storing substantial strain energy; breaking a C-O bond releases that strain, which strongly drives the ring-opening reaction forward.

epoxides.q: Why does switching from basic to acidic conditions change where a nucleophile attacks an unsymmetrical epoxide, even though the same general C-O bond region is ultimately broken?
options: Acid always breaks the bond on the side nearer the larger substituent for purely steric reasons

Protonating the epoxide oxygen gives the transition state significant carbocation-like character at the more substituted carbon, while under base the epoxide is unprotonated and attack is governed simply by steric accessibility
Base-catalyzed openings never actually break a C-O bond
The identity of the solvent, not the catalyst, controls the regiochemistry
epoxides.why: Under acid, protonation weakens the C-O bonds and shifts positive character toward whichever carbon can better stabilize it (the more substituted one), directing even weak nucleophiles there; under base, the unprotonated, still-strained ring is simply attacked wherever the strong nucleophile can approach most easily, favoring the less hindered carbon.

epoxides.q: Under acidic conditions, even weak nucleophiles such as water or alcohols can open an epoxide, whereas under neutral or basic conditions only strong nucleophiles react efficiently.
epoxides.why: Protonating the epoxide oxygen makes the ring vastly more electrophilic, so weak nucleophiles that would otherwise be unreactive can now attack; without that activation, only strong, good nucleophiles can open the strained but un-activated ring at a useful rate.

epoxides.q: An epoxide reacting with an amine nucleophile under neutral or basic-type conditions opens to give:
options: A beta-amino alcohol, with the amine attacking the more hindered carbon
An imine with loss of the oxygen entirely
A beta-amino alcohol, with the amine attacking the less hindered carbon
No reaction; amines do not open epoxides
epoxides.why: Amines are good, strongly basic nucleophiles, so like other strong nucleophiles they attack the less sterically hindered carbon of the epoxide via an SN2-like pathway, generating a beta-amino alcohol.

epoxides.q: Opening a meso epoxide with an achiral nucleophile under SN2-like (basic) conditions produces:
options: A mixture of diastereomers, not enantiomers
A racemic (1:1) mixture of two enantiomeric products
epoxides.why: A meso epoxide has two carbons that are enantiotopic to each other; an achiral nucleophile has no way to distinguish between them, so it attacks each one with equal probability, producing equal amounts of both resulting enantiomers.

epoxides.q: Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis of 2,2-dimethyloxirane (isobutylene oxide) directs the incoming water molecule mainly to:
options: The more substituted carbon (the one bearing the two methyl groups), since it better stabilizes the partial positive charge in the transition state
The unsubstituted CH2 carbon, exactly as it would under basic conditions
Either carbon with statistically equal likelihood
Neither carbon; tertiary epoxide carbons do not react with water
epoxides.why: Protonation of the epoxide oxygen gives the more substituted carbon significant carbocation-like character in the transition state, so water (even though it is a weak nucleophile) is directed there preferentially, just as with other acid-catalyzed epoxide openings.

epoxides.q: The fundamental driving force behind epoxide ring-opening reactions, under both acidic and basic conditions, is:
options: Formation of a new pi bond
Relief of angle strain stored in the three-membered ring
Loss of a proton from the nucleophile
epoxides.why: The highly strained bond angles of the oxirane ring store considerable potential energy; opening the ring to form a less strained, acyclic product is thermodynamically favorable and is the underlying reason epoxides react so readily compared to ordinary ethers.

epoxides.q: Which statement correctly contrasts the behavior of an epoxide versus an ordinary dialkyl ether toward aqueous NaOH at room temperature?
options: Both react at similar, moderate rates
The ordinary ether reacts faster because it has more accessible carbons
The epoxide reacts readily (ring-opening), while the ordinary ether is essentially inert, because ring strain makes the epoxide's C-O bond far easier to break via nucleophilic attack
Neither reacts with aqueous NaOH under any conditions
epoxides.why: An unstrained ether's C-O bond is simply too strong and the oxygen too poor a leaving group for hydroxide to displace at room temperature, but the epoxide's ring strain dramatically lowers the barrier for the same kind of backside nucleophilic attack.

epoxides.q: Acid-catalyzed ring-opening of an epoxide proceeds through a fully formed, free carbocation intermediate, exactly as in a classic SN1 substitution on an alkyl halide.
epoxides.why: The reaction is usually described as borderline or concerted, with the nucleophile beginning to attack as the C-O bond breaks rather than waiting for a fully independent, freely rotating carbocation to form first; this is why some stereochemical and regiochemical control is retained even under acidic conditions.

epoxides.q: Protonation of an epoxide's oxygen by a strong acid makes subsequent ring-opening much easier mainly because it:
options: Permanently removes the ring strain before any bond breaks
Converts the epoxide into an ether with no further reactivity
Reduces the electrophilicity of the ring carbons
Converts the epoxide oxygen into a much better leaving group and increases the electrophilicity of the ring carbons
epoxides.why: A neutral ether oxygen is a poor leaving group, but once protonated it becomes a much better one (similar to protonating an alcohol); this protonation also pulls electron density away from the ring carbons, making them more attractive targets for even weak nucleophiles.
