ir.why: Both alkynes and nitriles absorb in this triple-bond region; an aromatic ring or ketone would show very different characteristic bands instead.

ir.q: IR spectroscopy alone can usually determine the complete three-dimensional structure of an unknown molecule.
ir.why: IR reveals which functional groups are present from characteristic bond vibrations, but not the full connectivity or 3D arrangement of atoms; other tools like NMR and mass spec are needed for that.

ir.q: A sharp absorption near 2250 cm⁻¹ that is NOT accompanied by a sharp C-H stretch near 3300 cm⁻¹ most likely belongs to a:
ir.why: Both nitriles and alkynes absorb near 2100-2260 cm⁻¹, but only a terminal alkyne also shows the sharp sp C-H stretch near 3300 cm⁻¹; a nitrile has no such C-H to produce that band.

ir.q: The 'fingerprint region' of an IR spectrum, used to distinguish very similar molecules from each other, spans roughly:
ir.why: Below about 1500 cm⁻¹, absorptions arise from complex combinations of bending and skeletal vibrations unique to each molecule, making this region a usable fingerprint even when individual bands are hard to assign.

ir.q: A bond between two lighter atoms, such as C-H, generally stretches at a higher wavenumber than a bond between a carbon and a heavier atom, such as C-Cl, all else being roughly equal.
ir.why: Vibrational frequency increases as reduced mass decreases, so light-atom bonds like C-H vibrate much faster, and thus at higher wavenumber, than heavier-atom bonds like C-Cl.

ir.q: An ester C=O stretch typically appears at a slightly higher wavenumber (about 1735-1750 cm⁻¹) than a ketone C=O (about 1715 cm⁻¹) mainly because:
options: Esters always contain an aromatic ring
The ester oxygen's inductive electron withdrawal stiffens the C=O bond more than the oxygen's resonance donation softens it, relative to a ketone
Esters contain an extra hydrogen atom that ketones lack
Esters absorb water more readily than ketones
ir.why: The alkoxy oxygen withdraws electron density inductively and its resonance donation into the carbonyl is weaker than an amide nitrogen's, leaving the ester C=O stiffer and higher in frequency than a simple ketone.

ir.q: Aldehydes can often be distinguished from ketones in IR by the presence of:
options: A broad O-H band near 3300 cm⁻¹
Two weak C-H stretching bands near 2720 and 2850 cm⁻¹ in addition to the carbonyl stretch
A complete absence of any carbonyl absorption
ir.why: The C-H bond directly on the carbonyl carbon of an aldehyde gives a characteristic weak doublet near 2720 and 2850 cm⁻¹ that ketones, lacking that C-H, do not show.

ir.q: An amide carbonyl typically absorbs at a lower wavenumber (about 1630-1695 cm⁻¹) than a ketone (about 1715 cm⁻¹) because:
options: Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, which weakens the C=O only inductively
Amides are always less polar overall than ketones
Amides contain no hydrogen atoms at all
Resonance donation from the nitrogen lone pair gives the C=O bond more single-bond character, lowering its force constant
ir.why: Nitrogen's lone pair delocalizes strongly into the carbonyl pi system, increasing single-bond character in C=O and lowering its stretching frequency relative to a ketone.

ir.q: Conjugating a ketone's carbonyl with an adjacent C=C double bond, forming an enone, typically lowers the C=O stretching frequency compared to the unconjugated ketone.
ir.why: Conjugation delocalizes pi electron density between the alkene and the carbonyl, giving the C=O bond more single-bond character and a lower force constant, shifting the stretch lower.

ir.q: Compared to a simple alcohol's O-H stretch, a carboxylic acid's O-H stretch in IR is typically:
options: Broader and extending to lower wavenumber because of strong hydrogen-bonded dimer formation
ir.why: Carboxylic acids hydrogen-bond strongly to form dimers even in dilute solution, producing a very broad O-H absorption from roughly 2500-3300 cm⁻¹, broader than a typical alcohol O-H band.

ir.q: An unknown compound's IR spectrum shows a single, moderately broad N-H stretch near 3300 cm⁻¹ with no second N-H band nearby. This is most consistent with:
options: An amide with two N-H bonds
ir.why: A primary amine's two N-H bonds give two stretching bands, and a tertiary amine has no N-H at all, so a single N-H band points to a secondary amine.

ir.q: A sharp, strong absorption near 3300 cm⁻¹ together with a weak triple-bond stretch near 2120 cm⁻¹ is most diagnostic of:
ir.why: The sharp high-frequency band near 3300 cm⁻¹ comes from a C-H bonded directly to an sp carbon, which only a terminal alkyne has; an internal alkyne lacks that C-H band.

ir.q: A higher carbonyl stretching wavenumber generally corresponds to a carbonyl bond with a higher force constant, meaning a stiffer, more double-bond-like C=O.
ir.why: Stretching frequency scales with the square root of the force constant divided by reduced mass, so for similar atoms a stiffer, more double-bond-like bond vibrates at a higher wavenumber.

ir.q: Cyclopentanone's carbonyl stretch appears at a noticeably higher wavenumber than cyclohexanone's. This ring-size effect is best explained by:
options: Cyclopentanone simply contains more hydrogen atoms
Cyclopentanone cannot hydrogen bond at all
Increased ring strain in the smaller ring raises the s-character and stiffness of the carbonyl carbon's bonds, increasing the C=O force constant
ir.why: As ring size decreases and angle strain increases, the carbonyl carbon's bonding shifts in a way that stiffens the C=O bond, shifting the stretch to higher wavenumber; this trend continues for even smaller rings.

ir.q: Why does conjugating a carbonyl with an aromatic ring, as in acetophenone, lower the C=O stretching frequency relative to a simple aliphatic ketone?
options: Resonance delocalizes electron density from the ring into the carbonyl pi system, increasing single-bond character and lowering the force constant
The ring physically blocks the vibration from occurring
Aromatic rings are heavier, lowering the frequency purely by mass effects
Aromatic ketones do not contain a true C=O bond
ir.why: The ring donates electron density through conjugation, reducing the double-bond character of C=O, which softens the bond and lowers its stretching frequency compared to an unconjugated ketone.

ir.q: A dilute solution of an alcohol in an inert solvent shows a sharp O-H stretch near 3600 cm⁻¹, but a concentrated solution of the same alcohol shows a broader band shifted toward 3300 cm⁻¹. This is best explained by:
options: Decomposition of the alcohol at higher concentration
Increased intermolecular hydrogen bonding at higher concentration, which weakens and broadens the O-H stretch
The alcohol becoming more acidic at higher concentration
A change in the alcohol's molecular formula
ir.why: At low concentration, alcohol molecules are mostly isolated with a free O-H; at higher concentration, extensive hydrogen bonding weakens the O-H bond and broadens and lowers its absorption.

ir.q: A carboxylic acid anhydride typically shows two distinct C=O stretching bands rather than one, due to vibrational coupling between the two carbonyl groups.
ir.why: The two nearby carbonyls in an anhydride couple vibrationally, splitting the absorption into two bands, often one near 1820 and one near 1760 cm⁻¹, both higher than a typical ester.

ir.q: Even though the aldehyde C-H stretch near 2720-2850 cm⁻¹ overlaps with other C-H absorptions, it remains diagnostically useful mainly because:
options: It is always the strongest band in the entire spectrum
It exactly overlaps the carbonyl stretch itself
It appears as a distinct weak doublet in a relatively open part of the spectrum, usually alongside a carbonyl stretch
Aldehydes otherwise show no identifying features at all
ir.why: Although weak, the aldehydic C-H doublet falls below most alkane and alkene C-H stretches, so even a small, distinct pair of bands there is a reliable clue when paired with a carbonyl absorption.

ir.q: Rank the following from LOWEST to HIGHEST typical carbonyl stretching wavenumber: amide, ketone, ester, acid chloride.
options: Acid chloride, then ester, then ketone, then amide
Ketone, then amide, then ester, then acid chloride
Ester, then amide, then acid chloride, then ketone
Amide, then ketone, then ester, then acid chloride
ir.why: Stronger resonance donation and weaker inductive withdrawal (as in an amide) lowers the frequency, while poor resonance donation with strong inductive withdrawal (as in an acid chloride) raises it the most, placing amide lowest and acid chloride highest.

ir.q: An unknown shows a strong absorption near 1715 cm⁻¹ and a very broad absorption spanning roughly 2500-3300 cm⁻¹ that overlaps the C-H stretches, with no separate sharp O-H band near 3600 cm⁻¹. This pattern most strongly suggests:
options: A simple ketone with no other functional groups
ir.why: A carbonyl stretch combined with a very broad, hydrogen-bonded O-H absorption smeared across the C-H region, rather than a sharp free O-H, is the classic signature of a carboxylic acid dimer.

ir.q: IR spectroscopy using standard, non-polarized techniques can readily distinguish between two enantiomers of a chiral molecule.
ir.why: Enantiomers have identical bond types and strengths, so their standard IR spectra are essentially indistinguishable; other techniques are needed to tell them apart.

ir.q: An acid chloride's C=O stretch, around 1790-1815 cm⁻¹, is higher than both an ester's and an amide's mainly because:
options: Chlorine atoms are lighter than oxygen or nitrogen atoms
Chlorine is a poor resonance donor into the carbonyl while still strongly withdrawing electron density inductively, stiffening the C=O without the softening seen in esters and amides
Acid chlorides contain no true carbon-oxygen double bond
Acid chlorides are always gases at room temperature
ir.why: Good pi donors, like an amide nitrogen, soften the C=O bond by adding single-bond character; chlorine's lone pairs overlap poorly with carbon, so its strong inductive pull dominates and stiffens the bond.

ir.q: Why is water generally avoided as a solvent when preparing a sample for IR spectroscopy, especially when looking for O-H or N-H functional groups?
options: Water is simply too expensive to use as a solvent
Water has essentially no effect on an IR spectrum
Water strongly absorbs in the same O-H and N-H regions of interest and can damage traditional salt-plate IR cells
Water is always completely immiscible with organic compounds
ir.why: Water's own strong, broad O-H absorption overlaps exactly where chemists look for O-H and N-H stretches in the sample, and liquid water can dissolve traditional salt-plate cells, so it is usually avoided.

h-nmr.q: ¹H NMR chemical shift (in ppm) tells you mainly about a hydrogen’s:
h-nmr.why: Electron-withdrawing groups nearby deshield a proton, shifting its signal downfield (higher ppm); shielded protons appear upfield.

h-nmr.q: The n+1 rule in ¹H NMR predicts that a proton with n chemically equivalent neighboring protons will show how many peaks (splitting)?
h-nmr.why: Spin-spin coupling with n equivalent neighbors splits a signal into n+1 peaks (e.g., 3 neighboring H’s give a quartet).

h-nmr.q: Why do aromatic (benzene-ring) protons typically appear far downfield (~7-8 ppm) in ¹H NMR compared to typical alkyl protons (~1-2 ppm)?
options: Aromatic protons are shielded more, not less
Aromatic protons have a different isotope
Ring current effects from the circulating pi electrons create a deshielding magnetic field at the ring’s edge where the protons sit
There is no real difference — it’s a measurement artifact
h-nmr.why: The delocalized aromatic pi electrons circulate in the applied magnetic field, generating a local magnetic field that reinforces the external field right at the ring’s edge, deshielding those protons and pushing their signal downfield.

h-nmr.q: In ¹H NMR, the integrated area under a peak tells you mainly about:
options: The exact chemical shift of the peak
The relative number of protons giving rise to that peak
h-nmr.why: Integration is proportional to the number of protons contributing to a signal, so comparing integrated areas gives the ratio of protons in each chemically distinct environment.

h-nmr.q: Tetramethylsilane (TMS) is used as the standard reference in ¹H NMR mainly because its protons are:
options: Very shielded, appear far upfield, and TMS is chemically inert and volatile for easy removal
Highly deshielded and appear far downfield, away from most signals
Identical in shift to water protons
Split into many peaks for easy calibration
h-nmr.why: TMS's methyl protons are more shielded than almost any organic proton, so they appear as a single peak at the upfield end of the spectrum (defined as 0 ppm), and TMS is unreactive and easily evaporated from the sample afterward.

h-nmr.q: A proton's chemical shift in ppm is essentially independent of the specific magnetic field strength of the NMR spectrometer used to record it.
h-nmr.why: Reporting shift as a ratio (ppm) relative to the operating frequency cancels out the field-strength dependence, which is exactly why ppm, rather than raw Hz, is used for comparing spectra from different instruments.

h-nmr.q: Deuterated chloroform (CDCl3) is a commonly used NMR solvent mainly because:
options: It is the cheapest solvent available
Its deuterium atoms produce no interfering ¹H signal in the spectrum
It reacts with the sample to improve resolution
It has the same chemical shift as TMS
h-nmr.why: Replacing ordinary hydrogens with deuterium removes the solvent's own strong ¹H signal, leaving a largely clean baseline so the sample's proton signals can be seen clearly.

h-nmr.q: An aldehyde's C-H proton typically appears much further downfield (around 9-10 ppm) than a typical vinyl proton (around 5-6 ppm) mainly because:
options: Aldehyde protons are attached to a different element than carbon
Vinyl protons are always shielded completely
The aldehyde proton experiences deshielding from both the electronegative carbonyl oxygen and the anisotropic effect of the C=O pi system
There is no real difference between the two shifts
h-nmr.why: The carbonyl's electron-withdrawing oxygen and its magnetic anisotropy both pull electron density away from the adjacent aldehyde proton, pushing its signal further downfield than an ordinary vinyl proton.

h-nmr.q: Hydroxyl (O-H) and amine (N-H) proton signals in ¹H NMR are often broader and appear at less predictable chemical shifts than typical C-H signals mainly because:
options: They are always the most intense peaks in the spectrum
They never couple to any other protons under any conditions
They only appear in samples run at very high temperature
They undergo rapid exchange with other O-H or N-H protons, including trace water, which varies with sample conditions
h-nmr.why: Fast proton exchange (often catalyzed by trace acid, base, or water) averages the local environment and can broaden or shift the O-H/N-H signal, making it variable from sample to sample and solvent to solvent.

h-nmr.q: Spin-spin coupling between protons in ¹H NMR occurs primarily through space rather than through the chemical bonds connecting them.
h-nmr.why: Coupling is transmitted through the bonding electrons connecting the nuclei, which is why it typically falls off sharply beyond three bonds, not through direct spatial proximity.

h-nmr.q: Vicinal coupling, the most common type discussed in an introductory course, refers to coupling between protons that are separated by how many bonds?
h-nmr.why: Vicinal coupling is coupling between protons on adjacent (neighboring) carbons, which are three bonds apart (H-C-C-H), and is the basis of the simple n+1 splitting rule.

h-nmr.q: For a hydrogen nucleus to be observable in ¹H NMR, it must have a nonzero nuclear spin.
h-nmr.why: Only nuclei with nonzero spin (¹H has spin 1/2) behave like tiny magnets that can align with or against an external field and absorb energy at a characteristic radiofrequency, which is what NMR detects.

h-nmr.q: Comparing CH3Cl, CH2Cl2, and CHCl3, the chemical shift of the carbon-bound proton(s) moves progressively further downfield as the number of chlorine atoms increases. This trend is best explained by:
options: More chlorine atoms make the molecule heavier, which directly shifts the signal downfield
Each additional electronegative chlorine further withdraws electron density from the carbon and its attached protons, increasing deshielding
Chlorine atoms decouple the protons from each other
The trend is actually reversed; more chlorine shifts the signal upfield
h-nmr.why: Each electronegative chlorine pulls electron density away inductively; stacking more of them on the same carbon compounds this effect, progressively deshielding the remaining protons and pushing the shift downfield.

h-nmr.q: Geminal coupling and vicinal coupling differ in that:
options: Geminal coupling only occurs in aromatic rings
Vicinal coupling is always stronger than geminal coupling
Geminal coupling is between protons on the same carbon, while vicinal coupling is between protons on adjacent carbons
There is no real difference between the two terms
h-nmr.why: Geminal protons share one carbon (two bonds apart), while vicinal protons sit on neighboring carbons (three bonds apart); both can show coupling, but the structural relationship and typical coupling constants differ.

h-nmr.q: For an ethyl bromide fragment, CH3-CH2-Br, the n+1 rule predicts what splitting pattern for the two proton environments?
options: The CH3 appears as a singlet and the CH2 as a singlet
The CH3 appears as a quartet and the CH2 as a triplet
The CH3 appears as a triplet and the CH2 as a quartet
h-nmr.why: The CH3 protons have two neighboring CH2 protons, giving n+1 = 3 peaks (a triplet); the CH2 protons have three neighboring CH3 protons, giving n+1 = 4 peaks (a quartet).

h-nmr.q: Two protons on the same carbon can be diastereotopic and show different chemical shifts if replacing each one individually (in turn) with a test group would create distinguishable stereochemical outcomes.
h-nmr.why: When a molecule contains another stereocenter or similar feature, the two protons on a CH2 are no longer related by a simple symmetry operation, so they occupy genuinely different environments and can show different shifts and even couple to each other.

h-nmr.q: A terminal alkyne's C-H proton typically appears around 1.8-3.0 ppm, noticeably more upfield than a typical vinyl proton (around 4.5-6.5 ppm), even though the alkyne carbon is more electronegative (more s-character). This is best explained by:
options: The cylindrical symmetry of the triple bond's pi system creates an anisotropic shielding effect at the proton's position along the bond axis
The alkyne has no electronic effects on its proton at all
Alkyne protons are not actually attached to carbon
Vinyl protons are always more shielded than any other type
h-nmr.why: Unlike the carbonyl or aromatic pi systems, the circulating electrons around a linear triple bond generate an induced field that shields, rather than deshields, a proton sitting along the bond's axis, pulling its shift upfield despite the carbon's high s-character.

h-nmr.q: Vinyl (alkene) protons typically appear downfield, around 4.5-6.5 ppm, compared to ordinary alkyl protons. This is mainly due to:
options: Vinyl protons having a different number of neutrons
The anisotropic magnetic field generated by the circulating pi electrons of the double bond, which deshields protons in the alkene plane
A simple increase in molecular weight near the double bond
Vinyl protons never experiencing any magnetic effects
h-nmr.why: The pi electrons of the C=C double bond circulate under the applied field and generate a local induced field that adds to the external field in the plane of the alkene, deshielding the attached protons and shifting them downfield.

h-nmr.q: A highly symmetric molecule like tert-butanol, (CH3)3C-OH, shows how many distinct ¹H NMR signals?
h-nmr.why: The nine equivalent methyl protons give one signal, and the single O-H proton gives a separate signal, for two total distinct environments despite there being ten hydrogens overall.

h-nmr.q: A typical vicinal coupling constant (3J) between protons on adjacent sp3 carbons usually falls in roughly what range?
h-nmr.why: Vicinal (three-bond) proton-proton coupling constants in freely rotating alkyl chains commonly fall around 6-8 Hz, a useful benchmark when analyzing splitting patterns.

h-nmr.q: Protons that are chemically equivalent to each other by molecular symmetry do not produce visible splitting from coupling to one another.
h-nmr.why: Although equivalent protons can technically couple, the splitting is not observed because identical nuclei in identical environments produce overlapping, indistinguishable transitions, so equivalent protons appear to ignore each other.

h-nmr.q: Why does adding a drop of D2O to an NMR sample often cause an O-H or N-H peak to shrink or disappear from the ¹H NMR spectrum?
options: The exchangeable O-H or N-H proton rapidly swaps with deuterium from D2O, removing it from the pool of detectable ¹H nuclei
D2O reacts chemically with the carbon skeleton of the molecule
D2O always increases the intensity of every peak in the spectrum
h-nmr.why: O-H and N-H protons exchange rapidly with any other exchangeable protons present, including the large excess of deuterium in added D2O, converting O-H/N-H into O-D/N-D, which is invisible in a standard ¹H NMR spectrum.

h-nmr.q: For an isopropyl group, -CH(CH3)2, attached to a larger chain, the n+1 rule predicts what splitting for the central CH proton and the two equivalent CH3 groups?
options: The CH appears as a doublet and the CH3 groups appear as a septet
The CH appears as a septet and the CH3 groups appear as a doublet
The CH appears as a quartet and the CH3 groups appear as a triplet
h-nmr.why: The central CH proton is flanked by six equivalent methyl protons, giving n+1 = 7 peaks (a septet), while each methyl group's protons see only the one CH neighbor, giving n+1 = 2 peaks (a doublet).

h-nmr.q: A CH2 group flanked by a stereocenter elsewhere in the molecule can show an unusually complicated splitting pattern (such as an ABX-type pattern) rather than a simple doublet, because:
options: CH2 groups can never show splitting of any kind
The molecule must contain a triple bond nearby
The two hydrogens of that CH2 are diastereotopic, have slightly different chemical shifts, and can couple to each other as well as to other neighboring protons
This pattern only happens in aromatic rings
h-nmr.why: When the two CH2 protons are diastereotopic due to a nearby stereocenter, they are no longer chemically equivalent, so each can have its own shift and couple to the other proton on the same carbon as well as to outside neighbors, producing a more complex multiplet.

h-nmr.q: The simple n+1 rule for predicting splitting patterns assumes that a proton couples equally (with the same coupling constant) to all of its neighboring protons; when neighboring protons have noticeably different coupling constants, more complex multiplets than the simple n+1 prediction can result.
h-nmr.why: The n+1 rule is a simplification that works cleanly only when all relevant coupling constants are similar; unequal coupling constants to different sets of neighbors produce more complex patterns that must be analyzed as separate couplings rather than a single n+1 multiplet.

h-nmr.q: Rank the following methyl groups from most upfield to most downfield based on typical ¹H NMR chemical shift: CH3 attached to a plain alkyl carbon, CH3 attached to a carbonyl (as in a methyl ketone), CH3 attached directly to an aromatic ring, CH3 attached to an oxygen (as in a methyl ether).
options: Alkyl CH3, then aromatic CH3, then carbonyl CH3, then O-CH3
O-CH3, then carbonyl CH3, then aromatic CH3, then alkyl CH3
Aromatic CH3, then alkyl CH3, then O-CH3, then carbonyl CH3
Alkyl CH3, then carbonyl CH3, then aromatic CH3, then O-CH3
h-nmr.why: Plain alkyl CH3 is least deshielded (around 0.9 ppm); a carbonyl-adjacent CH3 is pulled somewhat downfield (around 2.1 ppm) by the electron-withdrawing carbonyl; an aromatic-ring CH3 is shifted further by ring anisotropy (around 2.3 ppm); and an O-CH3 is most deshielded (around 3.3-3.8 ppm) by the directly attached electronegative oxygen.

h-nmr.q: Why do long-range couplings across four or more bonds usually fail to produce visible splitting in a routine ¹H NMR spectrum of a simple flexible molecule?
options: Coupling constants generally fall off rapidly with increasing number of bonds, becoming too small to resolve beyond about three bonds in most saturated systems
Long-range coupling is physically impossible under any circumstances
Only aromatic rings are capable of long-range coupling
Splitting always increases without limit as more bonds are added
h-nmr.why: Coupling is transmitted through bonding electrons, and its magnitude typically shrinks quickly as the number of intervening bonds grows, so beyond three bonds the coupling constant in a flexible, saturated system is usually too small to resolve as visible splitting.

h-nmr.q: An ethanol sample's O-H proton integrates to 1H in theory, but the measured integration can vary noticeably between samples and conditions. The most likely explanation is:
options: The molecular formula of ethanol changes between samples
Rapid exchange of the O-H proton with trace water or other exchangeable protons in the sample can alter its apparent integration and shift
O-H protons never integrate correctly under any circumstances
Ethanol does not actually contain an O-H proton
h-nmr.why: Because O-H protons exchange rapidly with any available exchangeable protons (like trace water), the effective population and position of this signal is sensitive to moisture and sample purity, making its integration and shift less reproducible than for non-exchangeable C-H protons.

h-nmr.q: Given that aromatic ring protons are deshielded by the ring's induced magnetic field while a proton located directly above or below the ring plane (if one existed in a rigid system) could actually be shielded, this anisotropic behavior shows that a functional group's effect on chemical shift depends only on:
options: The electronegativity of the group alone, regardless of geometry
The molecular weight of the entire molecule
Both the electronic character of the group and the geometric position of the observed proton relative to that group's induced magnetic field
The number of carbons in the ring alone
h-nmr.why: Anisotropic shielding effects, like those from aromatic rings, alkenes, and alkynes, depend on where a proton sits relative to the induced field lines, which is why the same functional group can deshield some nearby protons while shielding others in a different spatial position.

h-nmr.q: Two protons related by an internal mirror plane of symmetry within an otherwise achiral, conformationally averaged molecule will typically give the same ¹H NMR chemical shift.
h-nmr.why: Protons related by a genuine symmetry operation of the molecule, such as reflection through an internal mirror plane, occupy equivalent environments on a time-averaged basis and therefore resonate at the same chemical shift.

c-nmr.q: ¹³C NMR typically shows each chemically distinct carbon as:
options: A single peak (carbons are rarely coupled to each other at natural abundance)
A large multiplet split by neighboring carbons
The same peak as all other carbons
c-nmr.why: ¹³C is only ~1.1% natural abundance, so two ¹³C atoms are rarely adjacent — carbon-carbon coupling is negligible, giving simple, usually unsplit peaks (with standard decoupling).

c-nmr.q: A carbonyl carbon in ¹³C NMR typically appears:
c-nmr.why: Carbonyl carbons are strongly deshielded by the adjacent electronegative, pi-bonded oxygen, pushing their signal far downfield (160–220 ppm).

c-nmr.q: Why is ¹³C NMR generally less sensitive (requiring more sample/scans) than ¹H NMR?
options: Carbon atoms do not exist in organic molecules
NMR spectrometers cannot detect carbon at all
¹³C is both low in natural abundance (~1.1%) and has a smaller magnetic moment (gyromagnetic ratio) than ¹H
¹³C NMR is actually more sensitive than ¹H NMR
c-nmr.why: Both the rarity of the ¹³C isotope and its inherently weaker NMR signal (lower gyromagnetic ratio) compared to ¹H make ¹³C NMR much less sensitive, requiring longer acquisition times.

c-nmr.q: In a standard proton-decoupled ¹³C NMR spectrum, each peak generally corresponds to:
options: One hydrogen atom in the molecule
The total number of atoms in the molecule
One chemically distinct carbon environment in the molecule
c-nmr.why: Each unique carbon environment gives rise to its own peak, regardless of how many hydrogens are attached to that carbon, which is different from how ¹H NMR integration works.

c-nmr.q: A ketone or aldehyde carbonyl carbon in ¹³C NMR typically appears in roughly what chemical shift range, making it the most downfield common signal?
c-nmr.why: Carbonyl carbons are strongly deshielded by the attached oxygen and the carbon's bonding, placing their signals well downfield of essentially all other common carbon environments.

c-nmr.q: ¹³C NMR spectra are referenced to tetramethylsilane (TMS), just as ¹H NMR spectra are, with TMS's carbons defined as 0 ppm.
c-nmr.why: TMS is used as the zero-point reference for both ¹H and ¹³C NMR because its carbons (and protons) are highly shielded, inert, and give a single clean reference peak.

c-nmr.q: The typical chemical shift range for ¹³C NMR signals (roughly 0-220 ppm) is much wider than for ¹H NMR (roughly 0-12 ppm). This is best explained by:
options: Carbon nuclei are simply heavier than hydrogen nuclei, which alone explains the wider range
Carbon's chemical shift is more sensitive to hybridization, substituents, and electronic environment, spreading signals over a wider range
¹³C NMR instruments always use a larger magnet
There is no real difference in range between the two techniques
c-nmr.why: Because carbon sits at the center of bonding with more direct exposure to hybridization and substituent effects, its chemical shift is more sensitive to structural differences, spreading ¹³C signals over a much wider ppm range than ¹H signals.

c-nmr.q: In a standard proton-decoupled ¹³C NMR spectrum, peak height or area reliably indicates the number of carbons contributing to that signal, the same way integration works in ¹H NMR.
c-nmr.why: Differences in relaxation times and the nuclear Overhauser effect between different carbons (especially quaternary versus protonated carbons) make simple peak height or area an unreliable guide to the number of carbons in ¹³C NMR, unlike in ¹H NMR.

c-nmr.q: Aromatic ring carbons typically appear in ¹³C NMR in roughly what chemical shift region?
c-nmr.why: The delocalized pi system and partial double-bond character of aromatic carbons deshield them into the roughly 100-150 ppm region, distinct from both simple alkyl carbons and carbonyl carbons.

c-nmr.q: In a standard proton-decoupled ¹³C NMR spectrum, why do we typically NOT observe splitting of one carbon's signal due to coupling with a neighboring carbon (carbon-carbon coupling)?
options: Carbon atoms are never bonded to each other
Carbon nuclei are incapable of any spin-spin coupling under any circumstances
All carbon-carbon coupling constants happen to be exactly zero
Because ¹³C makes up only about 1.1 percent of natural carbon, any given carbon's neighbor is almost always the NMR-silent ¹²C isotope, so there is essentially no ¹³C neighbor to couple with
c-nmr.why: Because ¹³C is rare (about 1.1 percent natural abundance), the odds that two bonded carbons are both the ¹³C isotope in the same molecule are very low, so carbon-carbon coupling is statistically almost never observed in a routine spectrum.

c-nmr.q: In a standard proton-decoupled ¹³C NMR spectrum, each carbon peak typically appears as a single, unsplit line even though most carbons have one or more attached hydrogens. This is because:
options: Broadband proton decoupling actively removes the carbon-hydrogen coupling during the experiment, simplifying each signal to a singlet
Carbons never actually couple to their attached hydrogens
Hydrogen atoms are invisible to the NMR magnet
The spectrometer only detects carbons with no attached hydrogens
c-nmr.why: A decoupling pulse sequence continuously flips the attached protons' spins during the ¹³C experiment, averaging out C-H coupling so each unique carbon gives one clean singlet instead of a complex multiplet.

c-nmr.q: A ketone's carbonyl carbon (around 205-220 ppm) appears at a higher chemical shift than an ester's carbonyl carbon (around 165-175 ppm). This difference is mainly explained by:
options: Esters contain no carbonyl carbon at all
The ester's alkoxy oxygen donates electron density into the carbonyl by resonance, shielding the carbon relative to a ketone's carbonyl carbon
Ketones always have more carbons overall
The difference is purely due to molecular weight
c-nmr.why: The ester oxygen's lone pair donates into the carbonyl pi system by resonance, increasing electron density at the carbonyl carbon and shielding it relative to a ketone, which lacks that extra donating oxygen.

c-nmr.q: Alkyne carbons typically appear around 65-90 ppm in ¹³C NMR, noticeably more upfield than alkene or aromatic carbons (roughly 100-150 ppm), even though all are unsaturated. The best explanation is:
options: Alkyne carbons have no electronic effects on their chemical shift
Alkynes never appear in ¹³C NMR spectra
The cylindrical symmetry and anisotropy of the triple bond's pi system, along with greater s-character, shields the sp carbons relative to sp2 carbons
Alkyne carbons are always attached to oxygen
c-nmr.why: The linear, cylindrically symmetric pi system of a triple bond interacts with the applied field differently than a planar double bond's pi system, producing an anisotropic effect that shields sp alkyne carbons relative to sp2 alkene or aromatic carbons.

c-nmr.q: Because of its molecular symmetry, how many distinct ¹³C NMR signals would toluene (methylbenzene) show, given that the ring carbons pair up by symmetry?
c-nmr.why: Toluene has a mirror plane that makes the two carbons ortho to the methyl group equivalent to each other, and the two meta carbons equivalent to each other, giving five unique carbons total: the methyl carbon, the ipso carbon, the equivalent ortho pair, the equivalent meta pair, and the para carbon.

c-nmr.q: In a DEPT experiment, quaternary carbons (carbons with no attached hydrogens) are distinguished from CH, CH2, and CH3 carbons because:
options: Quaternary carbons disappear entirely from the DEPT spectrum since DEPT relies on the presence of attached hydrogens to generate its signal
Quaternary carbons always appear as the tallest peaks in DEPT
DEPT can only detect quaternary carbons and nothing else
Quaternary carbons are shown in a completely different color on the spectrum
c-nmr.why: DEPT transfers polarization from attached protons to the carbon nucleus, so a carbon with no attached hydrogens has nothing to receive that transfer from and simply does not show up in the DEPT spectrum.

c-nmr.q: Quaternary carbons typically show weaker peak intensities in a standard proton-decoupled ¹³C NMR spectrum compared to protonated carbons of similar abundance.
c-nmr.why: Quaternary carbons lack the nuclear Overhauser enhancement from directly attached protons and often relax more slowly, both of which tend to make their signals weaker relative to protonated carbons, even at equal molar amounts.

c-nmr.q: Between a simple aldehyde's carbonyl carbon and a simple ketone's carbonyl carbon, which is generally found further downfield in ¹³C NMR?
options: The aldehyde carbonyl carbon is always further downfield
The ketone carbonyl carbon is generally further downfield than the aldehyde carbonyl carbon
They are always identical in shift
Aldehydes have no carbonyl carbon at all
c-nmr.why: Ketone carbonyl carbons typically fall around 205-220 ppm, while aldehyde carbonyl carbons are usually a bit more shielded, around 190-205 ppm, due to differences in the groups attached to the carbonyl carbon.

c-nmr.q: An sp3 carbon directly attached to a hydroxyl oxygen (as in an alcohol) typically appears around 50-90 ppm in ¹³C NMR, well downfield of a typical alkane carbon (0-40 ppm). This shift is mainly due to:
options: Alcohols having no carbon atoms bonded to oxygen
Oxygen always shielding nearby carbons rather than deshielding them
The electronegative oxygen withdrawing electron density from the attached carbon, deshielding it
This shift only happens in aromatic alcohols
c-nmr.why: Oxygen's electronegativity pulls electron density away from the carbon it is bonded to, deshielding that carbon and shifting its signal downfield relative to an ordinary alkane carbon.

c-nmr.q: Two carbons related by an internal mirror plane of symmetry in an achiral molecule will typically give the same ¹³C NMR chemical shift.
c-nmr.why: Just as with ¹H NMR, carbons related by a genuine symmetry operation of the molecule occupy chemically equivalent environments and therefore resonate at the same shift.

c-nmr.q: A carboxylic acid's carbonyl carbon (roughly 170-185 ppm) and an ester's carbonyl carbon (roughly 165-175 ppm) can sometimes be distinguished mainly by:
options: Carboxylic acids never show a carbonyl carbon signal
Esters always appear further downfield than carboxylic acids
There is no possible way to distinguish the two by any NMR method
Their somewhat different, overlapping chemical shift ranges combined with the presence or absence of an O-H signature elsewhere in the spectrum
c-nmr.why: The shift ranges for these two carbonyl types overlap somewhat, so chemists often combine the ¹³C shift with other evidence, such as the presence of a broad O-H absorption in IR or an O-H proton in ¹H NMR, to tell them apart confidently.

c-nmr.q: A nitrile carbon (C of a C≡N group) typically appears around 115-120 ppm in ¹³C NMR, a range that is useful diagnostically mainly because:
options: It falls in a relatively open region, distinct from typical aromatic or alkene carbons, helping identify the nitrile group
Nitrile carbons are never detectable by ¹³C NMR
This range is identical to a typical aldehyde carbonyl carbon
Nitrile carbons always overlap exactly with TMS
c-nmr.why: Although close to the aromatic/alkene region, a nitrile carbon's shift around 115-120 ppm, especially combined with a sharp triple-bond stretch in IR, helps distinguish it from other unsaturated carbons.

c-nmr.q: A para-disubstituted benzene ring with two different substituents, which breaks the ring's six-fold symmetry down to a single mirror plane, would be expected to show how many distinct aromatic ¹³C signals?
c-nmr.why: The mirror plane running through the two substituted carbons makes the two carbons next to one substituent equivalent to each other, and the two carbons next to the other substituent equivalent to each other, giving four unique aromatic carbons: the two substituted carbons plus the two equivalent pairs.

c-nmr.q: Why do we not typically observe carbon-carbon (¹³C-¹³C) spin coupling in a routine ¹³C NMR spectrum, even though carbons are directly bonded to each other throughout the molecule?
options: Carbon-carbon bonds are incapable of transmitting any spin coupling
All carbon-carbon coupling constants are zero by definition

The low natural abundance of ¹³C (about 1.1 percent) makes it statistically very unlikely that two bonded carbons in the same molecule are both the ¹³C isotope, so there is almost never an NMR-active neighbor to couple with
The decoupler used for proton decoupling also removes all carbon-carbon coupling
c-nmr.why: Since roughly 99 percent of carbon atoms are the spin-inactive ¹²C isotope, the probability that a given ¹³C nucleus happens to be bonded to another ¹³C nucleus is small, so carbon-carbon coupling is rarely visible above the noise in a normal spectrum.

c-nmr.q: A molecule can sometimes show a different total number of distinct ¹H NMR signals than distinct ¹³C NMR signals for the same structure. What is one reasonable explanation for this?
options: The two techniques must always give exactly the same number of signals for any molecule
¹³C NMR always shows more signals than ¹H NMR for every molecule
¹H NMR cannot show more than one signal per molecule

Two or more structurally distinct carbons can happen to have very similar or coincidentally overlapping shifts in one technique but not the other, or symmetry can equate protons without equating the carbons bearing them, or vice versa
c-nmr.why: Because chemical shift differences and coincidental overlaps differ between ¹H and ¹³C environments, and because symmetry can relate protons without necessarily relating the carbons carrying them (or vice versa), the number of resolved signals does not have to match between the two spectra.

c-nmr.q: In a DEPT-135 experiment, CH and CH3 carbons appear as positive peaks, CH2 carbons appear as negative (inverted) peaks, and quaternary carbons are absent altogether. This pattern is useful mainly because it allows chemists to:
options: Distinguish the number of attached hydrogens on each carbon without needing the unreliable integration of a standard ¹³C spectrum
Directly count the total number of hydrogens in the molecule
Measure the exact bond angles in the molecule
c-nmr.why: Because DEPT signal phase and intensity depend on the number of attached protons, comparing a DEPT-135 spectrum to the standard ¹³C spectrum lets chemists sort carbons into CH3/CH, CH2, and quaternary categories, something ordinary ¹³C peak height cannot reliably do.

c-nmr.q: ¹³C NMR chemical shifts generally follow the same electronegativity-based deshielding trends seen in ¹H NMR, where attaching a more electronegative atom shifts the signal downfield, though the magnitude of the shift differs between the two techniques.
c-nmr.why: Both techniques respond to the same underlying electron-withdrawing inductive and resonance effects, so electronegative substituents deshield nearby carbons in ¹³C NMR in a way that parallels ¹H NMR trends, even though the absolute ppm shifts differ in scale.

c-nmr.q: Neopentane, (CH3)4C, has five carbon atoms but shows only two signals in ¹³C NMR. This is best explained by:
options: Neopentane actually contains only two carbon atoms
The molecule's high symmetry makes all four methyl carbons chemically equivalent to each other, distinct only from the single central quaternary carbon
¹³C NMR cannot detect quaternary carbons under any circumstances
The four methyl groups are not actually bonded to the central carbon
c-nmr.why: The four methyl groups are related by the molecule's high symmetry (effectively a tetrahedral arrangement around the central carbon), making them all chemically equivalent and giving just one methyl signal plus one signal for the unique central quaternary carbon.

c-nmr.q: Obtaining a good ¹³C NMR spectrum often requires longer acquisition times or more scans rather than simply increasing sample concentration, partly because:
options: ¹³C nuclei are immune to any relaxation effects
Increasing concentration always fully compensates for ¹³C's low natural abundance with no need for extra scans
Many carbons, especially quaternary ones, have relatively long relaxation times, so sufficient signal averaging over many scans is needed to build up an adequate signal-to-noise ratio
Longer scans have no effect on signal-to-noise ratio
c-nmr.why: Slow relaxation, particularly for quaternary carbons lacking nearby protons to help them relax, limits how quickly a ¹³C signal can be repeatedly sampled, so extending the number of scans (not just raising concentration) is often needed to achieve a usable spectrum.

c-nmr.q: Rank the following carbonyl-containing carbons from LOWEST to HIGHEST typical ¹³C chemical shift: amide carbonyl, ester carbonyl, ketone carbonyl.
c-nmr.why: The amide nitrogen donates electron density into the carbonyl most effectively by resonance, shielding its carbon the most, followed by the ester oxygen's somewhat weaker donation, while the ketone, lacking this extra heteroatom donation, appears furthest downfield.

c-nmr.q: In ¹³C NMR, a carbon's chemical shift is strongly affected by nearby electronegative atoms even two or three bonds away, similar to the pattern seen in ¹H NMR, though the size of the effect attenuates with distance in both techniques.
c-nmr.why: Inductive electron withdrawal from an electronegative atom propagates through several bonds in both ¹H and ¹³C NMR, deshielding nearby nuclei, with the effect weakening as the number of intervening bonds increases.

mass-spec.q: In mass spectrometry, the molecular ion peak (M+) corresponds to:
options: The intact molecule after losing one electron
mass-spec.why: The molecular ion forms when the neutral molecule loses an electron in the ionization source, giving a radical cation at the molecule’s full mass.

mass-spec.q: A mass spec fragmentation pattern showing loss of 15 mass units from the molecular ion is most consistent with loss of:
mass-spec.why: A mass loss of 15 corresponds to CH₃ (methyl, 12+3=15), a very common fragmentation for molecules with a methyl group attached to a stabilizing center.

mass-spec.q: In mass spectrometry, the "base peak" refers to:
options: The peak at the lowest mass
The tallest (most intense) peak in the spectrum, set to 100% relative abundance
mass-spec.why: The base peak is defined as the most intense peak in the spectrum (100% relative abundance) — it is often, but not always, the same as the molecular ion peak.

mass-spec.q: In mass spectrometry, the term m/z refers to:
options: The total mass of the neutral, un-ionized sample
The melting point of the sample
The number of fragments produced per second
The mass-to-charge ratio of an ion detected by the instrument
mass-spec.why: Mass spectrometers separate and detect ions based on their mass-to-charge ratio, m/z, which for most singly charged ions in an intro course is essentially equal to the ion's mass.

mass-spec.q: In electron ionization (EI) mass spectrometry, the molecular ion is typically formed by:
options: Removing a single electron from the neutral molecule, producing a radical cation
Adding a proton to the neutral molecule
Removing an entire atom from the molecule
Adding an electron to the neutral molecule
mass-spec.why: A high-energy electron beam knocks one electron out of the neutral molecule, leaving behind an odd-electron, positively charged species called the molecular ion or radical cation.

mass-spec.q: The molecular ion peak (M+) always corresponds to the most intense peak in the entire mass spectrum.
mass-spec.why: The most intense peak is called the base peak, and it is very often a fragment ion rather than the molecular ion, especially for molecules that fragment easily; M+ itself can be weak or even absent for some compounds.

mass-spec.q: The relative height of the M+1 isotope peak compared to M+ in a mass spectrum is mainly useful for estimating:
options: The number of nitrogen atoms in the molecule
The approximate number of carbon atoms in the molecule, based on the natural abundance of ¹³C
The boiling point of the compound
The number of oxygen atoms in the molecule
mass-spec.why: Since about 1.1 percent of carbon atoms are naturally ¹³C, the M+1 peak's relative intensity grows roughly in proportion to the number of carbons present, giving a rough estimate of carbon count.

mass-spec.q: A compound containing a single chlorine atom typically shows an M+2 peak with what approximate relative intensity compared to M+?
options: About 10 times the intensity of M+
mass-spec.why: Chlorine's two natural isotopes, 35Cl and 37Cl, occur in roughly a 3:1 ratio, so a single-chlorine compound's M+2 peak (containing 37Cl) appears at roughly one-third the height of the M+ peak (containing 35Cl).

mass-spec.q: A compound containing a single bromine atom typically shows M+ and M+2 peaks of roughly what relative intensity to each other?
options: M+2 is about ten times more intense than M+
Roughly equal intensity, close to a 1:1 ratio
mass-spec.why: Bromine's two natural isotopes, 79Br and 81Br, occur in nearly equal abundance, so a single-bromine compound shows M+ and M+2 peaks of roughly similar height, a distinctive pattern compared to chlorine.

mass-spec.q: Loss of a methyl radical, corresponding to a mass loss of 15 units, from the molecular ion is a common fragmentation for branched alkyl compounds.
mass-spec.why: Cleaving off a methyl group is a frequent and often favorable fragmentation pathway, especially when it generates a more stable remaining cation, which is common in branched structures.

mass-spec.q: A mass spectral fragment showing a loss of 18 mass units from the molecular ion most commonly indicates loss of:
options: A water molecule, common for alcohols
mass-spec.why: Loss of 18 mass units corresponds to H2O, a very common fragmentation pathway for alcohols (and some other oxygen-containing compounds) under electron ionization conditions.

mass-spec.q: The nitrogen rule states that, for typical organic compounds containing only carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, and similar common elements, the molecular weight will be odd if the molecule contains an odd number of nitrogen atoms.
mass-spec.why: Because nitrogen has an odd valence (typically three bonds) while carbon, oxygen, and hydrogen follow patterns that keep the overall mass even in their absence, each nitrogen atom added in a stable structure shifts the molecular weight's parity, making an odd number of nitrogens correspond to an odd molecular weight.

mass-spec.q: A loss of 28 mass units from a molecular ion is ambiguous on its own because it could correspond to either:
options: Loss of water or loss of ammonia
Loss of carbon monoxide (CO) or loss of ethylene (C2H4)
Loss of chlorine or loss of bromine
Loss of a proton or loss of a methyl group
mass-spec.why: Both CO (common from ketones, aldehydes, and aromatic ethers) and C2H4 (common from retro-type eliminations) have a mass of 28, so this loss alone does not uniquely identify the fragmentation pathway without additional supporting evidence.

mass-spec.q: Alpha cleavage, the preferential breaking of a bond adjacent to a heteroatom such as nitrogen or oxygen, is a favorable fragmentation pathway mainly because:
options: Alpha cleavage never actually occurs in real spectra
Breaking bonds near heteroatoms requires less energy than breaking any other bond in the molecule under all circumstances
The resulting cation can be stabilized by resonance donation from the heteroatom's lone pair
Heteroatoms always prevent any fragmentation nearby
mass-spec.why: When the bond next to an oxygen or nitrogen breaks, the heteroatom's lone pair can donate into the resulting cation through resonance, stabilizing it and making that fragmentation pathway especially favorable.

mass-spec.q: A McLafferty rearrangement in a carbonyl-containing compound requires the presence of what structural feature, and produces what kind of products?
options: Any aromatic ring, producing two radical fragments
A triple bond anywhere in the molecule, producing a gas
A halogen atom, producing an odd-electron radical cation only
A hydrogen on the carbon three atoms away from the carbonyl (a gamma-hydrogen), producing an even-electron ion plus a neutral alkene fragment
mass-spec.why: The McLafferty rearrangement requires a gamma-hydrogen relative to the carbonyl so that a six-membered transition state can form, transferring that hydrogen and cleaving a bond to release a neutral alkene while leaving behind a stable, even-electron cation.

mass-spec.q: The characteristic tropylium cation at m/z 91 is commonly observed in the mass spectra of which class of compounds?
options: Alkylbenzenes, such as toluene and its derivatives
Primary amines with no ring present
mass-spec.why: Benzylic cleavage of an alkylbenzene's side chain generates a benzylic cation that readily rearranges into the highly stable, resonance-delocalized seven-membered tropylium cation, observed at m/z 91.

mass-spec.q: More highly branched alkanes generally show a weaker molecular ion peak than their straight-chain isomers, because branching provides additional, more easily accessible fragmentation pathways that generate more stable carbocations.
mass-spec.why: Branch points allow formation of more stable secondary or tertiary carbocations upon fragmentation, making it energetically easier for the branched molecular ion to fall apart rather than survive intact, weakening the M+ peak relative to a straight-chain isomer.

mass-spec.q: A loss of 43 mass units from a molecular ion commonly corresponds to loss of which fragment(s)?
options: An isopropyl group (C3H7) or an acetyl group (CH3CO), both common losses of mass 43
mass-spec.why: Both the isopropyl radical (C3H7, mass 43) and the acetyl cation-forming group (CH3CO, also mass 43) are common fragments lost from molecular ions, so a loss of 43 alone is often ambiguous without further context.

mass-spec.q: In the mass spectrum of a simple aldehyde, a loss of 29 mass units from the molecular ion most commonly corresponds to loss of:
mass-spec.why: Alpha cleavage adjacent to the aldehyde carbonyl commonly ejects the formyl radical, CHO, which has a mass of 29, leaving behind a stabilized carbon-centered cation.

mass-spec.q: Aromatic compounds often show a strong, easily recognized molecular ion peak relative to many aliphatic compounds mainly because:
options: Aromatic compounds never undergo any fragmentation at all
Aromatic rings always weigh less than aliphatic chains
Aromatic compounds cannot be ionized by electron ionization
The aromatic ring's delocalized electron system stabilizes the radical cation, making the intact molecular ion more resistant to fragmentation
mass-spec.why: The aromatic ring can delocalize the positive charge and radical character of the molecular ion over the ring system, stabilizing it and making the intact M+ more likely to survive and be detected as a prominent peak.

mass-spec.q: In a standard mass spectrum plot, the x-axis (m/z) represents a peak's relative abundance, while the y-axis (intensity) represents its mass-to-charge ratio.
mass-spec.why: It is actually the reverse: the x-axis shows the mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) of each ion, while the y-axis shows that ion's relative intensity, or abundance, compared to the base peak.

mass-spec.q: When an alkane's molecular ion fragments by breaking a carbon-carbon bond, the fragmentation pathway that generates the most stable resulting carbocation (tertiary over secondary over primary) is generally favored. This principle is analogous to:
options: The general stability order of carbocations seen elsewhere in organic chemistry, where more substituted cations are more stable
A rule that applies only in mass spectrometry and nowhere else in organic chemistry
The idea that all carbocations are equally stable regardless of substitution
A rule that favors primary carbocations above all others
mass-spec.why: Fragmentation in the gas phase favors pathways that produce the most stable cation, following the same substitution-based stability trend (tertiary greater than secondary greater than primary) used to rationalize carbocation stability throughout organic chemistry.

mass-spec.q: An unknown compound's mass spectrum shows significant fragment peaks corresponding to loss of 15 (a methyl group) and loss of 29 (an ethyl-related fragment) from the molecular ion, both consistent with alpha cleavage next to a carbonyl. This pattern is most consistent with a ketone structure in which:
options: The molecule contains no carbonyl group at all
The carbonyl carbon is flanked on one side by a methyl group and on the other by an ethyl group, such as in 2-butanone (methyl ethyl ketone)
The molecule must be a symmetrical ketone with identical groups on both sides of the carbonyl
The molecule is necessarily an aromatic compound
mass-spec.why: Alpha cleavage on either side of an asymmetric ketone's carbonyl generates two different acylium-type cations, explaining why both a methyl loss (15) and a loss consistent with the other alkyl substituent pattern can appear together in the spectrum of a compound like methyl ethyl ketone.

mass-spec.q: Loss of a single hydrogen atom, a mass loss of just 1 unit, from the molecular ion is relatively uncommon as a dominant fragmentation pathway compared to loss of larger groups. Why?
options: Hydrogen atoms cannot be removed from a molecule under any circumstances
Molecular ions never lose hydrogen atoms in any real spectrum
Losing a lone hydrogen atom as a radical is generally less energetically favorable than losing a larger, more stabilized radical or undergoing a rearrangement that releases a stable neutral fragment
Losing a hydrogen atom always produces the most intense peak in every spectrum
mass-spec.why: Because forming larger, more stable radicals (or undergoing favorable rearrangements like McLafferty) is usually more thermodynamically favorable than simply ejecting a lone hydrogen atom, simple H-loss is typically a minor pathway rather than the dominant one.

mass-spec.q: A high-resolution mass spectrometer can distinguish between two different molecular formulas that share the same nominal (whole-number) mass, such as C2H4O and CO2, both of which equal 44 to the nearest whole number. This is possible because:
options: All atoms have exactly the same mass, so this distinction is actually impossible
High-resolution instruments simply guess the formula from the compound's color
Nominal mass and exact mass are always identical for every molecule
Different combinations of atoms have slightly different exact masses due to the small mass differences among protons, neutrons, and binding energy, even when their nominal masses are the same
mass-spec.why: Individual isotopes have exact masses that are not perfectly whole numbers (for example, carbon-12 is defined as exactly 12, but hydrogen and oxygen have slightly different fractional exact masses), so formulas with the same nominal mass usually have distinguishably different exact masses when measured with sufficient precision.

mass-spec.q: The relative intensity of a peak in a mass spectrum reflects the relative abundance of that particular gas-phase ion reaching the detector, which is governed by the kinetics and thermodynamics of fragmentation in the gas phase, not by the compound's stability or solubility in a liquid solution.
mass-spec.why: Mass spectral peak intensities depend on how readily a given ion forms and survives under gas-phase ionization and fragmentation conditions, a distinct context from solution-phase stability, solubility, or reactivity, which are not what mass spectrometry intensities measure.

mass-spec.q: A cyclic secondary alcohol's mass spectrum can show both a loss of 18 (water) and a loss of 28 (often consistent with ethylene or CO) from the molecular ion. A reasonable explanation for seeing multiple distinct losses like this is:
options: The molecular ion can fragment through more than one competing pathway, such as simple dehydration alongside a ring-opening or retro-type elimination, each producing a different characteristic mass loss
A molecule can only ever show exactly one fragmentation pathway in its entire spectrum
Loss of water and loss of ethylene must always occur together as a single simultaneous event
Cyclic alcohols never lose water under any circumstances
mass-spec.why: Molecular ions are not limited to a single fragmentation route; different bonds can break under the conditions of electron ionization, so a cyclic alcohol can plausibly show both a straightforward water loss and a separate ring-related elimination pathway in the same spectrum.

mass-spec.q: For a simple carboxylic acid, a loss of 45 mass units from the molecular ion typically corresponds to loss of:
mass-spec.why: Alpha cleavage adjacent to the carbonyl-bearing carbon of a carboxylic acid commonly ejects the COOH group, which has a combined mass of 45, leaving behind the remaining alkyl cation.

mass-spec.q: Why does electron ionization (EI) typically produce a radical cation (an odd-electron species) as the molecular ion, rather than an even-electron cation?
options: EI always adds an extra electron to the molecule instead of removing one
Even-electron cations are impossible to form under any ionization method
EI removes exactly one electron from the neutral, even-electron molecule, necessarily leaving one unpaired electron behind along with the positive charge
EI removes two electrons at once from every molecule
mass-spec.why: Since a neutral organic molecule normally has all its electrons paired, knocking out just one electron during EI necessarily leaves an odd, unpaired electron along with the resulting positive charge, producing a radical cation.

mass-spec.q: Combining the nitrogen rule with an observed odd molecular ion mass for a compound containing only carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen, what can be concluded about its nitrogen content?
options: The compound must contain an even number of nitrogen atoms
The compound cannot contain any nitrogen at all
No conclusion about nitrogen content can be drawn from the molecular ion mass
The compound must contain an odd number of nitrogen atoms
mass-spec.why: According to the nitrogen rule, an odd molecular weight for a typical CHNO compound implies an odd number of nitrogen atoms, since each nitrogen (with its odd valence pattern) shifts the overall parity of the molecular mass.
